query: What changes are reshaping the Industrial manufacturing industry, and what should companies focus on to support digital and green transformation?
final_answer: Industrial manufacturing is being reshaped by digital transformation, especially through digital economy innovations, Industry 4.0, cloud computing, IoT, big data, AI, and related digital technologies that are changing production methods, management models, and innovation capability [https://openalex.org/W4403107862||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4319599463||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4313238684||ABSTRACT||000]. Across the papers, digitalization is repeatedly linked to sustainability outcomes, including greener technology systems, sustainable performance, and stronger corporate sustainability, but it is also clear that digitalization does not automatically produce sustainability benefits [https://openalex.org/W4403107862||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4360777148||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4302303968||ABSTRACT||000]. A common recommendation is to integrate digitalization with green technologies inside business processes, products, and models rather than treating them separately [https://openalex.org/W3182760100||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4313238684||ABSTRACT||001]. Companies should also focus on the practical enablers of transformation, including digital infrastructure, access to modern manufacturing technologies, and coordinated use of multiple digital transformation types such as service, model, organization, and process digitalization [https://openalex.org/W4360777148||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3164306258||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4313238684||ABSTRACT||001]. Several summaries emphasize that digital transformation can improve efficiency, supply-chain coordination, demand prediction, energy conservation, and environmental conservation, while also lowering costs and increasing productivity and innovation [https://openalex.org/W4319599463||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4309609041||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, firms face barriers such as integration challenges, economic and regulatory constraints, talent barriers, management costs, and uneven access to infrastructure [https://openalex.org/W4403107862||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4309609041||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3164306258||ABSTRACT||001]. The evidence also suggests that transformation strategies should be sensitive to regional differences, because the digital economy’s effect on industrial green transformation varies across places and over time [https://openalex.org/W4387972406||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, companies are advised to strengthen green-tech innovation and environmental awareness, build the right infrastructure, and pursue collaborative, policy-supported digital-green integration to make transformation effective [https://openalex.org/W4387972406||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4403107862||ABSTRACT||001].

query: What does the ClinicalTrials.gov record say about the DECISION phase III study design, treatment schedule, endpoints, and trial registration identifier?
final_answer: The supplied evidence about the DECISION phase III study comes from one paper that explicitly describes it as a multicenter, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled phase III trial in patients with locally advanced/metastatic RAI-refractory differentiated thyroid cancer (DTC) [pmc_PMC3164634||ABSTRACT||001]. The treatment was continued until radiographically documented disease progression, unacceptable toxicity, noncompliance, or withdrawal of consent, and efficacy assessments were performed every 56 days (2 cycles) while safety was assessed every 28 days (1 cycle) for the first 8 months and every 56 days thereafter [pmc_PMC3164634||ABSTRACT||001]. The same source reports that after progression, patients could continue or start sorafenib depending on original assignment, at investigator discretion [pmc_PMC3164634||ABSTRACT||001]. Its primary endpoint was progression-free survival (PFS), and secondary endpoints included overall survival, time to disease progression, disease control rate, response rate, duration of response, safety, and pharmacokinetic analysis [pmc_PMC3164634||ABSTRACT||001]. The ClinicalTrials.gov registration identifier given for this DECISION study is NCT00984282 [pmc_PMC3164634||ABSTRACT||001]. Other provided summaries mention different trial registration numbers and do not supply additional DECISION ClinicalTrials.gov design or endpoint details, so the available answer is limited to this one source [pmc_PMC10387733||ABSTRACT||001][pmc_PMC5387979||ABSTRACT||002][pmc_PMC9806070||ABSTRACT||002][pmc_PMC9806046||ABSTRACT||001][pmc_PMC9806091||ABSTRACT||001][pmc_PMC9806002||ABSTRACT||001].

query: Why nano-enhancers better for workpiece burn?
final_answer: The supplied evidence suggests that nano-enhancers are considered better for workpiece burn mainly because they improve cooling and lubrication during machining, which helps reduce burn at the workpiece surface [https://openalex.org/W4313508734||ABSTRACT||001]. In titanium alloy grinding, the paper specifically says nano-enhancers are recommended because their high thermal conductivity helps solve the “burn puzzle” by improving cooling performance compared with traditional cutting fluids [https://openalex.org/W4313508734||ABSTRACT||001]. The same paper also notes that nano-enhancers with high hardness and spherical characteristics are better choices, implying that these properties further help address surface burn issues [https://openalex.org/W4313508734||ABSTRACT||001]. A related review adds that nano-enhanced biolubricants benefit MQL machining through advanced lubrication and heat-transfer mechanisms, as well as distinctive film formation, atomization, and infiltration behaviors that improve workpiece performance [https://openalex.org/W4206313494||ABSTRACT||000]. Across these sources, the common explanation is that nano-enhancers outperform conventional fluids because they can manage heat and friction more effectively while forming more functional lubricant films [https://openalex.org/W4313508734||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4206313494||ABSTRACT||000]. However, several provided summaries do not actually discuss workpiece burn or nano-enhancers, so the evidence base is limited and not fully direct for every context [https://openalex.org/W4207036872||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4322505914||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4324057306||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How do carbon dots compare with inorganic quantum dots as optical nanomaterials, and what sustainability issues are highlighted in the review?
final_answer: Across these reviews, carbon dots/carbon quantum dots are consistently portrayed as promising optical nanomaterials with attractive properties such as tunable fluorescence or luminescence, biocompatibility, low toxicity, and applications in bioimaging, sensing, optoelectronics, photocatalysis, and environmental monitoring [https://openalex.org/W4403909528||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W4406866034||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W4378391047||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W4313550231||ABSTRACT||000]. Several papers explicitly frame them as a functional and sustainable alternative to incumbent optical nanomaterials, especially inorganic quantum dots, noting advantages such as biomass-based synthesis and freedom from toxic or precious metals and critical raw materials [https://openalex.org/W4400778971||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W4401798421||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, the reviews do not provide a detailed side-by-side optical performance comparison with inorganic quantum dots; instead, they mainly position carbon dots as replacement candidates based on sustainability, cost, and biocompatibility rather than direct quantitative benchmarking [https://openalex.org/W4318483232||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W4401798421||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W4378391047||ABSTRACT||000]. Sustainability concerns recur throughout the literature and include the environmental burden of synthesis solvents, energy use, material inefficiency, safety, and waste management, with some methods described as wasteful because they rely on non-sustainable solvents and energy [https://openalex.org/W4400778971||ABSTRACT||000]. In response, the reviews emphasize green chemistry, Safe and Sustainable by Design approaches, standardization, improved purification, and renewable or waste-derived precursors such as biomass, food waste, plastics, and other natural sources [https://openalex.org/W4403909528||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W4406866034||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W4378391047||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W4313550231||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W4387573993||ABSTRACT||000]. Several reviews also identify practical limitations that constrain wider adoption, including low quantum yield, reproducibility problems, heterogeneity, scalability challenges, and the need for more precise control over properties [https://openalex.org/W4403909528||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W4401798421||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the evidence supports carbon dots as a greener, lower-toxicity class of optical nanomaterials with broad application potential, while also showing that sustainability is not automatic and depends on cleaner synthesis, better efficiency, and more transparent reporting of inputs and outputs [https://openalex.org/W4400778971||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W4403909528||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How FT's do they add their own personal interpretation to sustainability requirements when they fulfill their boundary-spanning role?
final_answer: Across the papers, the strongest direct evidence indicates that FTs do add their own interpretation when performing boundary-spanning work on sustainability requirements, rather than applying rules mechanically [https://openalex.org/W3205987731||ABSTRACT||001][https://openalex.org/W4410729659||ABSTRACT||001]. One study explicitly says FTs add personal interpretation and that their boundary-spanning actions can be compliance-oriented or improvement-oriented, showing that interpretation can change both the meaning and the direction of the action taken [https://openalex.org/W3205987731||ABSTRACT||001]. A related paper on sustainability standard-setting describes the arena as highly contested and says actors negotiate interoperability, materiality, and connectivity, implying that interpretation is strategic and shaped by competing priorities [https://openalex.org/W4410729659||ABSTRACT||001]. Another paper on sustainability reporting regulation similarly finds that harmonization is still far from achieved because actors have diverse objectives and cannot renounce their particular perspectives, which supports the idea that boundary-spanning actors bring their own perspectives to requirements [https://openalex.org/W4225388860||ABSTRACT||001]. The broader literature also aligns with this pattern by showing that sustainability materiality is ambiguous and contested, and that professionals’ subjective understandings and contextual circumstances shape how sustainability is operationalized [https://openalex.org/W4289767614||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4313908265||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, some papers only address sustainability models or reporting frameworks at a general level and do not directly study FT behavior, so they support interpretation as a general phenomenon rather than providing direct evidence about FTs specifically [https://openalex.org/W3157489939||ABSTRACT||001][https://openalex.org/W4382811259||ABSTRACT||001][https://openalex.org/W4313644972||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the synthesis suggests that FT boundary-spanning is not neutral rule transmission but a socially and contextually influenced interpretive role, with evidence pointing to both compliance and improvement orientations and to negotiation of contested sustainability meanings [https://openalex.org/W3205987731||ABSTRACT||001][https://openalex.org/W4410729659||ABSTRACT||001][https://openalex.org/W4313908265||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How mask mandates help Covid-19 cases, and what did the study find?
final_answer: Across the supplied studies, the strongest direct evidence on mask mandates and COVID-19 case counts comes from a U.S. state-level analysis that estimated mask mandates and compliance while controlling for mobility [pmc_PMC9663388||ABSTRACT||000]. That study found that higher mobility increased case growth, and that a mask mandate could offset about one third of that mobility-related increase in the most conservative estimates [pmc_PMC9663388||ABSTRACT||000]. It also reported that mask mandates were more effective in states with higher compliance, and that a national mask mandate on May 15, 2020 could have reduced total U.S. infections by 23.7% to 30.4% by November 15, 2020 [pmc_PMC9663388||ABSTRACT||000]. A separate study found that longer-lasting COVID-19 prevention measures, including face mask mandates, were associated with lower incidence than having the policy in place for less than one month, with the largest reductions seen in socially vulnerable communities [pmc_PMC9729715||ABSTRACT||001]. This same study reported that for face mask mandates, the difference in marginal mean monthly incidence ranged from -4 cases per 100,000 in low-SVI counties to -401 cases per 100,000 in high-SVI counties [pmc_PMC9729715||ABSTRACT||001]. Other papers in the set support the general protective role of masks, but they focus on PPE rather than mandates: a rapid review found face masks significantly protected healthcare workers from infection and concluded that PPE, especially N95 masks, reduces risk [pmc_PMC9190185||ABSTRACT||000][pmc_PMC9190185||ABSTRACT||001], and another study concluded that surgical masks provided better protection than cloth masks among healthcare workers [pmc_PMC9845060||ABSTRACT||001]. One broader non-pharmaceutical-interventions paper also suggests that measures within a larger containment strategy helped achieve rapid and sustained containment of COVID-19, though it does not specifically isolate mask mandates [https://openalex.org/W3215618709||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the evidence in these summaries suggests mask mandates help reduce COVID-19 cases, especially when compliance is higher and mandates are sustained longer, but the exact estimates come from observational analyses and may vary by setting [pmc_PMC9663388||ABSTRACT||000][pmc_PMC9729715||ABSTRACT||001].

query: What role did hexagonal boron nitride play in the study of canola oil as a bio-lubricant, and what details are provided about its evaluation?
final_answer: Hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) appears in the evidence as a solid nano-additive used in canola oil to improve tribological performance, addressing the fact that canola oil alone was described as weaker than petroleum-based oils [https://openalex.org/W4200600140||ABSTRACT||000]. In that study, hBN was tested in canola oil at 0.5, 1.0, and 1.5 wt.% [https://openalex.org/W4200600140||ABSTRACT||000]. Its evaluation relied on dynamic viscosity measurements and pin-on-disk testing in the boundary lubrication regime, with coefficient of friction and wear as the main outcomes [https://openalex.org/W4200600140||ABSTRACT||000]. The best result for hBN alone was at 1.0 wt.%, which produced the lowest coefficient of friction and was reported as 40% lower than the base oil [https://openalex.org/W4200600140||ABSTRACT||001]. The study also combined hBN with graphene nanoplatelet in mixed formulations, and these blends achieved 56% friction reduction and 90% wear reduction versus base oil [https://openalex.org/W4200600140||ABSTRACT||001]. Across the broader literature, hBN is also discussed as a tribologically functional additive in sustainable biolubricant formulations, but the other supplied papers do not provide canola-oil-specific evaluation details [https://openalex.org/W4390658388||ABSTRACT||000]. More generally, the reviews agree that plant-based or bio-based lubricants are renewable and biodegradable, while also noting that performance is often improved by adding nanomaterials [https://openalex.org/W4401870224||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4390658388||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How does organizational learning capability contribute to radical innovation?
final_answer: The strongest direct evidence suggests that organizational learning capability contributes to radical innovation by acting as an enabling organizational context rather than as a standalone output [https://openalex.org/W3194620278||ABSTRACT||000]. In one study, organizational learning capability fully mediated the relationship between stewardship leader behavior and radical innovation, indicating that leadership influences radical innovation through learning processes [https://openalex.org/W3194620278||ABSTRACT||000]. The same evidence specifies that this capability supports experimentation, dialog, participative decision-making, risk-taking, and interaction with the external environment, all of which are presented as conditions that foster radical innovation [https://openalex.org/W3194620278||ABSTRACT||000]. Related evidence from another paper shows that organizational learning is very vital for sustainable organizational performance and helps make innovation more informed and less disruptive, with organizational networking and information sources moderating the innovation–performance relationship [https://openalex.org/W4378746192||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4378746192||ABSTRACT||001]. Additional studies are consistent with the broader idea that learning-related capabilities support more ambitious organizational change: organizational learning positively influences sustainable value creation and mediates the CSR–value creation relationship, while stakeholder engagement strengthens CSR’s effect on learning [https://openalex.org/W4400127182||ABSTRACT||000]. Likewise, top management team ambidextrous learning is positively associated with adoption of sustainable business model innovations, and this learning is itself strengthened by TMT diversity and university-industry collaboration [https://openalex.org/W4323928282||ABSTRACT||000]. However, several summaries do not address radical innovation directly, so the evidence is strongest for learning as a facilitator of innovation-oriented change and weakest for making broad claims beyond the specific contexts studied [https://openalex.org/W3211385979||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W3119434529||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4320476375||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How is the SDG Index used to measur progres toward the SDGs at local and regional level in Romania, and what did the results show?
final_answer: The clearest evidence indicates that the SDG Index was used in Romania by calculating progress toward the SDGs at both local and regional levels through an integrated approach based on 90 indicators stored and processed in a PostgreSQL object-relational database [https://openalex.org/W3135800278||ABSTRACT||000]. This study’s results showed that the highest sustainable development performance was concentrated in specific geographical areas, while rural areas and extended peripheral regions in eastern and southern Romania were the poorest performers [https://openalex.org/W3135800278||ABSTRACT||000]. A related regional perspective from another paper suggests that SDG monitoring can be used as a strategic tool for benchmarking regions and supporting policymakers, but that it depends on robust regional data infrastructure and adaptable indicators [https://openalex.org/W4399724167||ABSTRACT||001]. Evidence from broader regional and global SDG Index work is consistent with the idea that performance varies markedly across places, with Europe and Central Asia scoring highest and other world regions scoring lower [https://openalex.org/W4396930956||ABSTRACT||001]. However, several papers in the set do not provide Romania-specific local or regional findings, and some summaries explicitly state that the evidence is insufficient to determine Romanian outcomes [https://openalex.org/W4396930956||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4284681716||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4319870717||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the available evidence shows that Romania’s SDG Index application is used as a spatial benchmarking instrument, and it reveals clear territorial disparities rather than even progress across the country [https://openalex.org/W3135800278||ABSTRACT||000].

query: What are biomasses converted into through thermochemical decomposition?
final_answer: Across the provided summaries, biomass is most consistently described as being converted by thermochemical decomposition into energy-related outputs, especially energy, heat, and biofuels [https://openalex.org/W4400734527||ABSTRACT||000]. Several papers broaden this to include fuels and other products, stating that biomass wastes can be converted into energy, fuels, and products through conversion technologies that include thermochemical approaches [https://openalex.org/W4320879845||ABSTRACT||001]. Other summaries similarly report conversion into chemicals, energy vectors, biofuels, platform molecules, and high-value-added products, indicating that thermochemical or related conversion pathways are used in biorefinery and catalytic contexts to generate multiple product classes [https://openalex.org/W4377108088||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4377108088||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W3125494550||ABSTRACT||000]. One paper specifically names combustion and gasification as thermal technologies used to convert biomass [https://openalex.org/W4400734527||ABSTRACT||000]. Another summary notes that biomass can be converted into bioethanol, biodiesel, and other bioenergy products through thermochemical decomposition-related processing of agro-industrial wastes [https://openalex.org/W4281784117||ABSTRACT||001]. However, not all papers specify the decomposition products directly: some only mention electricity and heat, or generic value-added products and energy vectors, without naming the outputs of thermochemical decomposition itself [https://openalex.org/W4320494881||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W3139112995||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4367312219||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the evidence supports a broad answer that biomass is converted into energy carriers, fuels, chemicals, and other value-added products, but the exact products vary by technology and are not specified in every source [https://openalex.org/W4377108088||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4400734527||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How do thermal pwer plants relate to the environmental issues described in the survey on energy-efficient techniques in sustainable cloud computing?
final_answer: Thermal power plants are linked to the environmental issues in these sustainable cloud computing surveys mainly as the upstream source of the electricity that powers data centers, computing devices, and network equipment [https://openalex.org/W4281251447||ABSTRACT||000]. In the clearest statement, one survey says this electricity is “mainly generate[d]” by thermal power plants that use fossil fuels such as coal and oil, and it connects those plants to global warming, ozone layer depletion, and premature deaths [https://openalex.org/W4281251447||ABSTRACT||000]. Other papers do not mention thermal power plants directly, but they describe the same environmental burden in terms of high data-center energy use, carbon emissions, cooling demand, water use, and electronic waste, which together define the sustainability problem cloud computing is trying to reduce [https://openalex.org/W3172706057||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4385490509||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4385723923||ABSTRACT||000]. Across the surveys, the response is consistent: reduce energy consumption and carbon footprint through virtualization, consolidation, power-aware management, efficient cooling, monitoring, low-power electronics, and better workload/resource management [https://openalex.org/W4281251447||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4385490509||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4385723923||ABSTRACT||001]. Some papers also extend the solution space to renewable energy integration and energy-mix improvements, suggesting that the environmental issue is not only the amount of electricity used but also how that electricity is produced [https://openalex.org/W3172706057||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4391045525||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4366762583||ABSTRACT||000]. One survey even quantifies how severe the operational consequences are, reporting that data centers may consume 20% of global electricity by 2025 and emit up to 5.5% of global carbon emissions, with much of the energy becoming heat that increases cooling needs and reduces reliability and device life expectancy [https://openalex.org/W4385723923||ABSTRACT||000]. Taken together, the papers suggest that thermal power plants matter because they intensify the carbon and pollution consequences of cloud energy demand, but several surveys only address this relationship indirectly and focus instead on data-center-side efficiency measures [https://openalex.org/W3172706057||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4410019315||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4391045525||ABSTRACT||001].

query: In hepatocellular carcinoma, what was found about macrophage migration inhibitory factor, and how did its knockdown affect tumor cell behavior and related protein expression?
final_answer: In hepatocellular carcinoma, macrophage migration inhibitory factor (MIF) was reported to be significantly upregulated in both tissues and cell lines compared with adjacent normal tissues or a normal liver cell line, and its expression positively correlated with cyclin D1 expression and tumor size [pmc_PMC4170598||ABSTRACT||000]. siRNA-mediated MIF knockdown inhibited proliferation of PLC and HepG2 cells, promoted apoptosis, did not change the cell cycle, and reduced tumor growth in an in vivo xenograft model [pmc_PMC4170598||ABSTRACT||000]. Mechanistically, after MIF knockdown, Bcl-2, p-caspase-3, BIM, and Bax were upregulated, while cyclin D1, p-Akt, and p-ERK were downregulated [pmc_PMC4170598||ABSTRACT||000]. This pattern suggests that MIF supports HCC growth and survival through pro-proliferative and pro-survival signaling, whereas its inhibition shifts cells toward apoptosis and slower tumor expansion [pmc_PMC4170598||ABSTRACT||000]. The other provided HCC summaries do not contain MIF data, so they do not add direct evidence about MIF-specific knockdown effects [pmc_PMC4169566||ABSTRACT||001] [pmc_PMC3162940||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC4176125||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC10140795||ABSTRACT||001] [pmc_PMC10063289||ABSTRACT||001] [pmc_PMC9890137||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC9194659||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC3166084||ABSTRACT||001].

query: How did the learning curve for DIEP breast reconstruction change over time in this study?
final_answer: In the study that directly examined DIEP reconstruction, the learning curve appeared to improve over time, with the clearest institutional change being a shorter hospital stay in the later group than in the early group for both single and double DIEP cases [pmc_PMC10140818||ABSTRACT||000]. At the surgeon level, total operative time also improved over the study period, dropping from 296.0 ± 78.7 minutes in the early group to a lower value later on, which the summary interprets as a better operative learning curve [pmc_PMC10140818||ABSTRACT||000]. Beyond these gains, the abstract reported no statistically significant differences between the start and end of the study for most other outcomes, suggesting that the main measurable improvements were length of stay and surgery time rather than a broad change across all endpoints [pmc_PMC10140818||ABSTRACT||000]. The other provided paper did not report a DIEP-specific learning curve and instead focused on revisions and secondary reconstructions across reconstruction types and follow-up intervals, so it does not add direct evidence about learning-curve change over time [pmc_PMC10364508||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC10364508||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the available evidence indicates a time-related efficiency improvement in DIEP reconstruction, but only within a single study and with limited outcome changes beyond operative duration and hospitalization [pmc_PMC10140818||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How cross-disciplinary collaborations help sustainability education for manufacturing teams facing digitalization and skill changes?
final_answer: Across the papers, cross-disciplinary collaboration is presented as a way to make sustainability education more holistic, practical, and better aligned with complex change, including digitalization and shifting skills needs [https://openalex.org/W4390432598||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4386455762||ABSTRACT||000]. Several sources converge on the idea that collaboration supports learning by combining diverse perspectives, linking education to real-world problem solving, and strengthening social interaction and competence development [https://openalex.org/W4390432598||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4386455762||ABSTRACT||000]. In manufacturing- and supply-chain-relevant contexts, the evidence suggests that sustainability gains from digitalisation depend on collaboration, because firms may otherwise face data-sharing concerns, rebound effects, or underdeveloped uses of Industry 4.0 technologies for sustainability purposes [https://openalex.org/W4220997944||ABSTRACT||001]. The literature also indicates that education for sustainability can promote inclusion and collaborative/cooperative work, which is relevant for workforce adaptation to digitalization and skill changes, while broader engineering education is being pushed toward curriculum reform under Industry 4.0 and external accreditation and policy pressures [https://openalex.org/W4386284045||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4390751453||ABSTRACT||001]. Partnerships and collaborations are not one-size-fits-all: one review found that sustainability partnerships differ by issue, type, and mechanism, and that social issues such as education and job development more often rely on cross-sector partnerships beyond firm boundaries [https://openalex.org/W4318833090||ABSTRACT||000]. Another framework emphasizes that collaboration can improve organizational sustainability efforts only when its limits are managed, and that partnership performance should be assessed and continuously improved [https://openalex.org/W3128291854||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4205707734||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the evidence supports cross-disciplinary collaboration as a useful enabler of sustainability education for changing workforces, but the direct manufacturing-team evidence is limited and much of the literature remains general rather than specifically focused on digitalization-driven skill change [https://openalex.org/W4283808475||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4390432598||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4318833090||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How are coronary artery calcifications associated with complications?
final_answer: Across the provided papers, coronary artery calcification is most consistently associated with higher cardiovascular risk and worse prognosis, rather than with a single specific complication. A review found that coronary artery calcium (CAC) is associated with future atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease independent of conventional risk factors and improves risk prediction when added to a global risk model [pmc_PMC5383538||ABSTRACT||000]. In symptomatic patients referred for cardiac CT, coronary artery calcification score predicted all-cause mortality during follow-up, and absolute CACS performed at least as well as MESA percentile-based measures for predicting this outcome [pmc_PMC9806039||ABSTRACT||000]. In a trauma registry, coronary artery calcification visible on routine CT was independently associated with in-hospital complications, with left main coronary artery calcification linked to any complication and the number of calcified coronary arteries showing a trend toward association with complications [pmc_PMC10229702||ABSTRACT||001]. By contrast, a heavily calcified-lesion registry showed that calcification mainly increased procedural complexity, but orbital atherectomy still achieved high procedural success and no primary safety events within 30 days, suggesting that complication risk depends on the clinical context and treatment strategy [pmc_PMC10140256||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC10140256||ABSTRACT||001]. The review also notes that for similar CAC levels, absolute ASCVD risk can differ by region and ethnicity, indicating that the complication risk associated with CAC may vary across populations [pmc_PMC5383538||ABSTRACT||000]. However, some papers in the set do not address coronary calcification at all, so the evidence is incomplete for defining a universal complication profile [pmc_PMC10140970||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC10141707||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC9806495||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How does the combined detecion of KAI1 and VEGF improve the diagnosis of HCC?
final_answer: The only paper in the supplied evidence that directly addresses KAI1 and VEGF reports that, in HCC patients, serum KAI1 is downregulated while VEGF is upregulated, and that both markers are associated with clinical features relevant to disease burden, including TNM stage and metastasis-related findings [pmc_PMC4164248||ABSTRACT||000]. Individually, KAI1 showed better diagnostic performance than VEGF, with an AUC of 0.907 versus 0.779, and KAI1 alone achieved 86.96% sensitivity and 83.06% accuracy [pmc_PMC4164248||ABSTRACT||001]. The combined detection of KAI1 and VEGF further improved performance, increasing sensitivity to 91.86%, accuracy to 84.68%, and negative predictive value to 78.79% [pmc_PMC4164248||ABSTRACT||001]. Based on these data, the combination appears to improve HCC diagnosis mainly by adding VEGF to an already strong KAI1 signal, yielding better sensitivity and slightly better overall accuracy and rule-out performance than KAI1 alone [pmc_PMC4164248||ABSTRACT||001]. The study’s conclusion is that the combined assay may greatly improve HCC diagnosis and could form a reliable diagnostic marker panel [pmc_PMC4164248||ABSTRACT||001]. However, the remaining supplied summaries do not provide additional corroborating evidence for KAI1 and VEGF, so the answer rests on a single directly relevant study [pmc_PMC8318739||ABSTRACT||001] [pmc_PMC9805748||ABSTRACT||001] [pmc_PMC9806080||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3178660840||ABSTRACT||001].

query: How does global public health get threat from microplastics in fishmeal?
final_answer: Across the summaries, the main public-health concern is that microplastics can move from aquatic environments into the food chain and ultimately into seafood consumed by humans [https://openalex.org/W4282929872||ABSTRACT||000], [https://openalex.org/W4408578227||ABSTRACT||000], [https://openalex.org/W4295412833||ABSTRACT||000]. Fishmeal is presented as an important transmission route because fish that already accumulate microplastics, especially small pelagic and oceanic fish, are processed into fishmeal used in aquaculture and livestock feeds [https://openalex.org/W4282929872||ABSTRACT||000]. One study summarized here reports that in Bangladesh all commercial fish feed samples were contaminated with microplastics, with mean levels of 500 to 2200 MPs/kg, supporting the idea that contaminated feed can directly introduce microplastics into farmed fish and the human food chain [https://openalex.org/W4388496957||ABSTRACT||000]. The review evidence also states that when microplastics-contaminated feed is given to cultured fish, microplastics may alter fish physiology and behavior and may accumulate in edible parts of the fish, which strengthens the pathway from feed to consumer exposure [https://openalex.org/W4282929872||ABSTRACT||000]. Several papers agree that microplastics can act as carriers of harmful contaminants such as persistent organic pollutants, making food-chain transfer a plausible route of human exposure and a broader threat to global public health [https://openalex.org/W4408578227||ABSTRACT||000], [https://openalex.org/W4295412833||ABSTRACT||000]. However, the evidence is mostly conceptual or based on feed contamination and aquatic exposure rather than direct human outcome data, so the summaries support a risk pathway rather than a quantified health impact [https://openalex.org/W4388496957||ABSTRACT||000], [pmc_PMC9967563||ABSTRACT||000]. Some papers also explicitly note that they do not provide fishmeal-specific evidence or enough information to explain the global public-health threat in detail, reinforcing that the fishmeal pathway remains under-studied in the provided evidence [https://openalex.org/W4401805195||ABSTRACT||000], [https://openalex.org/W4408490507||ABSTRACT||001], [https://openalex.org/W4367322982||ABSTRACT||001].

query: How did broiler chicks in Iraq compare in maternal derived antibodies against Newcastle disease vaccination, and which strain performed better in the study?
final_answer: In the Iraq study, 1-day-old imported broiler chicks of two strains—Cobb 500 and Ross 308—were compared for maternal derived antibodies against Newcastle disease using indirect ELISA on samples from 28 Ross 308 flocks and 17 Cobb 500 flocks in Nineveh governorate [pmc_PMC9805781||ABSTRACT||000]. Cobb 500 performed better than Ross 308 in this comparison, because all Cobb 500 chicks were antibody-positive (100%) versus 97.78% of Ross 308 chicks, and Cobb 500 also had a higher mean maternal antibody titer and a lower mean CV [pmc_PMC9805781||ABSTRACT||000]. The paper also states that both strains had high and uniform maternal antibody titers overall, but Cobb 500 had higher protective titers than Ross 308 [pmc_PMC9805781||ABSTRACT||001]. In addition, the vaccination index was higher for Cobb 500 than for Ross 308, further supporting better performance for Cobb 500 in this study [pmc_PMC9805781||ABSTRACT||001]. query: How do neonatal injury models help to know about adult hearts cardiac regeneration?
final_answer: Neonatal injury models are presented as useful because newborn mice have a brief period of full cardiac regenerative capacity after injury, and studying that window may also be relevant to the neonatal human heart [pmc_PMC9064850||ABSTRACT||000]. By examining this early regenerative state, researchers can identify molecular mechanisms that underlie cardiac regeneration and find factors that stimulate heart repair [pmc_PMC9064850||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC9064850||ABSTRACT||001]. The same paper suggests that these models can point to ways of inducing endogenous cardiomyocyte proliferation in the adult heart, which could guide novel therapies for diseased adult hearts [pmc_PMC9064850||ABSTRACT||001]. They are also described as translational in vivo platforms for testing drugs and treatments to promote cardiac regeneration, with the advantage that short-lived mice allow outcomes to be monitored across the life span [pmc_PMC9064850||ABSTRACT||000]. In contrast, the other supplied summaries do not provide evidence about neonatal injury models or adult cardiac regeneration, because they focus on LVAD-related myocardial recovery, fibrosis and arrhythmia after ablation, neonatal critical congenital heart disease monitoring, chronic ISO/PE treatment responses, or heart valve implants [pmc_PMC9806425||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC10141040||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC10230358||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC8921177||ABSTRACT||001] [pmc_PMC10143004||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the evidence supports the idea that neonatal injury models help by revealing regenerative mechanisms and candidate pro-regenerative factors that may be translated toward adult heart repair, but the provided summaries do not include direct proof that such findings have already been successfully applied in adult hearts [pmc_PMC9064850||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC9064850||ABSTRACT||001].

query: What link between the consumer and the Circular economy is denoted in the context, and what is said about it?
final_answer: Across the papers, the consumer is linked to the circular economy mainly through the idea that consumption must be rethought within finite resource limits, rather than assumed to rely on endless restocking, which makes the circular economy especially important “today, more than ever” [https://openalex.org/W4378472586||ABSTRACT||000]. Several summaries also frame the consumer as part of broader circular-economy action: one paper explicitly places consumer behaviour among the key areas where circular economy has a place, alongside sustainability, innovation, remanufacturing, operations management, supply chains, and recycling [https://openalex.org/W4211051495||ABSTRACT||000]. Another paper links consumers with circular-economy practices through “engagement of both companies and consumers,” arguing that policymakers should support this with favourable policies and incentives [https://openalex.org/W4396622004||ABSTRACT||001]. In that same context, advancing the circular economy is associated with pro-environmental behaviour, digital transformation, and incentives, which are said to have already produced notable advancements [https://openalex.org/W4396622004||ABSTRACT||001]. More broadly, the circular economy is described as a resource-related concept for sustainable development and as a pragmatic route toward sustainability, including positive synergies in economic, social, and environmental areas [https://openalex.org/W3137694958||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4211051495||ABSTRACT||001]. The literature also positions circular economy within sustainable development more generally, with one paper describing it through efficient material use, product life extension, and smart production and use of products, plus related business models and waste-utilization strategies [https://openalex.org/W4282921144||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, the evidence suggests the topic is still emerging and unevenly developed, with limited research until recently and implementation challenges in sectors such as food, indicating that practical guidance and targeted initiatives are still needed [https://openalex.org/W4211051495||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4396622004||ABSTRACT||001].

query: How do PAs create public value in sustainability reporting?
final_answer: Across the papers, public value in sustainability reporting is created by making organizations more transparent and accountable to stakeholders, including investors, customers, employees, local communities, and other affected groups [https://openalex.org/W4402984150||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4390267129||ABSTRACT||001]. Several studies also describe public value as emerging when reporting is stakeholder-oriented and tied to justice, fairness, and stakeholder impressions, rather than being treated only as a compliance exercise [https://openalex.org/W4297090192||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4390267129||ABSTRACT||001]. In public-sector settings, PAs create public value by preserving and disseminating public value, obtaining legitimacy and support from stakeholders, and building operational capacity [https://openalex.org/W4320719832||ABSTRACT||000]. Another public-sector study shows that PAs can create public value by hybridizing integrated reporting and the SDGs in planned accountability and reporting practices that support sustainability delivery in practice [https://openalex.org/W3121263816||ABSTRACT||000]. Relatedly, the literature review suggests that public administrations also create public value by improving knowledge and practice around sustainability and non-financial reporting in public entities [https://openalex.org/W3147261195||ABSTRACT||000]. A recurring mechanism across the literature is materiality determination: one chapter argues that public value is created primarily through the stakeholder accountability purpose of deciding what is material, and that this accountability purpose should be paramount [https://openalex.org/W4289767614||ABSTRACT||000]. More broadly, sustainability reporting is presented as a structured, theory-of-change-driven practice that uses reporting standards and frameworks to support continuous improvement and alignment with international standards [https://openalex.org/W4406062330||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4402984150||ABSTRACT||000]. However, the evidence is not fully consistent on the role of public administrations in every context: one paper explicitly says public value is created through reporting’s effects on multiple stakeholder groups but does not specify PAs’ exact role [https://openalex.org/W4390267129||ABSTRACT||001].

query: How do sustainable technologies and environmantal management relate in the context of Industry 4.0 and SDGs, and what did the study find about enterprises preference for environmental aspects in business management?
final_answer: Across the reviewed papers, sustainable technologies and environmental management are presented as closely linked through Industry 4.0’s potential to improve environmental sustainability, especially in manufacturing and logistics [https://openalex.org/W4392974914||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4226256571||ABSTRACT||001]. Several studies argue that Industry 4.0 technologies can improve understanding of production and supply chains, increase manufacturing efficiency, and reduce resource consumption, thereby supporting environmental sustainability [https://openalex.org/W4226256571||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4311719782||ABSTRACT||000]. Other papers extend this connection to SDGs, stating that the convergence of Industry 4.0 with the SDGs improves environmental sustainability and environmental performance and can create ecological support [https://openalex.org/W4398200114||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4389484631||ABSTRACT||000]. The literature also frames sustainable technologies such as clean energy, green logistics, reverse logistics, and renewable energy as enablers of industrial development and growth when combined with Industry 4.0 innovations under the SDGs [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, one study cautions that some Industry 4.0-related technologies can have negative environmental effects, including air pollution, improper waste disposal, and excessive use of raw materials, information, and energy [https://openalex.org/W4398200114||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the literature review papers suggest broad agreement that Industry 4.0 can support environmental management, but also note that the relationship has been fragmented and not fully clarified in the literature [https://openalex.org/W3170613256||ABSTRACT||000]. In terms of enterprises’ preferences, the Slovak enterprise study found that more than 70% preferred environmental aspects in business management and that more than 82% implemented the SDGs [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000]. That same study reported a significant relationship between environmental management in the context of SDGs and sustainability in production and logistics, including a significant relationship with renewable energy technology use in industry [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How do energy resourses and renewable energy in mining together help with environmental sustainability and sustainable development, and what good effects are said about using renewable energy in mining for sustainability?
final_answer: Across the papers, the main idea is that mining sustainability improves when energy use is reduced and cleaner energy sources are adopted, because mining is energy-intensive and often reliant on fossil fuels [https://openalex.org/W4386805143||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4294647036||ABSTRACT||001]. One paper argues that sustainable mining should minimize resource and energy consumption, waste, and other environmental harms such as dust pollution, greenhouse gas emissions, and acid mine drainage across all stages of mining [https://openalex.org/W4294647036||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4294647036||ABSTRACT||001]. Another study reports that green mining technologies, including electric vehicles and renewable energy sources, decrease carbon emissions and lower energy use while improving waste management compared with traditional methods [https://openalex.org/W4399883377||ABSTRACT||000]. In addition, renewable energy in mining is said to support Sustainable Development Goals by creating jobs, reducing environmental pollution, increasing knowledge in mining areas, promoting a circular economy, and lowering operating costs [https://openalex.org/W4386805143||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4386805143||ABSTRACT||001]. At the same time, the literature warns that renewable energy should not be judged only by carbon reduction, because hidden impacts in energy-generation processes can create broader sustainability tradeoffs and can either enable or inhibit progress toward the SDGs [https://openalex.org/W4396736229||ABSTRACT||000]. This broader view is consistent with MASI’s emphasis on assessing mining sustainability across environmental, social, and economic dimensions to support ecological preservation, social welfare, and economic viability [https://openalex.org/W4393928445||ABSTRACT||001]. Evidence from sustainability reporting also suggests that these benefits are not automatic, since many companies still showed increased air emissions, water use, and energy usage, with no improvement in renewable energy utilization or waste recycling [https://openalex.org/W3165375152||ABSTRACT||000]. query: How the sustainability assessment and evaluation frameworks in the district heating and PT evaluation studies are linked, and which method was most used, plus how do they relate to CO2 emissions reduction in the urban transport example?
final_answer: Across the district heating, Positive Energy Districts (PEDs), and public transport (PT) studies, sustainability assessment and evaluation are linked by a common use of indicators or KPIs to compare alternatives and support decision-making, but the emphasis differs by domain [https://openalex.org/W3208788408||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W3216865266||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4315708900||ABSTRACT||000]. In district heating and related energy-system work, the assessment framework is organized around multi-dimensional indicator sets, such as social, economic, environmental, technical, and institutional dimensions, while other studies broaden this further to include technological, political, and institutional indicators [https://openalex.org/W3208788408||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4220986058||ABSTRACT||000]. The PED review similarly relies on KPIs, European standards/initiatives, Sustainable Development Agenda indicators, and literature-based metrics, but stresses that the KPI framework still needs better integration and harmonization with Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) [https://openalex.org/W3216865266||ABSTRACT||000]. For PT, the dominant evaluation frameworks are Multi-Criteria Decision-Making (MCDM), followed by Assessment Indicator Models (AIM), and among MCDM methods the Analytical Hierarchy Process was the most frequently used approach [https://openalex.org/W4315708900||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4315708900||ABSTRACT||001]. That means the most-used method explicitly identified in the PT evidence is AHP, while in the PED evidence LCA is highlighted as the most used method, showing that “most used” depends on the study domain and review scope rather than a single universal method [https://openalex.org/W4315708900||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3216865266||ABSTRACT||000]. In the district heating study using MCDA, several methods were compared, including WSM, TOPSIS, PROMETHEE, ELECTRE, and DEA, and sensitivity analysis was used to judge which approach was most credible [https://openalex.org/W4220986058||ABSTRACT||000]. The urban sustainability/project-evaluation papers reinforce the same general logic that indicators are used to measure progress, performance, and weaknesses over time, but they do not provide a direct district-heating-to-PT linkage or a specific urban transport case study beyond the indicator framing [https://openalex.org/W4377861392||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3162569529||ABSTRACT||001]. On CO2 emissions reduction, the clearest link appears in the renewable-energy/district-heating evaluation framework, where CO2 emission and GHG emission reduction are explicitly listed as environmental indicators [https://openalex.org/W3208788408||ABSTRACT||001]. So, the shared thread is an indicator-based sustainability evaluation logic, with MCDM/AHP dominant in PT and LCA prominent in PEDs, while CO2 reduction is treated as a measured environmental outcome in the urban transport/energy-evaluation framing rather than as a standalone result across all studies [https://openalex.org/W4315708900||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3216865266||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3208788408||ABSTRACT||001].

query: How do innovation, CEOs' sustainability orientation, and green governance relate to sustainability and environmental performance in firms?
final_answer: Across the summaries, innovation appears to be consistently associated with better sustainability-related outcomes, but the strength and pathway of that relationship varies by context and outcome. Green innovation is reported to have a significant positive relationship with environmental sustainability in industrial firms, and this link is mediated by innovation climate, with green motivational strategies and green abilities strengthening the effect of innovation practices [https://openalex.org/W4388684227||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4388684227||ABSTRACT||001]. In another study, green innovation capabilities indirectly influence the effect of social and economic sustainability on firm performance, although they do not indirectly affect the relationship between environmental sustainability and firm performance [https://openalex.org/W3200508375||ABSTRACT||001]. Sustainability-oriented innovations also show a strong positive impact on firms’ economic performance, with green competitive advantage and green image serving as mediators, and green organizational identity further supporting green image through green commitment [https://openalex.org/W4367603834||ABSTRACT||000]. On the leadership side, the evidence points to environmentally aware leadership as beneficial: green transformational leadership is positively related to green performance, and this relationship is mediated by green organizational culture and green engagement [https://openalex.org/W4401652574||ABSTRACT||000]. For CEOs specifically, the available evidence does not directly test CEOs’ sustainability orientation, so no firm conclusion can be drawn about that variable from these summaries alone [https://openalex.org/W4367603834||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4282035384||ABSTRACT||000]. Green governance also appears important, but in a configurational rather than universal way: corporate governance bundles involving CEO power, board capital, and ownership structure generate multiple sufficient paths to high environmental innovation, and both powerful and weak CEOs can facilitate environmental innovation when paired with suitable governance arrangements [https://openalex.org/W4282035384||ABSTRACT||000]. More broadly, a genuinely implemented sustainable strategy improves firm performance and favorable environmental results, yet its effectiveness depends on ownership dispersion and board independence, and sector-specific differences mean there is no single governance formula that works across all industries [https://openalex.org/W4404618052||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the papers agree that innovation, leadership orientation, and governance design can support sustainability and environmental performance, but they also suggest that these effects are often indirect, mediated, and contingent on internal organizational and governance conditions [https://openalex.org/W4388684227||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4401652574||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4282035384||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How do the themes of "energy resources," "clean and distributed energy," and "energy transitions" connect across the context in explaining both environmental sustainability and workforce implications, and what does the context say about the role of clean energy, renewable electricity, and training in this transition?
final_answer: Across the papers, “energy resources,” “clean and distributed energy,” and “energy transitions” are connected as parts of a broader shift from conventional energy systems toward more sustainable, lower-carbon systems that must satisfy environmental, economic, social, and institutional goals [https://openalex.org/W4220773259||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W3154213043||ABSTRACT||000]. Several summaries emphasize that this transition is not only about emissions reduction but also about environmental sustainability, policy coherence, and broader development goals such as green growth, social inclusion, and climate protection [https://openalex.org/W4401335752||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4391762394||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4400513475||ABSTRACT||001]. The context also treats energy resources as unevenly distributed and the transition as technically and economically constrained, noting the need for renewable adoption, storage, resilient grids, and a sustainable mix of renewable and limited nonrenewable sources to maintain stability and flexibility [https://openalex.org/W4220773259||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4387418575||ABSTRACT||000]. Clean and distributed energy appears especially as part of a democratic, inclusive, and stakeholder-sensitive transition, where perceptions of centralized versus distributed models, sustainability, and the speed of decarbonization matter for how quickly the transition can proceed [https://openalex.org/W4283155889||ABSTRACT||000]. On the environmental side, renewable energy is repeatedly presented as helping combat climate change and advance sustainable development, while also being linked to resource conservation, environmental protection, and climate change policy priorities [https://openalex.org/W4407562904||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4400513475||ABSTRACT||001]. On the workforce side, the papers connect transition with job creation, economic growth, social equity, and green job formation, but also note uneven impacts across sectors and regions, implying that adaptation pressures will not be distributed evenly [https://openalex.org/W4391762394||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4407562904||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4387418575||ABSTRACT||000]. The context specifically says that renewable energy investment and workforce training should support green economic transformation, and another paper highlights human capital development as part of advancing the transition [https://openalex.org/W4407562904||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4400513475||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the evidence suggests that clean energy and renewable electricity are central mechanisms in the transition, but the transition is framed as requiring policy support, infrastructure, stakeholder coordination, and skills development rather than technology alone [https://openalex.org/W4220773259||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4400513475||ABSTRACT||001].

query: How do the themes of "Environmental sustainability", "Sustainability implementation barriers", and "Sustainable residential buildings" connect when comparing off-site construction research with the barrier analysis in Ghana and the "Mostadam" approach in Saudi Arabia, and what sustainability-related findings are highlighted across these contexts?
final_answer: Across the supplied papers, the clearest common thread is that environmental sustainability is treated as a practical building and housing problem, not just an abstract goal: Ghanaian construction research evaluates sustainability across the full project life cycle using indicators such as water quality, air quality, energy use and conservation, and environmental compliance and management [https://openalex.org/W3168941981||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3168941981||ABSTRACT||001]. In the Ghana barrier studies, sustainability implementation is shown to be constrained by multiple barrier sets, including cultural, economic, technical knowledge, regulatory, management, standards, society, and knowledge barriers, with management-related barriers and economics/regulation often emerging as especially important [https://openalex.org/W4293340752||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4310036329||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3132259306||ABSTRACT||000]. The Saudi Arabia Mostadam discussion connects most directly to sustainable residential buildings by presenting the rating system as a pathway toward sustainable development, practical strategies, future policy, and Vision 2030 city transformation [https://openalex.org/W3120903819||ABSTRACT||001]. Read together, these papers suggest that sustainability in the built environment depends both on defining environmental performance goals and on overcoming implementation barriers that slow adoption in real projects [https://openalex.org/W3168941981||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4293340752||ABSTRACT||001]. The residential-building literature reinforces this by showing that sustainability can also be linked to affordability and lifecycle economics, with design techniques, passive design, recycled and local materials, and socio-technical innovation improving both sustainability and cost outcomes [https://openalex.org/W4385389240||ABSTRACT||001]. Similarly, prefabricated construction research in Southern Africa reports higher overall sustainability performance for innovative prefabricated methods, tying environmental sustainability to sustainable affordable housing and lifecycle energy and cost assessment [https://openalex.org/W4386401188||ABSTRACT||000]. A broader pattern across contexts is that sustainability-related findings are framed as actionable guidance for policymakers, designers, and industry stakeholders, whether through barrier removal, better education and policy support, or design and rating-system strategies [https://openalex.org/W3145060410||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4310036329||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W3120903819||ABSTRACT||001]. However, the evidence does not provide direct off-site construction results or a full side-by-side comparison between the specific Ghana, Saudi Arabia, and off-site construction contexts, so that linkage remains limited by the supplied summaries [https://openalex.org/W4310036329||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3120903819||ABSTRACT||001].

final_answer: Across the supply chain management papers, environmental sustainability is advanced by embedding it into core supply chain strategy and practice rather than treating it as a separate concern [https://openalex.org/W4364359925||ABSTRACT||000]. One framework does this through a systems perspective and the “Knowing,” “Doing,” and missing “Being” dimensions, which are meant to align supply chain practice with Sustainable Development Goals [https://openalex.org/W4364359925||ABSTRACT||000]. Another organizes 789 sustainable business practices into 11 categories under a triple-bottom-line lens, including environmental aspects, to guide industrial solutions toward sustainable supply chains [https://openalex.org/W4283697438||ABSTRACT||000]. Several papers also show that sustainability can improve business outcomes: strategic sustainability orientation, shaped by employee motivation and managerial attitude, is said to work through corporate environmental management and CSR to improve firm performance, and environmental sustainability itself is reported to have a direct effect on financial performance [https://openalex.org/W3128290205||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3132273715||ABSTRACT||001]. A supply chain view that identifies stakeholders and unsustainable production and consumption patterns is also presented as a way to build a sustainability mindset across the network and improve resilience and sustainability performance [https://openalex.org/W4308101885||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4308101885||ABSTRACT||002]. Taken together, these summaries suggest that sustainability is advanced through strategic orientation, stakeholder coordination, and concrete operational practices, while also being linked to performance and managerial value [https://openalex.org/W4280505603||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W3132273715||ABSTRACT||001]. However, the provided evidence does not include the sustainable marketing article, so there is not enough information to explain directly how it links environmental sustainability to company image [https://openalex.org/W4362600777||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4394697557||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How does the text link economic sustainability and decoupling consumption from economic growth in these two contexts, and what is suggested about making space tourism environmentally sustainable?
final_answer: In the space tourism context, the text links economic sustainability to the “costing side” of the activity: reusable rockets have reduced budget requirements, but the economic burden is said to remain, along with environmental costs, unless the “tyranny of the rocket equation” is overcome [https://openalex.org/W4315646741||ABSTRACT||002]. It therefore presents economic sustainability as inseparable from environmental and ethical feasibility, and says sustainability indicators for space tourism are still unclear and not well defined [https://openalex.org/W4315646741||ABSTRACT||003]. In the broader sustainable tourism context, the text argues that sustainability should be assessed through indicators combining economic, social, and environmental dimensions rather than relying on economic growth alone [https://openalex.org/W4315646741||ABSTRACT||014]. This suggests a form of decoupling consumption from economic growth by building a more robust indicator framework, though the literature is described as having focused more on environmental and social sustainability than on economic indicators [https://openalex.org/W4315646741||ABSTRACT||014]. Across both contexts, the text implies that sustainability cannot be reduced to growth or lower costs, but must be defined through clearer preconditions and multidimensional measures [https://openalex.org/W4315646741||ABSTRACT||002] [https://openalex.org/W4315646741||ABSTRACT||014]. For making space tourism environmentally sustainable, it recommends a theoretically grounded conceptual model adapted from sustainable tourism frameworks and developed through Dubin’s two-stage theory-building approach to assess frontier tourism and address environmental impact and ethical concerns [https://openalex.org/W4315646741||ABSTRACT||003].

query: How do regional integration and multistakeholder partnerships support Sustainable Development Goal 8 in the Yangtze River Delta?
final_answer: Regional integration can support SDG 8 in the Yangtze River Delta by using subnational, cross-regional analysis to identify where economic and sustainability strengths and weaknesses lie, then coordinating targeted action across places with similar or complementary SDG profiles [https://openalex.org/W4220857404||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4220857404||ABSTRACT||001]. In the YRD, sustainability research shows that progress is uneven: socio-economic sustainability improved in most counties from 2000 to 2015, but environmental sustainability declined, suggesting that integrated policies must address trade-offs rather than assume all dimensions improve together [https://openalex.org/W3194996912||ABSTRACT||000]. The YRD literature also frames the region as a global city-region where sustainable development should be linked to regional integrative development through the SDGs, and calls for multi-scale, interdisciplinary analysis of regional social-ecological systems and governance institutions [https://openalex.org/W4320729134||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4320729134||ABSTRACT||001]. Multistakeholder partnerships are presented more generally as a way to reduce implementation gaps in the 2030 Agenda by bringing in more non-state actors and focusing on interlinked issues across sectors, scales, and actors [https://openalex.org/W4380882019||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4205386374||ABSTRACT||000]. For SDG implementation, these partnerships are also described as needing clearer scope, responsibilities, indicators, and actor selection, because identifying the right participants is a major obstacle [https://openalex.org/W4205386374||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, the partnership literature warns that SDG partnerships often still face limits in effectiveness and legitimacy, may reproduce earlier shortcomings, and are unlikely on their own to generate synergies or reduce trade-offs at large scale [https://openalex.org/W4400486548||ABSTRACT||000]. Taken together, the evidence suggests that SDG 8 in the YRD is best supported by combining regional integration, cross-scale coordination, and broad partnerships that align economic planning with environmental and social dimensions, rather than relying on partnerships alone [https://openalex.org/W3185034769||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4320729134||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4400486548||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How do environmental sustainability reporting practices in Bahrain\"s large industrial sector relate to environmental management and Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), and what evidence from the Industry 4.0 study shows similar links between SDGs, environmental aspects, and renewable energy technologies in industrial enterprises?
final_answer: In Bahrain’s large industrial sector, the strongest available evidence suggests that sustainability reporting is used to integrate sustainability into industrial development and improve environmental performance, with materiality analysis helping companies monitor and measure environmental performance and implement SDGs more effectively [https://openalex.org/W4200252599||ABSTRACT||000]. The Bahrain study also indicates that materiality matrices improve report content by incorporating stakeholder views and by helping firms identify and prioritize the most significant sustainability issues for future reporting [https://openalex.org/W4200252599||ABSTRACT||000]. Across the broader industrial reporting literature, SDG-linked reporting is relevant but not always straightforward because the SDG framework was not designed for corporate reporting and practices vary widely across companies, industries, and contexts [https://openalex.org/W4286447895||ABSTRACT||000]. That same line of evidence suggests reporting patterns are shaped by company size, geographical area, internationalisation, and economic performance, which helps explain why industrial sustainability reporting may differ across firms [https://openalex.org/W4286447895||ABSTRACT||000]. A separate metals-industry study similarly shows that sustainability reporting can be used to gauge SDG engagement, with firms emphasizing some goals more than others and with differences across subsectors, underscoring that environmental sustainability reporting reflects wider environmental management priorities [https://openalex.org/W3217154997||ABSTRACT||000]. For the Industry 4.0 side of the question, the available evidence shows a clear linkage between Industry 4.0 technologies, circular economy practices, and sustainable operations, especially SDGs 6, 7, 9, 12, and 13 [https://openalex.org/W4210290448||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4210290448||ABSTRACT||001]. Another Industry 4.0 study likewise reports that these technologies can enhance sustainability performance, address environmental concerns, and help achieve the SDGs, while organizing the relationship between 17 SDGs and 9 technologies in a systematic review [https://openalex.org/W4389484631||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4389484631||ABSTRACT||001]. A third model-based study reinforces this pattern by explicitly mapping the SDGs onto an environmental sustainability performance model to show their usefulness in sustainability transition and organizational implementation [https://openalex.org/W3157489939||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the evidence points to a common theme: in industrial settings, both sustainability reporting and Industry 4.0 frameworks connect environmental management with SDG implementation, but the exact reporting-to-performance link remains uneven and context dependent [https://openalex.org/W4200252599||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4286447895||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4210290448||ABSTRACT||001].

query: In the context of Environmental sustainability reporting and Sustainability reporting, how do the Bahrain industrial companies" materiality matrices relate to improved environmental performance, and how does this compare with the UK evidence on whether reporting that follows guidelines and a business-case approach actually improves sustainability performance?
final_answer: The Bahrain evidence generally suggests that using materiality analysis and materiality matrices in sustainability reporting is associated with better monitoring and measuring of environmental performance, and that these matrices help companies identify and prioritize significant sustainability issues for future reporting and environmental performance improvement [https://openalex.org/W4200252599||ABSTRACT||000]. The same Bahrain study also says materiality matrices can improve report contents by incorporating stakeholders’ views, which in turn improves sustainability report quality and supports SDG implementation [https://openalex.org/W4200252599||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4200252599||ABSTRACT||001]. A related Bahrain/GCC study finds that stronger materiality assessment disclosures are associated with better corporate governance and higher financial performance, and argues that improved disclosures can raise sustainability reporting quality, transparency, and accountability [https://openalex.org/W3134875937||ABSTRACT||001]. However, that evidence does not directly show that materiality matrices themselves cause improved environmental performance, and it also notes a decline in how reporters identify material issues that may indicate managerial capture [https://openalex.org/W3134875937||ABSTRACT||001]. By contrast, the UK evidence indicates that reporting aligned only with guidelines and a business-case approach does not necessarily improve sustainability performance; in fact, compliance-oriented and business-centered reporting is reported to have negative effects, while reporting grounded in a broader sustainability worldview is associated with positive effects [https://openalex.org/W4220852241||ABSTRACT||000]. Taken together, the papers imply that Bahrain’s materiality-matrix approach may be more strongly linked to practical environmental monitoring and report improvement than the UK’s guideline-driven, business-case framing, which appears insufficient on its own to improve sustainability performance [https://openalex.org/W4200252599||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4220852241||ABSTRACT||000]. Still, the comparison is limited because the Bahrain studies emphasize associations and reporting quality rather than direct causal evidence on environmental outcomes, while the UK evidence is specific to the broader orientation of reporting rather than materiality matrices themselves [https://openalex.org/W3134875937||ABSTRACT||001][https://openalex.org/W4220852241||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How doeas sustainable marketing relate to enviromental sustainability in shaping a company"s image, and what kinds of consumption changes are described as ways to advance sufficiency transitions?
final_answer: Across the papers, sustainable marketing is generally presented as a way for firms to signal commitment to sustainability, build legitimacy, and strengthen competitiveness or market position, which in turn can support a more favorable company image [https://openalex.org/W4392716256||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W3137258271||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4388661115||ABSTRACT||001]. Several summaries tie this image effect to environmental sustainability specifically: green marketing is said to position a company as socio-environmentally responsible, and sustainability communication is described as involving green advertising, CSR communication, and pro-sustainable behavior messaging [https://openalex.org/W4392716256||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4400608740||ABSTRACT||000]. Other papers emphasize that sustainable marketing works by aligning firms with environmentally conscious consumers and by adapting marketing to consumer preferences, values, and changing behavior trends [https://openalex.org/W4396847081||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4388661115||ABSTRACT||001]. At the same time, one paper distinguishes a profit-centric sustainable marketing approach from a sustain-centric one that prioritizes social and ecological well-being, while warning that greenwashing can occur when firms mimic sustain-centric practices piecemeal [https://openalex.org/W4379928390||ABSTRACT||000]. On sufficiency transitions, the evidence is narrower: sustainable marketing is framed as moving beyond short-term growth-oriented marketing toward sustainability and sufficiency, and as supporting sustainable consumption patterns, but the summaries do not give concrete consumption-change types in most cases [https://openalex.org/W3126349936||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4400608740||ABSTRACT||000]. The only related descriptions are broad references to sustainable consumption, ethical consumerism, and promoting pro-sustainable behaviour, alongside a degrowth-oriented critique that points toward transformative business models and policies rather than specific consumer behavior changes [https://openalex.org/W4400608740||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4282834253||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the papers agree that sustainable marketing is linked to environmental sustainability through consumer-facing practices and pro-environmental firm behavior, but they differ in emphasis between image/competitiveness, legitimacy, and deeper systemic transition [https://openalex.org/W3137258271||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4392716256||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4282834253||ABSTRACT||000].
