query: How sustainability reporting link with SDGs and sustainability performance, it matter from the supply chain framework too?
final_answer:
Across the papers, sustainability reporting is generally treated as a way to connect corporate or supply-chain activities to the SDGs and to assess sustainability performance, but the strength of that connection varies by study [https://openalex.org/W4392003298||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4220859323||ABSTRACT||000]. Several studies support a positive link: sustainability reporting can be monitored against the SDGs, and reporting score indices have been built to help investors and stakeholders measure sustainable performance and commitment to the global sustainability agenda [https://openalex.org/W4392003298||ABSTRACT||001]. Relatedly, integrated reporting is framed as a corporate strategy for achieving SDGs and assessing SDG performance using common metrics, although the paper notes comparisons between companies remain difficult [https://openalex.org/W4362609606||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, evidence from a large study of 8,500 companies suggests that SDG reporting can be disconnected from actual sustainability performance and may involve arbitrary selection of goals rather than a grounded performance basis [https://openalex.org/W4394576889||ABSTRACT||000]. This creates an important contradiction: some papers present reporting as a useful performance tool, while others show that current reporting practices may not reliably reflect real sustainability outcomes or progress across multiple SDGs [https://openalex.org/W4394576889||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4220859323||ABSTRACT||000].

From a supply chain framework, the evidence is strong that sustainability matters beyond the firm boundary. One paper finds that sustainable supply chain practices have positive and significant relationships with both financial performance and the SDGs, and explicitly recommends implementing sustainability from supplier to customer to improve efficiency and reduce negative environmental and social impacts [https://openalex.org/W4394886303||ABSTRACT||001]. Another study proposes a supply-chain sustainability assessment framework grounded in GRI that measures both a company’s and its suppliers’ sustainability performance, while improving communication of environmental and social progress to stakeholders [https://openalex.org/W4400657024||ABSTRACT||000]. A further paper argues that SSCM, technology adoption, and performance measurement are important for sustainability and proposes frameworks for achieving SDGs through SSCM and deploying sustainability indicators [https://openalex.org/W4327714039||ABSTRACT||000].

However, the literature also shows that supply-chain or life-cycle links to SDGs are not yet fully harmonized. One study notes that some indicators have no direct or indirect connection to any SDG because SDGs lack a life-cycle-thinking perspective and there is limited discussion of workers, consumers, and value-chain actors [https://openalex.org/W4281493513||ABSTRACT||001]. Another review says SDGs and LCSA are complementary but there is still no generally agreed way to set up their connections, so further research is needed to consistently link metrics to SDG goals [https://openalex.org/W4380365728||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the best-supported conclusion is that sustainability reporting can matter for SDGs and sustainability performance, especially when it is tied to materiality, indicators, and supply-chain assessment rather than just symbolic disclosure [https://openalex.org/W4200252599||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4400657024||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How do the circular economy and sustainable recycling approaches in textile waste and polymeric membranes reduce environmental impact?
final_answer:
Across the papers, circular economy approaches are presented as a way to reduce environmental impact by keeping materials in use longer, lowering waste, and reducing demand for new resource extraction in both textiles and polymeric materials. In textile waste, reuse, repair, recycling, reduction, and related strategies are repeatedly described as mechanisms for cutting waste from fast-fashion production and consumption cycles, with repair extending garment life and reducing the need for new production [https://openalex.org/W4403242376||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4403242376||ABSTRACT||001]. Several textile studies also argue that circular models can turn waste into valuable outputs such as recycled yarn, regenerated fibers, biofilms, biodegradable composites, and biofuels, while reducing water, resource, and energy consumption [https://openalex.org/W4406270757||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4406270757||ABSTRACT||002]. Another textile paper frames a closed-loop system in which post-consumer items are transformed into recycled fiber, explicitly aiming to reduce pollution and resource waste [https://openalex.org/W4206622324||ABSTRACT||000]. The textile literature agrees that recycling is important but not sufficient on its own, because technological, awareness, investment, and policy barriers can limit effectiveness and existing waste-management programs have often been unsuccessful [https://openalex.org/W4403242376||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4403242376||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4407071446||ABSTRACT||000].

For polymeric materials, the review emphasizes that persistent plastic waste makes traditional mechanical recycling insufficient, and it presents chemical and biological options such as pyrolysis, depolymerization, and enzyme-based degradation as more efficient and sustainable alternatives [https://openalex.org/W4407870591||ABSTRACT||000]. These approaches are explicitly linked to closed-loop and circular plastic economy strategies, which are described as key steps toward reducing environmental impact [https://openalex.org/W4407870591||ABSTRACT||000]. The textile papers and the polymer review converge on the same general principle: sustainability improves when waste is treated as a resource and processes are designed for circularity rather than linear disposal [https://openalex.org/W4406270757||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3206222416||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4407870591||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, the textile literature suggests that better environmental outcomes depend on designing materials and finishes for end-of-life recycling, and on supportive systems such as traceability and improved waste-management infrastructure [https://openalex.org/W3206222416||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4406270757||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4407071446||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the evidence supports the view that circular economy and sustainable recycling reduce environmental impact by extending product life, increasing material recovery, and lowering pollution and resource use, but their success depends on overcoming technological and institutional barriers [https://openalex.org/W4403242376||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4407870591||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4283362208||ABSTRACT||001].

query: How textile waste management can use waste conversion and the adsorption properties in these materials?
final_answer: Across the papers, textile waste management is consistently framed as needing a shift away from dumping and toward circular, resource-recovery systems that support reuse, recycling, and closed-loop production [https://openalex.org/W3205047951||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3206222416||ABSTRACT||000]. Several studies show that waste conversion can be used to transform textile waste into valuable outputs, including recycled fibers, separable fiber fractions, and even new products or clean energy through biotechnologies [https://openalex.org/W4206622324||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4323545673||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4407071446||ABSTRACT||001]. More specific conversion routes include chemical and biotechnological methods such as acid hydrolysis, enzymatic recycling, solvent recovery, optimized pretreatment, and fluidized-bed pyrolysis, with the review reporting up to 70% glucose recovery for acid hydrolysis and about 20% less energy use for enzymatic recycling than conventional methods [https://openalex.org/W4408599276||ABSTRACT||000]. The papers also agree that textile waste is technically difficult to process because of mixed fibers, finishes, dyes, and additives, so pretreatment, enzyme time, and repeated treatment may be needed to make conversion efficient [https://openalex.org/W4408599276||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4323545673||ABSTRACT||000]. On the adsorption side, the strongest evidence comes from textile wastewater treatment, where adsorption is described as one of the most feasible ways to remove dyes and metals because it is cost-effective and can use a variety of adsorbents [https://openalex.org/W4309710850||ABSTRACT||000]. That same paper places adsorption within a broader treatment train combining primary, secondary, and tertiary phases, emphasizing flexible multi-step treatment for complex effluents and reuse-oriented goals such as zero liquid discharge and resource recovery [https://openalex.org/W4309710850||ABSTRACT||000]. However, most of the papers do not provide direct evidence that textile materials themselves have adsorption properties for waste conversion, and several summaries explicitly state that adsorption-based use is not described [https://openalex.org/W4408599276||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3206222416||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4206622324||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the evidence supports combining conversion technologies for solid textile waste with adsorption-based treatment for textile wastewater, but it does not show a unified adsorption-centered conversion strategy for textile materials [https://openalex.org/W4309710850||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4408599276||ABSTRACT||000].

key_claims.notes: The cited chunks explicitly contrast a linear model and dumping with sustainability, recycling, and closed-loop circular systems.

key_claims.notes: The chunks mention recycled fiber production, separation into purified product streams, glucose recovery, and bio-oil yield improvements.

key_claims.notes: The cited review directly states both the 70% glucose recovery and approximately 20% energy reduction.

key_claims.notes: Both chunks describe mixed fibers, dyes, and finishing chemicals as barriers and explicitly mention pretreatment, sufficient time, enzyme amount, and repeated treatment.

query: How is the translational regulation of NEDD4 linked to the IGF1 signaling pathway, and what does the context say about NEDD4 in cells that depend on this pathway?
final_answer: The strongest evidence connecting NEDD4 to the IGF1 pathway comes from the gastric cancer study, which divided GC cell lines into IGF1R-dependent and IGF1R-independent groups based on Akt phosphorylation after OSI906 treatment [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||000]. In that context, Dox-induced NEDD4 knockdown reduced tumor growth only in IGF1R-dependent cells, while NEDD4 overexpression promoted their growth, indicating that NEDD4’s effect is selective for cells reliant on IGF1/IGF1R signaling [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||000]. The same study reports that NEDD4’s translational regulation is linked to the IGF1 pathway through a PTEN-IRS1 axis, and rescue experiments showed this axis is required for NEDD4-mediated regulation of Akt activation and tumor growth [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||001]. It further concludes that NEDD4 promotes proliferation of GC cells dependent on IGF1/IGF1R signaling by antagonizing PTEN’s protein phosphatase activity to IRS1 [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||001]. In that IGF1-related setting, NEDD4 was higher in IGF1-high GC tissues than in IGF1-low or normal tissues, and co-high expression of NEDD4 and IGF1 predicted worse prognosis [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||001]. By contrast, another cancer study found NEDD4 to be translationally upregulated in pancreatic cancer cells through an undefined translational activation mechanism and linked it to PTEN/PI3K/AKT signaling rather than IGF1 signaling [pmc_PMC5386762||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC5386762||ABSTRACT||001]. That pancreatic study also reported heterogeneous but elevated NEDD4 expression versus normal ductal epithelial cells, and NEDD4 depletion reduced proliferation and migration of PDAC cells [pmc_PMC5386762||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC5386762||ABSTRACT||001]. Other provided papers do not add evidence for an IGF1–NEDD4 link, instead discussing unrelated systems such as DYRK3/SNAPIN or Nedd4-2 in glutamate transporter regulation [pmc_PMC9803678||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC5386455||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the evidence suggests that translational upregulation of NEDD4 can support growth signaling, but the direct IGF1 connection is specifically demonstrated in IGF1R-dependent gastric cancer cells and not established in the other summaries [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||001].

query: How are the SDOs linked to policy coherance for sustainable development in the EU context?
final_answer: Across these studies, the SDGs are linked to policy coherence for sustainable development in the EU as both a measurement framework and a policy integration agenda that should align environmental, social, and economic objectives without creating trade-offs that undermine progress on other goals [https://openalex.org/W3134571733||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W4200315183||ABSTRACT||000]. Several papers emphasize that coherence requires matching EU strategies and instruments with the SDGs, including mapping the SDGs against the European Green Deal, the European Semester’s Country-specific Recommendations, and the EU Recovery Plan to improve alignment of policy priorities [https://openalex.org/W3194602120||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W3194602120||ABSTRACT||001]. Related work argues that tools such as Life Cycle Assessment can support EU policy design and monitoring, and that these links to the SDGs and Planetary Boundaries can be existing, missing, or dependent on the specific framework used, suggesting that coherence is partly a technical and methodological problem [https://openalex.org/W4210270578||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, the literature cautions that policy coherence is not purely technical: one paper on the Dutch context argues that SDG arrangements can present an apolitical façade that may limit transformative change, while another stresses that ideas, institutions, and interests shape which policy options are prioritized and whose interests coherence serves [https://openalex.org/W4200315183||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W4308113945||ABSTRACT||000]. The papers also indicate that some SDG domains are more difficult to align than others, with environmental goals described as the most complex and least coherent, and with a need to strengthen coherence particularly within and between biodiversity and climate goals [https://openalex.org/W3134571733||ABSTRACT||000]. In addition, studies of circular economy and SDG implementation suggest that coherence depends on whether SDGs are treated as a homogeneous set and whether member states implement related policies consistently, while work on SDG 9 and SDG 11 shows that sector-specific goals remain central to sustainable development in the EU but are not in themselves direct evidence of coherence [https://openalex.org/W3209532954||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W4362550191||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W4312225363||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the evidence suggests that in the EU the SDGs function as a coordinating framework for policy coherence, but successful coherence requires better monitoring, stronger cross-policy alignment, attention to trade-offs, and explicit handling of political and institutional constraints [https://openalex.org/W4366975340||ABSTRACT||001; https://openalex.org/W3134571733||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W4308113945||ABSTRACT||000].

key_claims.claim: The SDGs are used in the EU as a framework for tracking sustainability across environmental, social, and economic dimensions, with policy coherence treated as a central challenge [https://openalex.org/W3134571733||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W4200315183||ABSTRACT||000].
key_claims.notes: The cited chunks explicitly say the SDGs provide a framework to track multiple dimensions of sustainability and that ensuring policy coherence across environmental, social and economic goals is a key challenge.

key_claims.notes: The chunk directly states that a 3D-mapping approach is proposed for aligning the CSRs, the SDGs, and the EGD, and that this supports reinforcing policy priorities.

key_claims.notes: The abstract states that LCA can strengthen and further enable EU policies toward achieving the SDGs while remaining within the physical limits of the planet, and that interlinkages depend on the LCA framework.

key_claims.notes: One chunk explicitly says technocratic understandings overlook political drivers such as vested interests and ideologies, and the other says coherence addresses inherently political incoherencies and can be limited by apolitical framing.

key_claims.notes: The cited abstract directly says environmental goals are the most complex and least coherent, and calls for better data availability plus strengthened monitoring of biodiversity and climate SDGs.

limitations_and_uncertainty: Several summaries focus on specific policy areas or tools, so the evidence does not provide a single comprehensive assessment of EU-wide SDG policy coherence across all goals and institutions.

Some findings are context-specific, such as the Dutch case or particular EU instruments, so their generalizability to the whole EU is limited [https://openalex.org/W4200315183||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W3194602120||ABSTRACT||001].

The evidence is uneven across SDGs: environmental goals are discussed as especially difficult, while SDG 9 and SDG 11 are presented mainly as sectoral implementation cases rather than direct tests of policy coherence [https://openalex.org/W3134571733||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W4362550191||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W4312225363||ABSTRACT||000].

The summaries do not provide quantitative results for most papers, so the strength of the reported relationships and the comparative effectiveness of different coherence mechanisms remain unclear [https://openalex.org/W4210270578||ABSTRACT||000; https://openalex.org/W3209532954||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How does the study use predictive analytics in the 1-hop work, and what does the 2-hop AI impact assessment say about AI"s role for sustainable development?
final_answer: Across the 1-hop papers, predictive analytics is used as part of AI methods for forecasting, optimization, and real-time or quantitative analysis in sustainability contexts such as climate change, biodiversity, resource management, cleaner production, and environmental risk prediction [https://openalex.org/W4401831154||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4392169541||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4412514975||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4402735735||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4396752219||ABSTRACT||000]. Several papers specifically link these predictive tools to improved monitoring, reduced waste, optimized agriculture or industrial processes, and support for climate and biodiversity goals [https://openalex.org/W4401831154||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4402735735||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4392169541||ABSTRACT||000]. The 2-hop impact assessments are broadly consistent in portraying AI as an important or transformative enabler of sustainable development, especially through data-driven insights, predictive modeling, optimization, and support for SDG implementation [https://openalex.org/W4401831154||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4392169541||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4412514975||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4405499395||ABSTRACT||001]. At the same time, the papers stress that AI’s sustainability benefits are conditional rather than automatic: supportive policy and infrastructure are needed, responsible governance and risk management are required, and ecological footprint, bias, privacy, and cost concerns must be addressed [https://openalex.org/W4401831154||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4414098400||ABSTRACT||000]. One paper goes further and argues AI should play a central role in the sustainability process, while another frames AI as potentially both enabling and inhibiting sustainability, showing some variation in emphasis rather than direct disagreement [https://openalex.org/W4412514975||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3135629427||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the shared conclusion is that AI can contribute to sustainable development across environmental, economic, and social dimensions, but its impact depends on careful integration and governance [https://openalex.org/W4402735735||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4414098400||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3135629427||ABSTRACT||000].

key_claims.claim: In the 1-hop work, predictive analytics is used for forecasting, optimization, and quantitative or real-time analysis in sustainability applications such as climate change, biodiversity, resource management, cleaner production, and environmental risk prediction [https://openalex.org/W4401831154||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4392169541||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4412514975||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4402735735||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4396752219||ABSTRACT||000]

query: How do the methods described for road transport sustainability and sustainable urban transport contribute to sustainable transportation systems, and what role do simulation, optimization, machine learning, and fuzzy sets play in designing and operating such systems?
final_answer: Across the papers, sustainable transportation systems are consistently framed as systems that must balance environmental, social, and economic goals rather than minimizing monetary cost alone, with particular emphasis on reducing emissions, congestion, and other transport externalities [https://openalex.org/W3126489268||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3160296158||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4386954171||ABSTRACT||002]. In road transport sustainability and sustainable urban transport, methods contribute by supporting analysis, planning, evaluation, policy-making, and operational decision-making for urban mobility and freight contexts [https://openalex.org/W3126489268||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3126404096||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W3142667272||ABSTRACT||000]. Several papers stress that better sustainability assessment and indicator frameworks are needed so decisions are more reliable, comparable, inclusive, and grounded in multiple sustainability dimensions [https://openalex.org/W3126404096||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4388202057||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3177488261||ABSTRACT||001]. Simulation, optimization, machine learning, and fuzzy sets are presented most clearly as tools for designing and efficiently operating sustainable transportation systems, including improving system design and operational performance [https://openalex.org/W3126489268||ABSTRACT||000]. Within this broader methodological toolkit, predictive modeling is described as helping planners, policymakers, and urban designers optimize traffic flow, reduce emissions, and take proactive measures to improve sustainability under a green innovation paradigm [https://openalex.org/W4390272563||ABSTRACT||001]. Fuzzy-set-based decision-making appears in the urban transport literature through Archimedean t-based operators and a MADM method that supports evaluation of sustainable urban transport strategies and public transport expansion decisions such as fare reduction [https://openalex.org/W4388440263||ABSTRACT||001]. More generally, system dynamics is characterized as a holistic and efficient method for analyzing transportation systems with dynamic complexity and policy resistance, especially for developing and implementing sustainable transport policies in urban contexts [https://openalex.org/W3160296158||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, the literature reviews show that many studies emphasize technical solutions, business models, and integrated planning instruments such as SUMPs and ITS, while behavioral aspects receive less attention [https://openalex.org/W4366773389||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W3142667272||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the evidence suggests these methods help not only diagnose sustainability problems but also support planning, evaluation, and continuous improvement of transport systems, though the exact role of simulation, optimization, machine learning, and fuzzy sets varies across studies and is not always specified in every excerpt [https://openalex.org/W3126489268||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4366773389||ABSTRACT||001].

query: How the Higher Education internationalization thing help sustainability in higher education institutions, and what the bibliometric analysis find about it from Scopus database?
final_answer: Across the summaries, internationalization in higher education is presented as a way to help sustainability by widening interaction between HEIs and their surroundings, expanding collaborative networks, and bringing global perspectives into teaching, learning, and research development [https://openalex.org/W4285797265||ABSTRACT||000]. It is also linked to mobilizing students and educators for partnerships, supporting SDG implementation, and affecting organizational culture, educational processes, and international cooperation activities [https://openalex.org/W3201485561||ABSTRACT||000]. More broadly, sustainability in higher education is described as a research niche that can deepen openness and interaction, while whole-institution and transformative approaches are said to be needed so universities can act as living labs, integrate SDGs across departments, and move beyond teaching alone [https://openalex.org/W4223628254||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3202265498||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4400413260||ABSTRACT||000]. Several papers agree that HEIs are important for sustainability and that their efforts need to be assessed, transformed, and supported by policies and tools for more effective implementation [https://openalex.org/W3212231498||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4400413260||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4392374449||ABSTRACT||000]. On the bibliometric side, Scopus-based studies show that research on higher education, sustainability, and internationalization has grown strongly over time, with one study identifying 4,410 Scopus publications on higher education and sustainability and another identifying 1,412 journal articles on higher education internationalization from 1974 to 2020 [https://openalex.org/W4223628254||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4285797265||ABSTRACT||000]. A separate Scopus-based review of education for sustainable development found 2,221 documents initially, screened to 1,013 eligible articles, with output rising especially since 2018 and peaking in 2022 [https://openalex.org/W4406778824||ABSTRACT||000]. These bibliometric studies consistently highlight leading countries, journals, and researchers, suggesting that the field is concentrated in a relatively small set of places and actors even as publication volume increases [https://openalex.org/W4406778824||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4223628254||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4285797265||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the evidence suggests that internationalization can support sustainability by strengthening collaboration, global engagement, and institutional change, but the bibliometric literature still mainly maps publication trends rather than proving which specific internationalization practices are most effective [https://openalex.org/W4285797265||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4400413260||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How does the theme of "Green Cluod Computing" connect the discussion of Green IoT with the systematic survey of energy-efficient techniques in sustainabl cloud computing, especially regarding why data centers and cloud technologies are being optimized for lower energy use and reduced environmental harm?
final_answer: The theme of “Green Cloud Computing” connects Green IoT and the systematic survey of energy-efficient techniques in sustainable cloud computing through a shared sustainability problem: expanding digital infrastructure is raising energy use and environmental harm, so cloud and data-center systems are being optimized to reduce both [https://openalex.org/W4280503421||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4385723923||ABSTRACT||000]. In the Green IoT framing, IoT’s own energy consumption, toxic pollution, and electrical waste create the need for green ICT, and Green Cloud Computing and Green Data Centers are explicitly described as enabling technologies for that response [https://openalex.org/W4280503421||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4280503421||ABSTRACT||001]. The survey paper on sustainable cloud computing similarly treats high energy use in cloud data centers as the reason to study energy-efficient techniques such as VM virtualization and consolidation, power-aware methods, bio-inspired methods, and thermal-management techniques [https://openalex.org/W4281251447||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4281251447||ABSTRACT||001]. Several papers agree that the basic motivation is environmental: data centers consume vast power, generate heat, increase cooling demands, and contribute to carbon emissions and other harms, including global warming and ozone layer depletion [https://openalex.org/W4385723923||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4281251447||ABSTRACT||000]. Other summaries add that green data centers are also linked to lower operational costs, compliance with environmental regulations, and a more sustainable digital future, showing that the push for efficiency is both environmental and operational [https://openalex.org/W4391045525||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4391566264||ABSTRACT||000]. The Green IoT review also ties the same logic to IoT devices and sensors: they support environmental monitoring and real-time data collection, while cloud technologies are improved by optimizing energy consumption and lowering carbon footprints [https://openalex.org/W4391917929||ABSTRACT||000]. Across the papers, there is broad agreement that cloud technologies and data centers must become more energy-efficient because the growth of connected devices is increasing cloud demand and making sustainability central to cloud design and management [https://openalex.org/W4385723923||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3172706057||ABSTRACT||000]. The main difference is emphasis: some papers focus on specific technical methods for cloud efficiency, while others frame green cloud computing more broadly as part of environmentally sustainable computing and regulatory compliance [https://openalex.org/W4281251447||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4391566264||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How do sustainable technologies, such as clean energy in manufacturing and green and reverse logistics, support Industry 4.0 innovation and SDG-based growth in industrial enterprises, and what did the analysis find about enterprise adoption and environmental management?
final_answer: Across the reviewed papers, sustainable technologies are consistently presented as enablers of Industry 4.0-driven innovation and SDG-aligned growth in industrial enterprises, especially when they are embedded in manufacturing and logistics systems [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4398200114||ABSTRACT||001]. One study specifically states that clean energy in manufacturing, green logistics, and reverse logistics create conditions for industrial development and future growth by supporting Industry 4.0 technologies and innovations in the context of the SDGs [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000]. Broader reviews similarly conclude that Industry 4.0 technologies support environmentally sustainable manufacturing by improving efficiency, lowering resource consumption, and enhancing environmental performance, while also linking these technologies to multiple SDGs and sustainability targets [https://openalex.org/W4226256571||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4389484631||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4398200114||ABSTRACT||001]. Several papers also emphasize that Industry 4.0 can reduce environmental impact, support social inclusion, and help organizations align innovation with sustainability goals through sustainable management and technology adoption [https://openalex.org/W4311719782||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4392974914||ABSTRACT||001]. In the Slovakia-based qualitative study of 105 enterprises, more than 82% reported implementing the SDGs and more than 70% preferred environmental aspects in business management, suggesting substantial enterprise-level openness to sustainability-oriented practices [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000]. That same study found a significant relationship between enterprise environmental management and sustainability in production and logistics, and it also confirmed a relationship between renewable energy technology use in the industrial sector and sustainability in logistics [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, the literature is not uniformly optimistic: one review notes that some Industry 4.0 technologies can have detrimental environmental effects through air pollution, improper waste disposal, and excessive consumption of raw materials, information, and energy [https://openalex.org/W4398200114||ABSTRACT||000]. Other studies also stress that sustainability-practices adoption remains limited in emerging economies and that further investigation is needed to fully understand Industry 4.0’s environmental dimensions [https://openalex.org/W3120619572||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4392974914||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the evidence suggests that sustainable technologies can support innovation, environmental management, and SDG-based growth, but their benefits depend on implementation quality and context, and the current literature still shows fragmentation and knowledge gaps [https://openalex.org/W3170613256||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4389484631||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How was ARDL used to test the nexus, and what long-run association did it reveal for human capital and renewable energy?
final_answer: Across the provided studies, ARDL was used as a time-series framework to test relationships among variables by first checking stationarity with the Augmented Dickey-Fuller test and then estimating the nexus in short- and long-run terms [https://openalex.org/W4313181844||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4315784444||ABSTRACT||000]. In one China-based study, the ARDL model was applied to test the nexus among human capital, renewable energy consumption, renewable energy production, carbon emissions, and sustainable development outcomes [https://openalex.org/W4313181844||ABSTRACT||000]. That study reported that human capital, renewable energy consumption, and renewable energy production were negatively associated with carbon emissions and positively associated with sustainable development goals, which is the closest long-run-type result available in the evidence set for the human capital–renewable energy nexus [https://openalex.org/W4313181844||ABSTRACT||000]. However, the evidence does not provide a separate explicit long-run coefficient or dedicated long-run estimate for the relationship between human capital and renewable energy itself [https://openalex.org/W4313181844||ABSTRACT||000]. A separate Pakistan study used novel dynamic ARDL simulations and found that GDP and institutional quality had positive short- and long-run effects on energy consumption, while technological innovation had a long-term positive influence, showing that ARDL was also used more broadly to assess long-run dynamics in energy-related systems [https://openalex.org/W4315629505||ABSTRACT||000]. Other papers in the set used ARDL or ARDL-type approaches to test related nexuses, but they did not report human capital–renewable energy results, so they do not resolve the specific association asked about [https://openalex.org/W4315784444||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4388450586||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the evidence supports that ARDL was used to examine nexus relationships and long-run effects, but it does not yield a clean, standalone long-run estimate specifically linking human capital with renewable energy [https://openalex.org/W4313181844||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4312213521||ABSTRACT||000].

query: In the context of Sustainable Consumption, what did the systematic review conclude about the concept’s complexity, its relationship to the circular economy, and the role of government in supporting sustainable consumption?
final_answer: The systematic review literature portrays sustainable consumption as a complex and nebulous concept, with theoretical fragmentation that creates both breadth and overlapping ideas rather than a single settled definition [https://openalex.org/W4381591906||ABSTRACT||000]. Across the reviews, sustainable consumption is also treated as closely connected to the circular economy, but not reducible to it: several papers describe the consumer–circular economy link as important yet difficult, and others stress that circularity alone does not guarantee social, economic, or environmental sustainability [https://openalex.org/W4381591906||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3120864615||ABSTRACT||000]. This means the relationship is often framed as promising but contingent, requiring critical reflection on strengths, shortcomings, and theoretical flaws rather than simple enthusiasm for circular solutions [https://openalex.org/W3132132623||ABSTRACT||000]. The reviews also suggest that the concept is methodologically challenging, because existing indicators and assessment methods are incomplete and may miss important dimensions of sustainability impacts [https://openalex.org/W3120864615||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3163949760||ABSTRACT||001]. On government’s role, the literature consistently emphasizes that public authorities matter: one review explicitly highlights the importance, role, and tools of government in sustainable consumption, while another says that policy guidance and public support are needed so collaborative consumption can deliver sustainable outcomes rather than becoming a missed opportunity [https://openalex.org/W4381591906||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4289130621||ABSTRACT||001]. A broader review likewise places governments among the key actors needed to support the transition from linear to circular models [https://openalex.org/W4409544928||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the evidence converges on three points: sustainable consumption is conceptually contested, it is linked to but not synonymous with the circular economy, and government action is seen as necessary to make the transition effective [https://openalex.org/W4381591906||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3120864615||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4289130621||ABSTRACT||001].

query: What clinical and laboratory findings are associated with elevated FSH in men with non-obstructive azoospermia and chromosomal anomalies, and how do KS and testicular XX DSD compare with the undefined cause group?
final_answer: In men with non-obstructive azoospermia and chromosomal anomalies, elevated FSH is associated with a more severe testicular and hormonal phenotype, including lower average testicular volume, shorter penile length, lower total testosterone, higher height and arm span, and higher LH; gynecomastia is also reported more frequently in Klinefelter syndrome (KS) and was absent in the undefined-cause group [pmc_PMC10065101||ABSTRACT||000][pmc_PMC10065101||ABSTRACT||001]. The same study reports that testicular XX DSD shows LH, FSH, and penile length values intermediate between KS and the undefined-cause group, with testicular volume similar to KS and other data similar to the undefined group [pmc_PMC10065101||ABSTRACT||001]. This suggests KS is the more severe end of the spectrum, while testicular XX DSD has a mixed phenotype that falls between KS and undefined causes [pmc_PMC10065101||ABSTRACT||001]. The authors conclude that clinical and laboratory data can help differentiate men with chromosomal anomalies, especially KS and testicular XX, from men with undefined causes [pmc_PMC10065101||ABSTRACT||001]. Separately, in a broader NOA cohort, elevated FSH and LH were associated with failed sperm retrieval, whereas larger testicular volume and a higher testosterone-to-LH ratio were associated with successful retrieval, and multivariate analysis found FSH level and bilateral testicular volume were significantly associated with sperm extraction success [pmc_PMC10307674||ABSTRACT||000][pmc_PMC10307674||ABSTRACT||001]. However, the provided summaries do not give detailed laboratory or clinical comparisons for other chromosomal-anomaly subgroups beyond KS and testicular XX DSD, and they do not provide direct comparative data on sperm retrieval outcomes for KS versus testicular XX DSD versus undefined-cause groups [pmc_PMC10307663||ABSTRACT||000][pmc_PMC10307663||ABSTRACT||001].

query: How do Sustainable Catalytric Technologies support global resource securty and sustainability?
final_answer: Sustainable catalytic technologies support global resource security and sustainability by enabling cleaner production pathways, reducing dependence on finite fossil resources, and improving how energy and materials are produced and used [https://openalex.org/W4323925755||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4397002662||ABSTRACT||000]. Across the papers, catalysis is repeatedly framed as central to addressing climate change, pollution, sustainable energy, and the manufacture of the products that underpin welfare and sustainability [https://openalex.org/W3136963614||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W3214828424||ABSTRACT||000]. One major pathway is the conversion of renewable electricity and distributed energy into solar fuels and commodity chemicals, which the literature says can support the water-energy-food nexus and multiple end-use sectors while preserving human wellbeing [https://openalex.org/W4323925755||ABSTRACT||000]. Another pathway is circularity: catalytic systems can transform sustainable waste resources and biomass into fuels, biofuels, and high-value products, thereby increasing biorefinery sustainability and shifting industry away from a linear fossil-based model [https://openalex.org/W4397002662||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4377108088||ABSTRACT||001]. Several papers also emphasize design strategies that make catalysis itself more sustainable, including green chemistry and engineering principles, earth-abundant catalyst design, and methodological best practices to overcome catalyst scarcity [https://openalex.org/W3156019499||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4401191227||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W3214828424||ABSTRACT||000]. The evidence further suggests that these technologies matter not only for immediate sustainability gains but also for long-term systems change, helping accelerate progress toward post-2030, 2050, and 2100 targets [https://openalex.org/W4284690057||ABSTRACT||000]. However, the papers also caution that wide adoption depends on technical, economic, societal, and planetary stewardship considerations, and that quantitative sustainability metrics, techno-economic analysis, and environmental assessment are needed to verify real-world benefits [https://openalex.org/W4323925755||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W3156019499||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4377108088||ABSTRACT||001].

query: In the sustainability assessment of district heating systems, which multi-criteria decision analysis methods were compared, and what did the sensitivity analysis reveal about their suitability and differences in calculation and interpretation?
final_answer: In the district-heating sustainability assessment paper, five MCDA methods were compared: WSM, TOPSIS, PROMETHEE, ELECTRE, and DEA, using 8 criteria across 12 district heating companies [https://openalex.org/W4220986058||ABSTRACT||000]. The sensitivity analysis tested robustness by changing criterion weights in three ways: varying them individually to find stability ranges for alternatives, varying them individually by a fixed value to examine effects on average scores, and comparing AHP-derived weights with equal weights [https://openalex.org/W4220986058||ABSTRACT||000]. The paper reports that, together with a literature review, the sensitivity analysis showed all five methods are suitable for sustainability analysis of district heating systems [https://openalex.org/W4220986058||ABSTRACT||000]. It also found that the methods differ in their calculation procedures and in how their results are interpreted, even though they are all considered applicable for this task [https://openalex.org/W4220986058||ABSTRACT||000]. Broader review evidence aligns with this by indicating that MCDM methods are the preferred evaluation approach in district heating sustainability frameworks and that AHP is the most frequently used method among them, although that review does not report a comparable method-by-method sensitivity analysis [https://openalex.org/W4315708900||ABSTRACT||001]. Other reviewed papers discuss sustainability assessment with multi-criteria methods or indicator prioritization, but they do not add specific comparisons of MCDA methods for district heating or further sensitivity-analysis findings on calculation and interpretation differences [https://openalex.org/W4311545548||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3204246278||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4367856736||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4206600484||ABSTRACT||001].

query: Based on the review of "sustainable innovations," what factors are said to encourage or block farmers" adoption of these innovations, and how do environmental values, in contrast with complexity, innovation aversion, and low perceived control, shape this adoption behavior?
final_answer: Across the reviewed papers, farmers’ adoption of sustainable innovations is described as being encouraged by a mix of innovation characteristics, producer and farm characteristics, and broader institutional or market supports [https://openalex.org/W4385875829||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4210468156||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4383033841||ABSTRACT||002]. The review on sustainable innovations specifically says adoption is fostered by certain innovation characteristics and by individual psychological and socio-demographic features, while another review adds that producer demographics, land tenure, labor and credit availability, and beliefs about what it means to be a “good farmer” shape attitudes, norms, and perceived capacity to adopt [https://openalex.org/W4385875829||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4210468156||ABSTRACT||000]. Additional encouraging factors mentioned include self-efficacy, perceived production risks, social-environmental altruism, communication and networking, use of other conservation practices, diversity of cash crops, livestock operations, farming size, and participation in demonstration trials [https://openalex.org/W4387228452||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W3174938154||ABSTRACT||001]. Policy incentives, improved access to credit and resources, stronger research and extension services, and consumer demand for sustainably produced food are also described as mechanisms that can motivate adoption through institutional and market channels [https://openalex.org/W4383033841||ABSTRACT||002]. In contrast, the clearest barriers identified in the sustainable-innovation review are complexity of the innovation, high innovation aversion, and low perceived control over the innovation [https://openalex.org/W4385875829||ABSTRACT||000]. The evidence also suggests that adoption is easier when practices fit producers’ beliefs and capabilities, and harder when they do not [https://openalex.org/W4210468156||ABSTRACT||000]. Environmental values appear to encourage adoption: the review notes that organic farmers are characterized by a stronger environmental view and by placing less weight on economic gains, and another paper links environmental motivation to social-environmental altruism as an adoption factor [https://openalex.org/W4385875829||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4387228452||ABSTRACT||001]. By contrast, complexity, innovation aversion, and low perceived control are framed as blocking adoption because they reduce perceived capability and willingness to adopt, but the provided summaries do not give a direct head-to-head comparison or quantify their relative importance [https://openalex.org/W4385875829||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4210468156||ABSTRACT||000]. More broadly, multiple reviews emphasize that adoption is multidimensional and heterogeneous, and that explanations are limited when studies focus too narrowly on farmer-level variables or borrow constructs from other contexts [https://openalex.org/W4387228452||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3118303193||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4309605934||ABSTRACT||001].

query: What did the interviews with retailers and service providers in North America reveal about managing product returns sustainably?
final_answer: The interviews with North American retailers and service providers found that sustainability in product returns was constrained by several practical barriers in the reverse e-commerce supply chain, including the need to encourage reverse-e-commerce producers to compete and the lack of governmental support for sustainable supply chain solutions [https://openalex.org/W4317888257||ABSTRACT||001]. The broader interview study also indicated that retailers were chiefly focused on the financial impact of returns and had limited awareness of the environmental scale of those returns [https://openalex.org/W4322500966||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4322500966||ABSTRACT||001]. In addition, these retailers lacked a comprehensive approach to reducing the environmental impact of returns, suggesting that sustainability was not yet integrated into returns decision-making [https://openalex.org/W4322500966||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4322500966||ABSTRACT||001]. Across these studies, the common message is that sustainable returns management requires first identifying the barriers that prevent environmental planning and then implementing strategies to reduce the impact of returns [https://openalex.org/W4322500966||ABSTRACT||001]. The interviews therefore point less to a mature sustainability system than to an area where awareness, incentives, and policy support are still weak [https://openalex.org/W4322500966||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4317888257||ABSTRACT||001]. The evidence also suggests that resale and second-hand channels can support more sustainable product use by giving products a “second life,” but the provided material does not connect that channel development directly to the North American interview findings [https://openalex.org/W4205116137||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How is the public sector related to corporate governance, and what did the study say was stopping sustainable procurement in the Nigerian public construction sector?
final_answer: The papers suggest that the public sector is linked to corporate governance through its role in supporting sustainability, with one study explicitly stating that corporate governance is important in the public sector and is related to the sustainability of modern organisations [https://openalex.org/W10420025||ABSTRACT||000]. Another study on public sector organisations found that sustainable procurement implementation is supported by institutional isomorphism and sustainable leadership, with coercive and mimetic forces positively influencing leadership and procurement practices [https://openalex.org/W4386268572||ABSTRACT||000]. This is consistent with the broader public-sector framing in the literature, where prior work had already examined barriers to sustainable procurement in the public sector and treated the public sector as a key setting for sustainability implementation [https://openalex.org/W3162983557||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3138706393||ABSTRACT||000]. In the Nigerian public construction sector, sustainable procurement was hindered by grouped barriers of attitude and poor fiscal incentive, financial restrictions, insufficient leadership and knowledge, and regulatory constraints [https://openalex.org/W4308695771||ABSTRACT||000]. The study further specified major barriers as lack of government commitment, poor economic conditions, lack of knowledge, and the absence of a sustainable procurement regulatory framework in Nigeria [https://openalex.org/W4308695771||ABSTRACT||001]. It also reported that tenders were usually awarded to the lowest bidder, with little attention to contractors’ sustainability commitment [https://openalex.org/W4308695771||ABSTRACT||000]. query: How can the Paris Agreement be used in makin�27 healthcare or manufacturing teams push more sustainable practices, and what do the three I's say about why policy coherence with it can be helped or hindered?
final_answer: The Paris Agreement can be used as a policy reference point to push healthcare teams toward more sustainable practices by linking climate action with health promotion, decarbonisation, and cleaner public policy [https://openalex.org/W3166839458||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3128473151||ABSTRACT||002]. In the healthcare context, the evidence says health-system decarbonisation should be paired with reducing disease burden, and Health in All Policies is intended to support systematic, intersectoral policymaking that minimizes environmental impacts on population health [https://openalex.org/W3128473151||ABSTRACT||002]. The Paris Agreement is also described as a broader international agenda that can shape the ambition and importance given to goals and actors, which can help make sustainability a priority for organizational teams [https://openalex.org/W4308113945||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4308113945||ABSTRACT||001]. For manufacturing, the evidence is less direct, but related papers say sustainable practices are advanced by implementing safer and more sustainable production methods, and by using policy frameworks to align priorities with sustainability ambitions [https://openalex.org/W4312064827||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W3194602120||ABSTRACT||001]. The three I’s are ideas, institutions, and interests, and they help or hinder policy coherence with the Paris Agreement because they shape policy options, the ambition attached to agendas, and whose ideas and interests are served by coherence or non-coherence [https://openalex.org/W4308113945||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4308113945||ABSTRACT||001]. The evidence also says vested interests and ideologies may either encourage or obstruct coherence, so the three I’s are not automatically enabling; they can work in both directions depending on the political and institutional context [https://openalex.org/W4308113945||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4308113945||ABSTRACT||001]. More generally, the Paris Agreement is framed as a government-level signal for reducing emissions and reaching net zero by 2050, but the papers caution that fossil-fuel benefits, risk handling by governments and companies, and the fact that emissions are “everyone’s long-term problem” but “nobody’s short-term problem” create major barriers to change [https://openalex.org/W4313495531||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, one paper suggests that a clean energy transition could yield health-sector benefits that outweigh costs, which provides a practical incentive for teams to adopt more sustainable practices when policy coherence is in place [https://openalex.org/W3128473151||ABSTRACT||002].

query: How does the review link green nanotechnology with environmental remediation in agro-ecosystems, and why does it say biogenic nanoparticles matter for this?
final_answer: The reviews collectively link green nanotechnology with environmental remediation in agro-ecosystems by portraying nanomaterials as tools for sustainable agricultural technologies that also serve remediation roles, such as pollution abatement, water treatment, crop protection, and management of soil quality and moisture [https://openalex.org/W4324149138||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4403849839||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4225104982||ABSTRACT||000]. Several reviews also describe green nanotechnology as an eco-friendly approach that can reduce adverse environmental impacts, improve input efficiency, decrease losses, and support food security and sustainable farming [https://openalex.org/W4380075578||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4390194078||ABSTRACT||000]. In this framing, nanomaterials are not just agricultural inputs but “nano-remediators” or remediation-supporting tools that help with tasks like monitoring metal and organic toxins, managing pathogens and diseases, and enabling cleaner agricultural practices [https://openalex.org/W4324149138||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4225104982||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4390194078||ABSTRACT||000]. The review also broadens this idea by saying green nanotechnology should be integrated with conventional remediation techniques, advanced engineering tools, and real-time monitoring to support environmental restoration and pollution management in agro-ecosystems [https://openalex.org/W4410647264||ABSTRACT||001]. Biogenic nanoparticles matter because multiple reviews contrast them with conventional physical and chemical nanoparticle production, which is repeatedly described as economically unsustainable, ecologically harmful, or detrimental to the ecosystem [https://openalex.org/W4324149138||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4380075578||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4390194078||ABSTRACT||000]. By comparison, nanoparticles produced from plants, bacteria, fungi, or microorganisms are presented as sustainable, economical, biocompatible, eco-friendly, high-purity, and cost-effective alternatives that better fit the sustainability goals of agro-ecosystem remediation [https://openalex.org/W4324149138||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4390194078||ABSTRACT||000]. Some reviews further emphasize their functional value in agriculture, including targeted nutrient delivery, nanofertilizers, reduced pesticide use, and antifungal disease control [https://openalex.org/W4380075578||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4390194078||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4402449485||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, the literature is cautious: one review notes unresolved challenges such as scalability, control over nanoparticle properties, variability in biological sources, toxicity assessment, and regulatory concerns [https://openalex.org/W4410647264||ABSTRACT||001]. Another review warns that no single eco-friendly nanocompound is fully sustainable, implying that multiple routes and careful environmental evaluation are still needed [https://openalex.org/W4225104982||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How does the EU Taxonomy relate to global greenhouse gas emissions, and what does the labour force participation study say about reducing those emissions in developing countries?
final_answer: The EU Taxonomy is presented as a standardized classification system for sustainable economic activities that covers activities responsible for up to 80% of EU greenhouse gas emissions, and it is intended to channel investment toward low-carbon technologies [https://openalex.org/W4200364028||ABSTRACT||000]. The same evidence also warns that the Taxonomy’s impact depends on how strict its technical thresholds are, because current thresholds may be too weak to drive climate neutrality in emission-intensive sectors [https://openalex.org/W4200364028||ABSTRACT||000]. More broadly, the paper summaries show that global greenhouse gas emissions remain a major problem and are still rising overall, even though some countries have achieved sustained reductions through sectoral change and shifts toward green energy [https://openalex.org/W3215792940||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3128252787||ABSTRACT||000]. The labour force participation study adds that labour market dynamics affect global GHG emissions, with labour force participation generally improving environmental quality across 173 countries from 1996–2020 [https://openalex.org/W4387873299||ABSTRACT||000]. Its disaggregated results are mixed: male labour-force participation is described as environment-degrading, while female labour-force participation is environmental-augmenting [https://openalex.org/W4387873299||ABSTRACT||000]. For the specific question of reducing emissions in developing countries, the study reports that rising labour force participation significantly reduces GHG emissions in developing countries, while its effect is insignificant in developed economies [https://openalex.org/W4387873299||ABSTRACT||000]. It also finds reductions in low-income and high-income countries but environment-degrading effects in upper-middle-income countries, suggesting that the emission impact of labour participation varies by development level [https://openalex.org/W4387873299||ABSTRACT||000]. Taken together, the evidence suggests the EU Taxonomy is a policy instrument aimed at steering investment toward the sectors most linked to emissions, whereas the labour-force study points to labour participation as a potential emissions-reduction pathway specifically in developing countries [https://openalex.org/W4200364028||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4387873299||ABSTRACT||000].

query: In the context of OSC, what does the systematic review say about its environmental performance, its market penetration by 2018, and why is it considered timely to identify the factors that advanced and enhanced its environmental performance in developed and developing regions?
final_answer: The systematic review indicates that OSC has been proven to improve environmental outcomes, including reducing waste generation and carbon emissions [https://openalex.org/W4321507223||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4321507223||ABSTRACT||001]. It also reports that by 2018 no major market had exceeded 20% OSC penetration, even though OSC’s benefits were already recognized [https://openalex.org/W4321507223||ABSTRACT||000]. The review frames it as timely to identify the factors that advanced and enhanced OSC’s environmental performance because it sees a novel opportunity to compare developed and developing economies, understand their differences and similarities, identify critical success factors and future opportunities, and guide stakeholders toward greater adoption and improved environmental performance [https://openalex.org/W4321507223||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4321507223||ABSTRACT||001]. The broader evidence base also supports the idea that sustainability outcomes are context dependent: one review found positive sustainability indicator results on average, but with a substantial share of cases showing no difference or negative outcomes, and it noted that environmental outcomes must be measured appropriately [https://openalex.org/W3129330537||ABSTRACT||001]. That same review found no significant differences among sustainability pillars in the average share of positive and negative results, suggesting that environmental performance claims should be interpreted cautiously rather than assumed to be uniform across settings [https://openalex.org/W3129330537||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the evidence points to OSC as environmentally beneficial but still underpenetrated by 2018, making comparative analysis across developed and developing regions especially relevant for explaining how stronger performance can be achieved and scaled [https://openalex.org/W4321507223||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4321507223||ABSTRACT||001].

query: How did the study use Affective commitment in the framework, and what results it give about workplace spirituality, responsible leadership, and pro-environmental behavior in Pakistan SMEs?
final_answer: In the Pakistan SMEs study, Affective commitment (AC) was used as a mediating mechanism within a single unified framework linking workplace spirituality (WPS), responsible leadership (RL), and pro-environmental behavior (PEB). [https://openalex.org/W4385633441||ABSTRACT||000] The study analyzed survey data from 390 employees using structural equation modeling (SEM). [https://openalex.org/W4385633441||ABSTRACT||000] Its main finding was that workplace spirituality, responsible leadership, and pro-environmental behavior were all significantly and positively related in Pakistan’s SMEs. [https://openalex.org/W4385633441||ABSTRACT||000] The results also supported the mediating role of AC, indicating that WPS and RL can encourage PEB through affective commitment. [https://openalex.org/W4385633441||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4385633441||ABSTRACT||001] This aligns with other Pakistan-based studies showing that positive organizational or leadership-related practices can enhance pro-environmental outcomes, including micro-level CSR improving employee pro-environmental behavior and responsible leadership having a partial mediating link with pro-environmental conduct. [https://openalex.org/W3133017979||ABSTRACT||001][https://openalex.org/W4367316216||ABSTRACT||001] However, the broader SME evidence base in the provided summaries is mixed and limited, because one qualitative CSR study in Pakistani SMEs focused on social, economic, and environmental CSR without addressing AC, WPS, RL, or PEB, and found that environmental CSR was non-existent in small enterprises. [https://openalex.org/W3127159552||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W3127159552||ABSTRACT||001] Overall, the available evidence suggests AC functions as an important bridge between employee-centered leadership/spirituality and environmentally friendly behavior in Pakistan SMEs, but the conclusion rests on one SEM-based survey study rather than multiple directly comparable SME studies. [https://openalex.org/W4385633441||ABSTRACT||000]

query: How do digital tools in environmental education foster sustainability awareness among learners?
final_answer: Across the papers, digital tools in environmental education are consistently portrayed as supports for sustainability awareness because they make learning more engaging, connected to real sustainability goals, and more likely to influence attitudes and behavior [https://openalex.org/W4396495518||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4313362444||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4361975213||ABSTRACT||000]. A review of 21 articles found that digital tools in environmental education promote environmental learning gains and increase students’ concern for the sustainability of the planet, with virtual reality and climate change emerging as especially prominent topics [https://openalex.org/W4396495518||ABSTRACT||000]. More broadly, ICT in education is described as reshaping teaching and learning in ways that can support sustainable development and the SDGs, suggesting that digital learning fosters awareness by linking classroom activity to wider sustainability objectives [https://openalex.org/W4313362444||ABSTRACT||000]. Several summaries also emphasize that sustainability education works best when it is transformative and practice-oriented, giving learners knowledge, skills, values, critical thinking, and opportunities for social engagement rather than relying on lecturing alone [https://openalex.org/W4361975213||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4210723178||ABSTRACT||001]. In that sense, digital tools appear most effective when they help learners understand local environmental conditions, participate in solving local issues, and become active agents of change inside and outside school settings [https://openalex.org/W4399175475||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4311849879||ABSTRACT||001]. The papers also suggest that integrating digital technologies can strengthen sustainable digital learning in higher education, but this requires conceptual frameworks, teacher training, curriculum development, and innovative resources to organize practice effectively [https://openalex.org/W4361222029||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4361975213||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, the evidence notes barriers such as resistance to change, insufficient funding, and lack of awareness, and one paper explicitly cautions that digital learning itself raises sustainability concerns and needs further conceptual clarification [https://openalex.org/W4361975213||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4361222029||ABSTRACT||000].

query: What screening criteria and classification rules were used to select and categorize the 87 life cycle assessment studies?
final_answer: The clearest description of how the 87 life cycle assessment studies were selected comes from the review that searched Scopus for 2017–2023 publications using the keywords “Sustainability assessment” OR “Life cycle assessment” AND “Internal combustion engine*” OR “ICE*,” followed by careful screening before inclusion [https://openalex.org/W4393374431||ABSTRACT||001]. That paper does not give detailed inclusion or exclusion rules beyond the keyword search and screening step [https://openalex.org/W4393374431||ABSTRACT||001]. The same review then categorized the included studies across six dimensions: sustainability indicators, life cycle phases, life cycle inventories, ICE technologies (including alternative fuels), types of mobile sources, and powertrain systems [https://openalex.org/W4393374431||ABSTRACT||001]. Another review used the PRISMA protocol and an evaluation matrix, stating that papers were classified using “several integrated criteria” after database searching, but it does not provide the full screening rules for the 87 studies in question [https://openalex.org/W3130637975||ABSTRACT||000]. In that paper, the explicit categorization reported that 52 of 84 case studies used stand-alone LCA, 8 used LCC combined with other analyses, and none used S-LCA, while the studies were also distinguished by common indicators such as global warming potential, eutrophication, human toxicity, and ecotoxicity [https://openalex.org/W3130637975||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3130637975||ABSTRACT||001]. A broader review limited to peer-reviewed journal articles and using wide keyword searches for life cycle methods and quantitative methods also shows that screening strategies can be defined by database search terms and publication-type limits, but it identified 144 articles rather than 87 and does not explain the categorization of the 87-study set [https://openalex.org/W4403910234||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4403910234||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the evidence suggests the 87-study review relied on a targeted keyword search plus manual screening, then organized studies by methodological and system-level descriptors, but the exact inclusion/exclusion thresholds are not fully disclosed in the summaries provided [https://openalex.org/W4393374431||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W3130637975||ABSTRACT||000].

final_answer: The available summaries indicate that the DECISION phase III study was described as a multicenter, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial in patients with locally advanced/metastatic RAI-refractory differentiated thyroid cancer, designed to test whether sorafenib improves progression-free survival (PFS) [pmc_PMC3164634||ABSTRACT||001]. The primary endpoint was PFS, and secondary endpoints included overall survival, time to disease progression, disease control rate, response rate, duration of response, safety, and pharmacokinetic analysis [pmc_PMC3164634||ABSTRACT||001]. However, the summaries show inconsistent trial identifiers across records: one ClinicalTrials.gov record is given as NCT00984282 for DECISION [pmc_PMC3164634||ABSTRACT||001], while other summaries cite different registration numbers for different studies or records, including NCT02709408, NCT03976804, NCT05386225, DRKS00022563, and NL9261 [pmc_PMC5387979||ABSTRACT||002] [pmc_PMC9806070||ABSTRACT||002] [pmc_PMC9806091||ABSTRACT||001] [pmc_PMC9806046||ABSTRACT||001] [pmc_PMC10387733||ABSTRACT||001]. query: Why nano-enhancers better for workpiece burn?
final_answer: Nano-enhancers appear to be better for workpiece burn in machining mainly because they improve heat removal and lubrication compared with traditional cutting fluids [https://openalex.org/W4313508734||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4206313494||ABSTRACT||000]. In titanium alloy grinding, the literature specifically notes that nano-enhancers with high thermal conductivity help address the workpiece “burn puzzle,” and that high hardness and spherical characteristics are also favorable for reducing burn and improving grinding performance [https://openalex.org/W4313508734||ABSTRACT||001]. A broader review of nano-enhanced biolubricants similarly says they improve tool wear and surface integrity through advanced lubrication and heat-transfer mechanisms, with performance depending on film formation, atomization, infiltration, concentration, and dispersion [https://openalex.org/W4206313494||ABSTRACT||000]. The papers therefore agree that the main advantage is not simply that the additives are nanoscale, but that their physical and tribological properties make cooling and lubrication more effective under machining conditions that tend to cause burn [https://openalex.org/W4313508734||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4206313494||ABSTRACT||000]. One paper also contrasts traditional cutting fluids with biolubricants and nano-enhancers, stating that the latter are more effective because of improved lubrication and cooling performance [https://openalex.org/W4313508734||ABSTRACT||001]. However, the evidence is still limited because it is largely review-level and does not provide direct comparative burn-rate data or detailed mechanisms for all machining contexts [https://openalex.org/W4206313494||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4313508734||ABSTRACT||001]. Some supplied papers are unrelated to machining burn and therefore do not add support for this question [https://openalex.org/W4322505914||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4324057306||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How do carbon dots compare with inorganic quantum dots as optical nanomaterials, and what sustainability issues are highlighted in the review?
final_answer: Across the reviewed papers, carbon dots/carbon quantum dots are consistently presented as promising optical nanomaterials because they combine attractive optical behavior with low toxicity, biocompatibility, water solubility, and low cost or cost-effectiveness [https://openalex.org/W4378391047||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4401798421||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4406866034||ABSTRACT||000]. Several reviews further emphasize that these materials are being explored for sensing, bioimaging, optoelectronics, photocatalysis, environmental monitoring, biomedical uses, and packaging-related applications [https://openalex.org/W4378391047||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4387573993||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4403909528||ABSTRACT||000]. In contrast, the provided evidence does not offer a direct head-to-head performance comparison with inorganic quantum dots; instead, one review explicitly frames carbon dots as a possible “functional and sustainable alternative” to incumbent optical nanomaterials, notably inorganic quantum dots, while others simply highlight their own advantages without direct comparison [https://openalex.org/W4400778971||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4387573993||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4313550231||ABSTRACT||000]. Where sustainability is discussed, the dominant themes are green or environmentally friendly synthesis, use of biomass, food waste, natural sources, or other renewable feedstocks, and reduced reliance on toxic, precious, or critical raw materials [https://openalex.org/W4318483232||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4406866034||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4400778971||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4387573993||ABSTRACT||000]. The review literature also highlights sustainability concerns in the production chain itself, including solvent use, energy use, material efficiency, safety, waste management, and the need for quantitative reporting of inputs and byproducts [https://openalex.org/W4400778971||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, limitations recur across the papers: low quantum yield, reproducibility problems, heterogeneity, scalability challenges, and the need for better standardization and property control [https://openalex.org/W4403909528||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4401798421||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the reviews converge on carbon dots as a more sustainable and versatile class of optical nanomaterials, but the evidence supplied is largely qualitative and does not support a definitive direct comparison with inorganic quantum dots [https://openalex.org/W4400778971||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4324142846||ABSTRACT||000].
