query: How mask mandates help Covid-19 cases, and what did the study find?
final_answer: Across the relevant studies, mask mandates and mask use were generally associated with fewer COVID-19 cases or lower infection risk, though the strength of evidence varied by setting and study design [pmc_PMC9663388||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC9729715||ABSTRACT||001] [pmc_PMC9190185||ABSTRACT||000]. In a US state-level analysis from March to November 2020, mask mandates were estimated to offset about one third of the increase in case growth associated with higher mobility, and a hypothetical national mandate on May 15, 2020 was projected to reduce total US infections by 23.7% to 30.4% by November 15, 2020 [pmc_PMC9663388||ABSTRACT||000]. That same study found mask mandates were more effective in states with higher compliance, suggesting mandates work better when people actually follow them [pmc_PMC9663388||ABSTRACT||000]. A separate study found that keeping prevention measures in place for at least two months was linked to lower COVID-19 incidence, with face mask mandates showing larger reductions in monthly incidence in counties with higher social vulnerability than in counties with lower social vulnerability [pmc_PMC9729715||ABSTRACT||001]. Evidence from a rapid review and meta-analysis in healthcare workers also found that wearing face masks, especially N95 masks, significantly protected against infection, although gloves and gowns did not show an effect and some PPE components had unclear benefits [pmc_PMC9190185||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC9190185||ABSTRACT||001]. Another review emphasized that surgical masks provided better protection than cloth masks, reinforcing the idea that mask type matters [pmc_PMC9845060||ABSTRACT||001]. One modeling study added that masks can be counterproductive if poorly paired with ventilation, but the best strategy was combining a face mask with upward ventilation, which could reduce indoor infectious concentration by nearly 99.95% compared with no precautions [pmc_PMC9803700||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the studies suggest mask mandates help reduce cases most when compliance is high, duration is sustained, and masks are used properly alongside other measures such as ventilation [pmc_PMC9663388||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC9729715||ABSTRACT||001] [pmc_PMC9803700||ABSTRACT||001].

query: What role did hexagonal boron nitride play in the study of canola oil as a bio-lubricant, and what details are provided about its evaluation?
final_answer: Hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) played the role of a solid lubricant nano-additive in canola oil in the one study that actually evaluated this specific system, because canola oil alone was described as having weaker tribological performance than petroleum-based oils [https://openalex.org/W4200600140||ABSTRACT||000]. The study tested hBN loadings of 0.5, 1.0, and 1.5 wt.% in canola oil [https://openalex.org/W4200600140||ABSTRACT||000]. Its evaluation was done in a boundary lubrication regime using pin-on-disk tests, with coefficient of friction (COF) and wear as the measured outcomes [https://openalex.org/W4200600140||ABSTRACT||001]. Among the tested concentrations, 1.0 wt.% hBN produced the lowest COF, which was 40% lower than the base oil [https://openalex.org/W4200600140||ABSTRACT||001]. The same study reported that comparing hBN with graphene nanoplatelet additives and then combining them into mixed nano-lubricants created a positive synergy, reducing friction by 56% and wear by 90% versus base oil [https://openalex.org/W4200600140||ABSTRACT||001]. These improvements were attributed to a composite protective film and polishing mechanisms [https://openalex.org/W4200600140||ABSTRACT||001]. By contrast, the other provided papers are reviews that mention hBN or plant-based lubricants in general but do not provide canola-oil-specific experimental evaluation details [https://openalex.org/W4390658388||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4386898801||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4401870224||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How is the SDG Index used to measur progres toward the SDGs at local and regional level in Romania, and what did the results show?
final_answer: The clearest evidence shows that in Romania the SDG Index was used as a composite measure of progress toward the SDGs at the local and regional level by calculating it through an integrated approach based on 90 indicators, which were stored and processed in a PostgreSQL object-relational database [https://openalex.org/W3135800278||ABSTRACT||000]. This approach was designed to compare territorial performance and identify spatial patterns of sustainable development across the country [https://openalex.org/W3135800278||ABSTRACT||000]. The results indicated that the highest sustainable development performances were concentrated in specific geographical areas, rather than being evenly distributed [https://openalex.org/W3135800278||ABSTRACT||000]. In contrast, rural areas and extended peripheral regions in eastern and southern Romania performed the worst, showing clear territorial disparities in SDG progress [https://openalex.org/W3135800278||ABSTRACT||000]. Other papers in the set do not provide Romania-specific local or regional SDG Index results, but they do support the broader idea that regional SDG monitoring requires robust indicator sets, adaptive benchmarking, and data infrastructure [https://openalex.org/W4399724167||ABSTRACT||001]. One related framework study also suggests that structured indicator-selection methods can reduce bias and improve the scientific basis of SDG assessment, which is consistent with the Romanian study’s use of an integrated multi-indicator index [https://openalex.org/W4389430761||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the available evidence points to the SDG Index as a practical territorial benchmarking tool in Romania, but the observed pattern was one of concentrated high performance and weaker outcomes in rural and peripheral east-southern areas [https://openalex.org/W3135800278||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How do thermal pwer plants relate to the environmental issues described in the survey on energy-efficient techniques in sustainable cloud computing?
final_answer: Across the surveyed papers, the environmental issues in sustainable cloud computing are consistently framed around the large energy demand of data centres, the resulting carbon emissions, and heat-related cooling burdens [https://openalex.org/W4385723923||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4385490509||ABSTRACT||000]. One paper makes the relationship to thermal power plants explicit by stating that the electricity used by cloud data centres is mainly generated by thermal power plants, and that these plants, because they rely on fossil fuels like coal and oil, contribute to global warming, ozone layer depletion, and premature deaths [https://openalex.org/W4281251447||ABSTRACT||000]. Other papers do not directly mention thermal power plants, but they still connect the same environmental problem to the broader electricity supply and emphasize reducing energy use and carbon footprint through energy-efficient cloud techniques [https://openalex.org/W4385723923||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4385723923||ABSTRACT||001]. The common mitigation strategies across the surveys include innovative or effective cooling, virtualization and consolidation, energy management and monitoring, low-power electronics, automation, and advanced cooling technologies such as cold plates and immersion cooling [https://openalex.org/W3172706057||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4385490509||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4410019315||ABSTRACT||000]. Some papers also broaden sustainability beyond carbon emissions to include water use and electronic waste, showing that the environmental issues are multidimensional rather than limited to electricity alone [https://openalex.org/W4385490509||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, thermal power plants appear in the literature mainly as an upstream source of the electricity whose consumption by cloud infrastructure drives environmental harm, rather than as a direct focus of the cloud techniques themselves [https://openalex.org/W4281251447||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4385723923||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, one paper presents cloud computing itself as potentially beneficial for sustainability through energy efficiency and renewable energy integration, indicating that the literature is not entirely one-sided and also considers cloud systems as part of the solution [https://openalex.org/W4366762583||ABSTRACT||000].

query: In hepatocellular carcinoma, what was found about macrophage migration inhibitory factor, and how did its knockdown affect tumor cell behavior and related protein expression?
final_answer: In the provided HCC evidence, macrophage migration inhibitory factor (MIF) was reported to be significantly upregulated in HCC tissues and cell lines compared with adjacent normal tissues or a normal liver cell line, and its expression positively correlated with cyclin D1 expression and tumor size [pmc_PMC4170598||ABSTRACT||000]. siRNA-mediated MIF knockdown inhibited proliferation of PLC and HepG2 cells, promoted apoptosis, and reduced tumor growth in an in vivo xenograft model, while not affecting the cell cycle [pmc_PMC4170598||ABSTRACT||000]. The knockdown also altered apoptosis- and signaling-related proteins, with Bcl-2, p-caspase-3, BIM, and Bax upregulated and cyclin D1, p-Akt, and p-ERK downregulated [pmc_PMC4170598||ABSTRACT||000]. These findings suggest that MIF supports HCC cell growth and survival and is linked to proliferative signaling through cyclin D1, Akt, and ERK pathways [pmc_PMC4170598||ABSTRACT||000]. The other provided paper summaries do not contribute additional evidence about MIF in HCC, as they explicitly state that MIF was not mentioned or that there was insufficient evidence to address it [pmc_PMC3162940||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC4169566||ABSTRACT||001] [pmc_PMC4176125||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC10140795||ABSTRACT||001] [pmc_PMC9194659||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC10063289||ABSTRACT||001] [pmc_PMC9890137||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC3166084||ABSTRACT||001].

query: How did the learning curve for DIEP breast reconstruction change over time in this study?
final_answer: In this study, the DIEP breast reconstruction learning curve improved over time, but the pattern differed by level of analysis. At the institutional level, the late cases had a shorter length of hospital stay than the early cases for both single and double DIEP reconstructions, suggesting some overall improvement as experience accumulated [pmc_PMC10140818||ABSTRACT||000]. However, the study found no other statistically significant differences between the beginning and end of the study period at the center level, so the broader learning-curve gains were limited [pmc_PMC10140818||ABSTRACT||000]. At the single-surgeon level, the learning curve was more pronounced, with a significant reduction in total surgery time over time, indicating improved operative efficiency [pmc_PMC10140818||ABSTRACT||000]. The evidence provided for other papers does not add DIEP-specific learning-curve data, and some summaries explicitly state that they do not describe a DIEP learning curve over time [pmc_PMC10364779||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC10364508||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the clearest time-related improvement in this study was shorter hospital stay institutionally and faster total surgery time for the surgeon, rather than widespread changes across multiple outcomes [pmc_PMC10140818||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How are coronary artery calcifications associated with complications?
final_answer: Coronary artery calcifications are associated with several adverse outcomes across different clinical settings, but the strength and meaning of that association varies by study and population. In population-based studies, coronary artery calcium (CAC) is associated with future atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease independent of conventional risk factors, and it can improve risk prediction when added to a model such as the Framingham risk score [pmc_PMC5383538||ABSTRACT||000]. In symptomatic patients referred for cardiac CT, higher CAC scores had prognostic value for all-cause mortality over a median 4.4-year follow-up, and absolute CAC scores performed at least as well as sex-, age-, and race/ethnicity-specific MESA percentiles for mortality prediction [pmc_PMC9806039||ABSTRACT||000]. In trauma patients, left main coronary artery calcification was independently associated with any in-hospital complication, and a greater number of calcified coronary arteries showed a trend toward more complications and was significantly associated with an adverse discharge condition [pmc_PMC10229702||ABSTRACT||001]. The complications in that trauma cohort were commonly pneumonia or delirium, suggesting that calcification may mark broader vulnerability during acute illness rather than only cardiac-specific events [pmc_PMC10229702||ABSTRACT||001]. At the same time, the evidence base has important gaps: one review notes that no clinical trial has shown whether CAC screening improves clinical outcomes or healthcare costs, and that similar CAC levels may correspond to different absolute ASCVD risks across regions and ethnic groups [pmc_PMC5383538||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the papers support CAC as a marker of higher complication or mortality risk, but they also show that prognostic performance and clinical implications depend on setting, population, and how calcification is measured [pmc_PMC9806039||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC10229702||ABSTRACT||001] [pmc_PMC5383538||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How does the combined detecion of KAI1 and VEGF improve the diagnosis of HCC?
final_answer: Combined detection of KAI1 and VEGF appears to improve HCC diagnosis by complementing the information each marker provides individually. In the cited HCC study, serum KAI1 was downregulated while VEGF was upregulated, and each marker was associated with disease-related features such as TNM stage and metastasis for KAI1, and α-fetoprotein level for VEGF [pmc_PMC4164248||ABSTRACT||000]. The diagnostic performance of KAI1 alone was strong, with an AUC of 0.907, while VEGF alone had a lower AUC of 0.779 [pmc_PMC4164248||ABSTRACT||001]. When the two were combined, sensitivity increased from 86.96% to 91.86%, accuracy increased from 83.06% to 84.68%, and negative predictive value reached 78.79% [pmc_PMC4164248||ABSTRACT||001]. query: How does global public health get threat from microplastics in fishmeal?
final_answer: The strongest evidence suggests that microplastics in fishmeal threaten public health mainly by entering aquaculture and livestock feed, then moving into cultured fish and potentially into the human food supply [https://openalex.org/W4282929872||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4388496957||ABSTRACT||000]. One review states that microplastics are already abundant in marine environments, accumulate in fish that are turned into fishmeal, and can then interact with pond ecosystems and cultured fish when contaminated fishmeal is used in feed [https://openalex.org/W4282929872||ABSTRACT||000]. That same review says microplastics may alter cultured fish physiology and behavior, can accumulate in edible parts, and may cause severe physiological disorders in fish consumers, framing human exposure from cultured fish as a significant threat to global public health [https://openalex.org/W4282929872||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4282929872||ABSTRACT||001]. A Bangladesh study supports the exposure pathway by finding commercial fish feeds were 100% contaminated with microplastics, with mean abundance of 500 to 2200 MPs/kg, and it presents this as a major concern for sustainable aquaculture and a potential public health issue through fish consumed from aquaculture systems [https://openalex.org/W4388496957||ABSTRACT||000]. More generally, microplastics are described as persistent environmental pollutants that can carry hazardous chemicals such as persistent organic pollutants on their surfaces, making them a route for harmful contaminants in the food chain with serious consequences for human health [https://openalex.org/W4408578227||ABSTRACT||000]. Other papers reinforce the broader environmental and food-chain concern, noting that microplastics disrupt food chains, create public health challenges for seafood consumers, and are considered a worldwide aquatic pollution issue, but they do not directly establish a fishmeal-specific pathway [https://openalex.org/W4295412833||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4311705688||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the papers agree that the public-health threat is indirect but plausible: contamination of feed or fishmeal can transfer microplastics into farmed fish and seafood, increasing human exposure [https://openalex.org/W4282929872||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4388496957||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4408578227||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How did broiler chicks in Iraq compare in maternal derived antibodies against Newcastle disease vaccination, and which strain performed better in the study?
final_answer: In the Iraq study, 1-day-old imported Cobb 500 and Ross 308 broiler chicks were compared for maternal derived antibodies against Newcastle disease vaccination using blood samples from 28 Ross 308 flocks and 17 Cobb 500 flocks [pmc_PMC9805781||ABSTRACT||000]. Both strains showed high and uniform maternal antibody titers, indicating that both had strong passive immunity at hatch [pmc_PMC9805781||ABSTRACT||000]. However, Cobb 500 performed better overall than Ross 308 across the measured antibody-related outcomes [pmc_PMC9805781||ABSTRACT||000]. Specifically, Cobb 500 had higher positivity (100% vs 97.78%), a higher mean maternal antibody titer (9,871.47 vs 8,647.76), a lower mean CV (12.41% vs 15.18%), and a higher mean vaccination index (966.59 vs 821.60) [pmc_PMC9805781||ABSTRACT||000]. The study concluded that Cobb 500 produced chicks with higher protective titers than Ross 308 [pmc_PMC9805781||ABSTRACT||001]. Taken together, the evidence suggests that while both broiler strains had strong maternal antibody levels, Cobb 500 was the superior strain in this study [pmc_PMC9805781||ABSTRACT||000][pmc_PMC9805781||ABSTRACT||001].

query: What link between the consumer and the Circular economy is denoted in the context, and what is said about it?
final_answer: Across the summaries, the consumer is linked to the circular economy mainly through consumer behaviour, engagement in circular economy practices, and broader resource-use decisions in a finite world [https://openalex.org/W4211051495||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4396622004||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4378472586||ABSTRACT||000]. In one context, the consumer-circular economy relationship is explicitly identified as an area of review, and the circular economy is described as an emerging issue with limited theoretical and empirical research until recently [https://openalex.org/W4211051495||ABSTRACT||000]. Another summary states more directly that the link is consumer engagement in circular economy practices, and argues that policymakers should use specific policies and incentives to strengthen that engagement [https://openalex.org/W4396622004||ABSTRACT||001]. The same paper adds that progress depends on integrating pro-environmental behaviour, digital transformation, and incentives, while noting that the food industry faces implementation challenges that call for targeted initiatives [https://openalex.org/W4396622004||ABSTRACT||001]. More broadly, the circular economy is framed as a resource-related concept for sustainable development and as one of the pragmatic approaches to sustainability, while also being intertwined with industrial ecology, industrial symbiosis, and sustainable development [https://openalex.org/W3137694958||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3137694958||ABSTRACT||001]. A related context places the consumer within a finite and limited world of scarce resources, emphasizing that restocking is not possible infinitely and that circular economy thinking fits that constraint [https://openalex.org/W4378472586||ABSTRACT||000]. Other summaries show that the circular economy is also operationalized through material efficiency, product life extension, smart production and use, and business models such as resource recovery, sharing platforms, product as a service, and circular suppliers [https://openalex.org/W4282921144||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the papers agree that the consumer’s role is tied to participation in and support for circular practices, but they differ in emphasis: some stress behaviour and policy incentives, while others frame the connection more indirectly through sustainability transitions and resource limits [https://openalex.org/W4396622004||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4409544928||ABSTRACT||001].

query: How do PAs create public value in sustainability reporting?
final_answer: Across the papers, public value in sustainability reporting is created when reporting makes organizations more accountable, transparent, and responsive to stakeholders, while also helping them advance sustainability goals. In the public-sector and port-authority studies, PAs create public value by preserving and disseminating public value, obtaining legitimacy and stakeholder support, and building operational capacity, with hybrid reporting approaches used as a means to deliver sustainability and public value [https://openalex.org/W4320719832||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3121263816||ABSTRACT||000]. Several papers converge on the idea that stakeholder accountability is central: materiality determination is framed as primarily serving stakeholder accountability rather than valuation or stewardship, and sustainability reporting is also described as managing stakeholder impressions [https://openalex.org/W4289767614||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4390267129||ABSTRACT||001]. Other studies emphasize that public value comes from higher-quality reporting that improves transparency, comparability, clarity, accuracy, and reliability, thereby providing a clearer view of economic, social, and environmental impacts and supporting continuous performance improvement [https://openalex.org/W4402984150||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4313418383||ABSTRACT||001]. The literature also links public value creation to integrated or hybrid frameworks: one paper describes sustainability reporting as a joint project between firms and stakeholders that promotes integrated thinking and a roadmap using the SDG Compass logic model, while another says public-sector actors hybridize integrated reporting and SDGs to deliver sustainability and public value [https://openalex.org/W4297090192||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W3121263816||ABSTRACT||000]. More broadly, sustainability reporting is portrayed as part of public-value agendas tied to the UN Sustainable Development Goals, voluntary frameworks such as GRI and <IR>, and the evolution toward mandatory non-financial reporting [https://openalex.org/W3134875937||ABSTRACT||002] [https://openalex.org/W3147261195||ABSTRACT||000]. However, the evidence also suggests that the field is still developing, with public-sector research described as early-stage and reporting quality in some settings still limited or uneven, which means public value depends not just on reporting’s existence but on how well materiality, disclosure quality, and stakeholder engagement are handled [https://openalex.org/W3147261195||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4313418383||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4289767614||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How do sustainable technologies and environmantal management relate in the context of Industry 4.0 and SDGs, and what did the study find about enterprises preference for environmental aspects in business management?
final_answer: Across the papers, sustainable technologies and environmental management are consistently presented as mutually reinforcing within Industry 4.0 and SDG-oriented development [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4398200114||ABSTRACT||000]. Several studies describe clean energy in manufacturing, green and reverse logistics, renewable energy, and other Industry 4.0 applications as conditions that support industry development, future growth, and a more sustainable environment when aligned with the SDGs [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4226256571||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4389484631||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, the literature also frames environmental management as essential because these technologies can improve environmental performance, but they can also create harms such as air pollution, improper waste disposal, and excessive use of raw materials, information, and energy [https://openalex.org/W4398200114||ABSTRACT||000]. This means the relationship is not purely positive: environmental sustainability depends on how Industry 4.0 technologies are implemented and managed [https://openalex.org/W4398200114||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4311719782||ABSTRACT||000]. The review evidence further suggests that Industry 4.0 can reduce resource consumption and improve manufacturing efficiency, while broader synthesis work says researchers, policymakers, and practitioners should collaborate to integrate advanced technologies with sustainable practices and assess their environmental dimensions [https://openalex.org/W4226256571||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4392974914||ABSTRACT||001]. query: How the sustainability assessment and evaluation frameworks in the district heating and PT evaluation studies are linked, and which method was most used, plus how do they relate to CO2 emissions reduction in the urban transport example?
final_answer: Across the district heating and related sustainability studies, evaluation frameworks are consistently framed as indicator-based systems that assess environmental, economic, and social dimensions, sometimes expanded to technical, institutional, smartness, or flexibility criteria. In district heating and renewable-energy contexts, one paper explicitly organizes sustainability assessment around five indicator groups—social, economic, environmental, technical, and institutional—while another uses a three-phase framework of identification, refinement, and prioritisation to build indicators that holistically evaluate heating technologies and stakeholder preferences [https://openalex.org/W3208788408||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4367856736||ABSTRACT||000]. A broader district-scale sustainability paper also emphasizes a holistic methodology for Sustainable Plus Energy Neighbourhoods, including GHG emissions, life cycle costs, and social sustainability, showing that these frameworks are designed to connect multiple performance dimensions rather than single-issue metrics [https://openalex.org/W3185590208||ABSTRACT||000]. Methodologically, the district heating review says literature review, MCDM techniques, LCA, PCA, and statistical methods are all widely used, but it does not single out one best method, whereas another district heating MCDA study compares WSM, TOPSIS, PROMETHEE, ELECTRE, and DEA and concludes all are suitable despite differing calculations [https://openalex.org/W3208788408||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4220986058||ABSTRACT||000]. For public transport evaluation, however, the evidence is clearer: Multi-Criteria Decision-Making is the preferred framework type, Assessment Indicator Models are next, and the most frequently used MCDM method is the Analytical Hierarchy Process [https://openalex.org/W4315708900||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4315708900||ABSTRACT||001]. The link between these evaluation frameworks and CO2 reduction is made through environmental indicators: one district-heating/RE summary states that CO2 emission and GHG emission reduction are key environmental measures, and the neighborhood framework also includes GHG emissions as a performance indicator [https://openalex.org/W3208788408||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W3185590208||ABSTRACT||000]. In contrast, the PT review evidence provided does not itself report a CO2-emissions-reduction result for an urban transport example, so the CO2 connection is supported only at the level of indicator inclusion rather than demonstrated outcomes [https://openalex.org/W4315708900||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the studies agree that sustainability assessment is best treated as a multi-criteria, indicator-based decision framework, but they differ in the specific methods emphasized and in how explicitly they connect the framework to emissions-reduction results [https://openalex.org/W4377861392||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4362558773||ABSTRACT||001].

query: How do innovation, CEOs' sustainability orientation, and green governance relate to sustainability and environmental performance in firms?
final_answer: Across the papers, innovation is generally linked positively to sustainability-related outcomes, especially when it is green or sustainability-oriented: green innovation is reported to have significant positive relationships with environmental sustainability and innovation climate in industrial firms, and innovation climate mediates that link [https://openalex.org/W4388684227||ABSTRACT||000]. In another study, sustainability-oriented innovations are strengthened by dynamic capabilities, sustainable organizational innovations, and smart technologies, and they have a strong positive impact on firms’ economic performance [https://openalex.org/W4367603834||ABSTRACT||000]. However, the evidence is not uniformly positive for every sustainability dimension, because one study finds green innovation capabilities indirectly influence the effect of social and economic sustainability on firm performance but not the effect of environmental sustainability on firm performance [https://openalex.org/W3200508375||ABSTRACT||001]. Governance also matters: a configurational study finds six sufficient governance configurations leading to high environmental innovation in dirty firms, and concludes that both powerful and weak CEOs can support environmental innovation when paired with appropriate board and ownership structures [https://openalex.org/W4282035384||ABSTRACT||000]. More directly on governance quality, genuine sustainability strategy implementation improves firm performance and is associated with favorable environmental results, while dispersed ownership and board independence are described as pivotal conditions [https://openalex.org/W4404618052||ABSTRACT||000]. Leadership-oriented evidence points in the same direction, as green transformational leadership positively influences green performance through green organizational culture and green engagement [https://openalex.org/W4401652574||ABSTRACT||000]. By contrast, the provided summaries do not offer direct evidence on CEOs’ sustainability orientation specifically, and several papers explicitly note that they do not address that construct [https://openalex.org/W4367603834||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4401652574||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4282035384||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the synthesis suggests that innovation and green governance are usually beneficial for sustainability or environmental outcomes, but the strength and pathway of effects depend on mediators, moderators, sector, and governance configuration [https://openalex.org/W4388684227||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4404618052||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4282035384||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How do the themes of "Environmental sustainability", "Sustainability implementation barriers", and "Sustainable residential buildings" connect when comparing off-site construction research with the barrier analysis in Ghana and the "Mostadam" approach in Saudi Arabia, and what sustainability-related findings are highlighted across these contexts?
final_answer: Across the supplied studies, the three themes connect through a shared emphasis on making buildings and construction more environmentally sustainable while also confronting practical obstacles to implementation [https://openalex.org/W3168941981||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4310036329||ABSTRACT||001]. In the Ghanaian literature, sustainability is treated both as measurable environmental performance across the project life cycle—through water quality, air quality, energy use and conservation, and environmental compliance—and as a set of implementation barriers that must be overcome in residential buildings [https://openalex.org/W3168941981||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4310036329||ABSTRACT||000]. The Ghana residential-building study identifies management, standards, society, and knowledge barriers, with management-related barriers described as the most significant obstacle, and it argues that policy action can save costs while improving the environmental ecosystem and social cohesion [https://openalex.org/W4310036329||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4310036329||ABSTRACT||001]. The separate Ghana retrofit study similarly groups barriers into cultural, economic, technical knowledge, and regulatory categories, showing that sustainability implementation is constrained by human behavior, cost, skills, and legislation/policy [https://openalex.org/W4293340752||ABSTRACT||001]. In Saudi Arabia, the Mostadam discussion frames sustainable residential buildings as a pathway to sustainable cities and comprehensive sustainable development under Vision 2030, and it highlights categories of sustainable residential buildings plus strategies and future policies for transformation [https://openalex.org/W3120903819||ABSTRACT||001]. Off-site construction and prefabricated housing research align with this sustainability direction by showing that innovative prefabricated construction methods and sustainable design techniques can improve sustainability performance, affordability, and lifecycle outcomes in housing [https://openalex.org/W4386401188||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4385389240||ABSTRACT||001]. The broader pattern across contexts is that sustainability is not presented as a single technical fix but as a combination of environmental metrics, material and design innovation, and institutional or behavioral enablers needed for adoption [https://openalex.org/W3168941981||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4385389240||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4293340752||ABSTRACT||001]. A key contrast is that the Ghana papers focus on barriers and policy/management constraints, whereas the Saudi Mostadam paper emphasizes a strategic framework and policy pathway toward sustainable residential development [https://openalex.org/W4310036329||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W3120903819||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the sustainability-related findings highlighted across these contexts are that environmental sustainability can be measured and improved through life-cycle and performance indicators, while sustainable residential buildings are most feasible when supported by management capacity, regulations, knowledge, and appropriate construction innovations [https://openalex.org/W3168941981||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4386401188||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4385389240||ABSTRACT||001].

query: How can healthcare workers balanc innovation with sustainability when reducing workplace emissions and avoid the wasteful use of medical resources in imaging and other care, while still keepin AI benefits responsible?
final_answer: Healthcare workers can balance innovation with sustainability by treating emission reduction, resource stewardship, and responsible AI use as linked goals rather than competing priorities. In healthcare AI, sustainability is described as depending on health, justice, and resource conservation, not carbon calculations alone, and ethical reflection must include AI’s environmental impact because health care emits significant carbon and AI can worsen it if used carelessly [https://openalex.org/W4220793133||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4220793133||ABSTRACT||001]. Across radiology and nuclear medicine, AI is portrayed as a “double-edged sword”: it can improve diagnostic accuracy, workflow efficiency, and resource allocation, but it also brings energy use, carbon emissions, hardware waste, and other risks, so innovation should be paired with explicit efforts to reduce AI-related emissions and avoid wasteful use of medical resources [https://openalex.org/W4409540874||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4392191303||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4394008899||ABSTRACT||001]. The radiology literature also suggests practical sustainability gains from reducing low-value imaging and improving energy efficiency, which aligns with the broader healthcare AI review’s emphasis on optimizing workflows, reducing resource waste, and supporting telemedicine [https://openalex.org/W4409540874||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4399973910||ABSTRACT||001]. However, the interventional radiology study shows that awareness alone is not enough: although sustainability awareness was high, actual action remained limited because sustainability was not prioritized and change could not be made by a single department or hospital [https://openalex.org/W4327898048||ABSTRACT||000]. This points to the need for organizational and policy support, not just individual effort, and the healthcare AI review explicitly recommends policy and governance frameworks, global initiatives, and collaborative efforts [https://openalex.org/W4399973910||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4327898048||ABSTRACT||000]. To keep AI benefits responsible, the literature recommends eco-design, lifecycle assessment, responsible data management, continuous monitoring, and strategies at individual, institutional, and collective levels so that environmental preservation, economic sustainability, and social equity are addressed together [https://openalex.org/W4399973910||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4409540874||ABSTRACT||001]. More generally, the evidence suggests AI should be used where it adds real value—such as extending services to underserved areas or filling provider gaps—while remaining cautious about bias, dangerous recommendations, implementation costs, and other harms [https://openalex.org/W4220793133||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4409540874||ABSTRACT||000].

final_answer: The text links economic sustainability to space tourism by saying that most authors are optimistic about its economic sustainability, but it simultaneously emphasizes that high launch costs and the “tyranny of the rocket equation” keep the economic burden high and preserve associated environmental costs [https://openalex.org/W4315646741||ABSTRACT||003] [https://openalex.org/W4315646741||ABSTRACT||002]. In the broader sustainable tourism context, the literature is described as focusing mainly on economic and environmental sustainability, while social aspects receive less attention [https://openalex.org/W4315646741||ABSTRACT||014]. This suggests that decoupling consumption from economic growth is not presented as a solved issue here; instead, the text highlights that sustainability indicators for space tourism are still unclear and not clearly defined, which limits any firm claim that growth and consumption can be separated sustainably [https://openalex.org/W4315646741||ABSTRACT||014] [https://openalex.org/W4315646741||ABSTRACT||003]. For making space tourism environmentally sustainable, the article suggests that one must first critically assess whether space tourism can be sustainable and ethical at all, and identify the preconditions under which that might be possible [https://openalex.org/W4315646741||ABSTRACT||002]. It also calls for a robust, theoretically grounded analytical framework and space-tourism-specific sustainability indicators to evaluate environmental sustainability more clearly [https://openalex.org/W4315646741||ABSTRACT||003]. Overall, the evidence points to optimism about economic viability but substantial unresolved uncertainty about whether environmental sustainability can be achieved in practice [https://openalex.org/W4315646741||ABSTRACT||003] [https://openalex.org/W4315646741||ABSTRACT||002].

query: How do regional integration and multistakeholder partnerships support Sustainable Development Goal 8 in the Yangtze River Delta?
final_answer: The evidence suggests that regional integration and multistakeholder coordination can support SDG 8 in the Yangtze River Delta mainly by improving cross-scale planning, aligning actors, and balancing economic and environmental goals [https://openalex.org/W3185034769||ABSTRACT||001][https://openalex.org/W3194996912||ABSTRACT||000]. In the YRD, one study finds that sustainability improved overall from 2000 to 2015, but progress was uneven: socio-economic sustainability rose in most counties while environmental sustainability declined, implying that SDG 8-oriented development should be integrated with environmental safeguards [https://openalex.org/W3194996912||ABSTRACT||000]. Another paper frames the Yangtze River Delta as a subnational region where sustainable development should be studied through regional integrated development, regional social-ecological systems, and integrated-region assessment, and it calls for applicable governance structures and institutions [https://openalex.org/W4320729134||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4320729134||ABSTRACT||001]. This implies that regional integration supports SDG implementation by providing the governance and analytical infrastructure needed to coordinate development across sectors, scales, and regions [https://openalex.org/W4205386374||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4205386374||ABSTRACT||001]. Multistakeholder partnerships are presented in the broader SDG literature as complementary to state-led governance, with growing inclusion of non-state actors and a role in addressing cross-cutting goals [https://openalex.org/W4380882019||ABSTRACT||000]. However, the broader MSP literature also warns that such partnerships can suffer from limited effectiveness and legitimacy deficits, so their contribution depends on better accountability and institutional design [https://openalex.org/W4400486548||ABSTRACT||000]. In this sense, the strongest supported answer is that regional integration in the YRD helps create the spatial and institutional basis for coordination, while MSPs help assemble the actors needed to pursue SDG 8-related trade-offs and synergies across the region [https://openalex.org/W3185034769||ABSTRACT||001][https://openalex.org/W4205386374||ABSTRACT||001].

query: How do environmental sustainability reporting practices in Bahrain\"s large industrial sector relate to environmental management and Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), and what evidence from the Industry 4.0 study shows similar links between SDGs, environmental aspects, and renewable energy technologies in industrial enterprises?
final_answer: In Bahrain’s large industrial sector, sustainability reporting is described as using materiality matrices to identify and prioritize significant sustainability issues, with the goal of improving future reporting and environmental performance [https://openalex.org/W4200252599||ABSTRACT||000]. The Bahrain study says that firms using materiality analysis benefit from better monitoring and measuring of environmental performance and from implementing SDGs, indicating a direct connection between reporting practices, environmental management, and SDG alignment [https://openalex.org/W4200252599||ABSTRACT||000]. It also reports that a materiality matrix can improve report content by incorporating stakeholders’ views, which in turn improves the quality of environmental sustainability reporting and supports environmental performance improvements [https://openalex.org/W4200252599||ABSTRACT||000]. More generally, other studies in the set reinforce the idea that SDG-oriented reporting is used to assess corporate contributions to the SDGs, as shown in the metals industry where reporting revealed stronger attention to some goals than others and variation by subindustry [https://openalex.org/W3217154997||ABSTRACT||000]. The oil and gas study similarly finds SDG reporting relevant in corporate reporting and shows that company size, geography, internationalization, and economic performance influence how much firms use such reporting [https://openalex.org/W4286447895||ABSTRACT||000]. For the Industry 4.0 evidence, the studies show parallel links between sustainability, SDGs, and industrial transformation: one review states that Industry 4.0 technologies and circular economy practices are linked to sustainable operations and to SDGs 6, 7, 9, 12, and 13, and that these linkages can help organizations realign management practices toward those goals [https://openalex.org/W4210290448||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4210290448||ABSTRACT||001]. Another Industry 4.0 review adds that widespread adoption of Industry 4.0 technologies enhances sustainability performance and addresses environmental concerns, while also mapping SDGs to specific technologies, design principles, and enablers in industrial contexts [https://openalex.org/W4389484631||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4389484631||ABSTRACT||001]. Related evidence from a sustainability model study also shows that SDG mapping can increase environmental and sustainability performance and support a systematic sustainability transition in manufacturing [https://openalex.org/W3157489939||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the evidence converges on the view that both sustainability reporting and Industry 4.0 frameworks function as management tools that connect organizational practices to SDGs and environmental performance, although the specific Bahrain findings are grounded in materiality-based reporting rather than technology adoption [https://openalex.org/W4200252599||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4210290448||ABSTRACT||000].

query: In the context of Environmental sustainability reporting and Sustainability reporting, how do the Bahrain industrial companies" materiality matrices relate to improved environmental performance, and how does this compare with the UK evidence on whether reporting that follows guidelines and a business-case approach actually improves sustainability performance?
final_answer: The Bahrain industrial-company evidence suggests that materiality matrices are used as a practical tool for monitoring and measuring environmental performance, because they help companies identify and prioritize the most significant sustainability issues for future reporting and improved environmental performance [https://openalex.org/W4200252599||ABSTRACT||000]. It also indicates that materiality analysis can strengthen report content by incorporating stakeholders’ views, thereby improving the quality of sustainability reports [https://openalex.org/W4200252599||ABSTRACT||001]. A related Bahrain summary further links stronger materiality assessment disclosure with better sustainability reporting quality, and says that disclosure scores are positively influenced by higher financial performance, lower leverage, and better corporate governance [https://openalex.org/W3134875937||ABSTRACT||001]. However, that Bahrain evidence emphasizes reporting quality and disclosure rather than a directly measured environmental performance outcome, so the environmental-performance benefit is implied more than demonstrated in the supplied chunks [https://openalex.org/W3134875937||ABSTRACT||001]. By contrast, the UK evidence states that sustainability reports framed around living within planetary limits and harmony with nature are likely to improve sustainability performance [https://openalex.org/W4220852241||ABSTRACT||000]. The same UK evidence says that reporting that follows guidelines and uses a business-case, business-centred approach negatively affects sustainability performance, which is the opposite of the hoped-for effect [https://openalex.org/W4220852241||ABSTRACT||000]. Taken together, the supplied evidence points to a difference between Bahrain’s emphasis on materiality matrices as a way to improve reporting quality and environmental management, and the UK finding that guideline-compliant, business-case reporting does not necessarily improve sustainability performance and may be associated with worse performance [https://openalex.org/W4200252599||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4220852241||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How doeas sustainable marketing relate to enviromental sustainability in shaping a company"s image, and what kinds of consumption changes are described as ways to advance sufficiency transitions?
final_answer: Across the papers, sustainable marketing is generally presented as a way for firms to align their market activities with environmental sustainability while also strengthening how they are perceived by consumers and the market [https://openalex.org/W4392716256||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4396847081||ABSTRACT||001]. One paper says green/sustainable marketing demonstrates commitment to sustainability, gives competitive advantage, favors the company’s image, and positions the organization as socio-environmentally responsible [https://openalex.org/W4392716256||ABSTRACT||001]. Another adds that sustainable marketing can build stronger relationships with environmentally conscious consumers by adapting to their preferences and values, supporting long-term success and positive change in the market [https://openalex.org/W4396847081||ABSTRACT||001]. Several papers also link sustainable marketing to environmental sustainability through pro-sustainable behavior, sustainable consumption patterns, and broader sustainability frameworks that orient marketing toward sustainability and sufficiency [https://openalex.org/W4400608740||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3126349936||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, one paper warns that profit-centric firms may greenwash by inauthentically mimicking sustain-centric practices, suggesting that sustainable marketing can help shape image but also damage credibility when it is not genuine [https://openalex.org/W4379928390||ABSTRACT||000]. The literature also shows tension between growth-oriented approaches and more radical alternatives: one paper describes a dominant profit-centric triple bottom line approach, while another argues for a sustain-centric or degrowth framework because current sustainability debates contain contradictions when growth is reconciled with sustainability [https://openalex.org/W4379928390||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4282834253||ABSTRACT||000]. On sufficiency transitions, the evidence consistently mentions sustainable consumption, pro-sustainable behaviour, sustainability, and sufficiency as desired directions, but most summaries do not specify concrete consumption shifts beyond these broad terms [https://openalex.org/W3126349936||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4400608740||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4282834253||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How sustainability reporting link with SDGs and sustainability performance, it matter from the supply chain framework too?
final_answer: Across the papers, sustainability reporting is consistently presented as a way to connect business activity with the SDGs and to assess sustainability performance, but the strength of that connection varies by context and method. Several studies report a positive linkage: sustainability reporting can be monitored with reference to the SDGs to help investors and stakeholders assess firms’ sustainable performance [https://openalex.org/W4392003298||ABSTRACT||001], and integrated reporting is framed as a corporate strategy for achieving SDGs while evaluating implementation with shared metrics [https://openalex.org/W4362609606||ABSTRACT||000]. Other work also finds that sustainability reporting is linked to performance improvement, including through environmental performance measurement, SDG implementation, and materiality matrices that incorporate stakeholder views [https://openalex.org/W4200252599||ABSTRACT||001]. From a supply chain perspective, the evidence suggests this matters a lot: a sustainable supply chain is positively associated with financial performance and with SDGs, and the study explicitly argues that SMEs should implement sustainability from supplier to customer [https://openalex.org/W4394886303||ABSTRACT||001]. A supply-chain sustainability assessment framework built from GRI indicators similarly aims to measure both firms’ and suppliers’ performance and improve transparency and accountability in global supply chains [https://openalex.org/W4400657024||ABSTRACT||000]. However, not all evidence is aligned: one study finds no correlation in reporting specific SDGs and a disconnection between corporate sustainability performance and SDG reporting, suggesting companies may report SDGs arbitrarily rather than based on actual performance [https://openalex.org/W4394576889||ABSTRACT||000]. This is echoed by another study showing that companies may cite SDGs in reports without explaining how sustainability initiatives translate into an actual contribution [https://openalex.org/W4220859323||ABSTRACT||000]. The literature therefore supports the idea that sustainability reporting can be useful for SDG alignment and performance assessment, but it also warns that reporting quality, indicator selection, and transparency are often weak and need clearer guidance [https://openalex.org/W4394576889||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4220859323||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How do the circular economy and sustainable recycling approaches in textile waste and polymeric membranes reduce environmental impact?
final_answer: Across the textile papers, the circular economy is presented as a way to reduce environmental harm by moving away from a linear model that drives wasteful production and disposal toward reduce, reuse, recycle, repair, repurpose, rental, and resale strategies that extend product life and cut waste [https://openalex.org/W4406270757||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4403242376||ABSTRACT||000]. Several summaries state that these approaches reduce the need for new raw materials, lower water, resource, and energy consumption, and turn waste into useful outputs such as recycled yarn, regenerated fibers, biodegradable composites, biofuels, and recycled fiber [https://openalex.org/W4406270757||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4206622324||ABSTRACT||000]. The textile literature also emphasizes that recycling concepts and technologies are intended to protect resources, the environment, and people, with bio-based recycling highlighted as especially promising because its selectivity and benign processing conditions can help circularize the textile life cycle [https://openalex.org/W3206222416||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, the evidence notes important barriers: recycling is limited by technological and awareness constraints, requires substantial investment and supportive policy, and prior studies have sometimes overlooked its limitations [https://openalex.org/W4403242376||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4403242376||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4283362208||ABSTRACT||001]. The papers also link these textile strategies to broader sustainability goals, including responsible consumption and production and transparent supply chains through IoT traceability [https://openalex.org/W4406270757||ABSTRACT||000]. For polymeric membranes and plastics, the summary evidence is narrower but similarly frames chemical and biological recycling methods such as pyrolysis, depolymerization, and enzyme-based degradation as more efficient and sustainable than traditional mechanical recycling, because they support closed-loop circular plastic economy strategies and reduce the environmental burden of persistent polymer waste [https://openalex.org/W4407870591||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the papers agree that sustainable recycling reduces environmental impact mainly by diverting waste from disposal, recovering value from discarded materials, and decreasing demand for virgin inputs, but they also show that implementation depends on better technologies, policy support, and design for end-of-life recycling [https://openalex.org/W3206222416||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4403242376||ABSTRACT||001].

query: How textile waste management can use waste conversion and the adsorption properties in these materials?
final_answer: Textile waste management can use waste conversion as a way to move away from dumping and toward recovery, reprocessing, reuse, recycling, and circular-economy loops [https://openalex.org/W3205047951||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4206622324||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3206222416||ABSTRACT||000]. Several papers describe conversion routes that turn textile waste into valuable products, including biological treatment with micro-organisms and enzymes, chemical and biotechnological conversion to new products and clean energy, and recycling into recovered fibers such as FINEX fiber [https://openalex.org/W4407071446||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4408599276||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4206622324||ABSTRACT||000]. One study reports enzymatic deconstruction of cut fabrics into purified fiber fractions, showing that 100% cotton fabrics could be completely disintegrated into slurry and water-soluble degradation products under aggressive mechanical agitation plus cellulase hydrolysis [https://openalex.org/W4323545673||ABSTRACT||000]. The same study also shows that waste conversion is not straightforward because blended fibers and dyes/finishing chemicals interfere with recycling, and reactive dyes inhibited degradation, although longer time, more enzyme, and repeated treatment could reduce those barriers [https://openalex.org/W4323545673||ABSTRACT||000]. Across the reviews, the common message is that textile waste treatment should combine multiple modalities rather than rely on a single route, because there is no universally applicable solution for textile effluents or wastes [https://openalex.org/W4309710850||ABSTRACT||000]. In wastewater and effluent management, adsorption is highlighted as one of the most feasible methods for dye and metal removal because it is comparatively cost-effective and can use a variety of adsorbents [https://openalex.org/W4309710850||ABSTRACT||000]. This means textile waste management can use adsorption mainly as a treatment step for contaminated wastewater streams, while conversion routes handle the solid textile waste itself by turning it into reusable materials, bio-products, or energy [https://openalex.org/W4309710850||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4408599276||ABSTRACT||000]. The overall direction supported by these papers is an integrated system that combines eco-design, efficient waste management, regenerative production, and bio-based or chemical recycling to reduce pollution and dependence on virgin materials [https://openalex.org/W3205047951||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3206222416||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4408599276||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How is the translational regulation of NEDD4 linked to the IGF1 signaling pathway, and what does the context say about NEDD4 in cells that depend on this pathway?
final_answer: The evidence links translational regulation of NEDD4 to IGF1 signaling most directly in gastric cancer cells, where NEDD4 was shown to be translationally relevant to pathway-dependent growth and Akt activation rather than simply transcriptionally changed [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||001]. In that study, GC cell lines were classified as IGF1R-dependent or IGF1R-independent based on Akt phosphorylation after OSI906 treatment, and NEDD4 knockdown or overexpression altered tumor growth only in the IGF1R-dependent cells [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||000]. The mechanism described involved a PTEN-IRS1 axis, with NEDD4 antagonizing PTEN phosphatase activity toward IRS1 to promote Akt activation and proliferation in IGF1/IGF1R-dependent cells [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||001]. Clinically, NEDD4 was reported to be higher in IGF1-high gastric cancer tissues than in IGF1-low and normal tissues, and co-high expression of NEDD4 and IGF1 predicted worse prognosis [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||001]. A related but distinct pancreatic cancer study also found NEDD4 to be translationally upregulated, with polysomal profiling supporting translational activation as the basis for higher protein expression, although that paper linked NEDD4 to PTEN/PI3K/AKT rather than IGF1 signaling specifically [pmc_PMC5386762||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC5386762||ABSTRACT||001]. In PDAC cells, NEDD4 was significantly higher than in normal pancreatic ductal epithelial cells, and depleting NEDD4 reduced proliferation and migration, suggesting that cells relying on this axis are sensitive to NEDD4 loss [pmc_PMC5386762||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC5386762||ABSTRACT||001]. By contrast, another paper in Parkinson’s disease focused on Nedd4-2-mediated ubiquitination of glutamate transporters and did not address IGF1 signaling, highlighting that NEDD4 family members can act in different pathways depending on context [pmc_PMC5386455||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the strongest supported connection is that translationally upregulated NEDD4 promotes growth in IGF1/IGF1R-dependent gastric cancer cells, while evidence from other systems shows pathway-specific roles for NEDD4 but does not extend the IGF1 link beyond the gastric cancer context [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||001] [pmc_PMC5386762||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How are the SDOs linked to policy coherance for sustainable development in the EU context?
final_answer: Across these papers, the SDGs are presented as a central reference point for policy coherence for sustainable development in the EU, because they can be used to align EU and national priorities with the broader 2030 Agenda [https://openalex.org/W3194602120||ABSTRACT||000], [https://openalex.org/W4308113945||ABSTRACT||000]. Several studies frame coherence operationally: one maps the SDGs against the European Green Deal, the European Semester, Country-Specific Recommendations, and recovery planning to improve alignment across policy frameworks [https://openalex.org/W3194602120||ABSTRACT||000], while another argues that a system perspective is needed to boost coherence across governance levels and scales of implementation [https://openalex.org/W4366975340||ABSTRACT||001]. Other papers connect coherence to monitoring and evidence, suggesting that circular economy implementation, lifecycle assessment, and SDG tracking can help assess whether policy goals support each other and stay within planetary limits [https://openalex.org/W3209532954||ABSTRACT||000], [https://openalex.org/W4210270578||ABSTRACT||000], [https://openalex.org/W3134571733||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, the literature does not present SDG-based coherence as purely technical: one paper argues that incoherencies are fundamentally political and that “neutral” or “win-win” institutional arrangements can obscure conflict and limit transformative change [https://openalex.org/W4200315183||ABSTRACT||000]. Empirically, the evidence suggests uneven coherence across the EU, since environmental SDGs are described as the most complex and least coherent [https://openalex.org/W3134571733||ABSTRACT||000], and some major sustainability challenges are not captured by the Country-Specific Recommendations even when the EU has generally incorporated the SDGs into strategic priorities [https://openalex.org/W3194602120||ABSTRACT||001]. The papers also point to data and research gaps, including poor intra-cluster connections around the SDGs and the need for more transdisciplinary research [https://openalex.org/W4366975340||ABSTRACT||001], as well as the need for better data availability and monitoring to support coherence [https://openalex.org/W3134571733||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the evidence suggests that in the EU context the SDGs link to policy coherence both as a coordinating framework for aligning agendas and as a monitoring lens for detecting trade-offs, but their effectiveness depends on political context, institutional design, and the completeness of the underlying evidence base [https://openalex.org/W4308113945||ABSTRACT||000], [https://openalex.org/W4200315183||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How are Multi-Criteria Decision-Making (MCDM) and optimization used in sustainability evaluation frameworks for transport systems, and what methods are highlighted for road transport sustainability analysis?
final_answer: Across the reviewed transport-sustainability papers, MCDM/MCDA is consistently used to handle the fact that transport systems must be evaluated across multiple, often conflicting criteria rather than by a single score alone [https://openalex.org/W4280576525||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4406996777||ABSTRACT||000]. One review explicitly states that MCDM is the preferred framework type for public transport sustainability evaluation, with AHP the most frequently used method, while another argues that sustainability assessment is increasingly moving from classic sustainability indices toward MCDA methods that should be matched to the decision problem and context [https://openalex.org/W4315708900||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4311545548||ABSTRACT||000]. Several frameworks operationalize this by integrating indicators into a single sustainability index, such as the STPI for public transport, or by combining social, economic, and environmental factors through MCDM and normalization procedures [https://openalex.org/W4363679553||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4406996777||ABSTRACT||000]. The literature also emphasizes that method choice matters: one framework analyzes 28 MCDA methods to identify which are most suitable under different sustainability decision characteristics, and another notes that normalization technique can materially affect robustness and reliability [https://openalex.org/W4311545548||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4406996777||ABSTRACT||000]. In applied transport cases, MCDM is used not only for ranking alternatives but also for weighting criteria and structuring complex decisions, as shown by the integrated entropy–CoCoSo framework for road transport sustainability in OECD countries and the spherical fuzzy SWARA–MARCOS model for sustainable vehicle prioritization in Tehran [https://openalex.org/W4280576525||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4320918985||ABSTRACT||000]. For road transport sustainability analysis specifically, the highlighted methods are entropy-based objective weighting and CoCoSo ranking, with entropy reducing subjectivity and CoCoSo producing the final performance order [https://openalex.org/W4280576525||ABSTRACT||000]. Other transport studies show hybrid workflows as well, such as DEMATEL, REMBRANDT, and VIKOR in an expressway placement case, with results compared against EIA and alternative methods including AHP, Fuzzy AHP, TOPSIS, and PROMETHEE [https://openalex.org/W3196060399||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the papers agree that MCDM helps stakeholders compare sustainability dimensions, but they differ in whether the main contribution is a general method-selection framework, a composite index, or a specific ranking/weighting hybrid for a transport subdomain [https://openalex.org/W4378909343||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4366259790||ABSTRACT||001].

query: How do the methods described for road transport sustainability and sustainable urban transport contribute to sustainable transportation systems, and what role do simulation, optimization, machine learning, and fuzzy sets play in designing and operating such systems?
final_answer: Across the papers, sustainable transportation systems are consistently framed as requiring more than cost minimization: they must account for environmental, social, and economic impacts in both design and operation, including in urban contexts and for public transport systems [https://openalex.org/W3126489268||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4388202057||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4386954171||ABSTRACT||002]. Several papers emphasize that urban transport sustainability is advanced by reducing externalities such as air pollutant emissions, traffic congestion, and other undesirable effects while improving decision-making for planners, policymakers, and mobility managers [https://openalex.org/W3160296158||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4390272563||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W3177488261||ABSTRACT||001]. In that sense, methods for road transport sustainability and sustainable urban transport contribute by providing assessment, policy, and planning tools that make sustainability more measurable and actionable, including sustainability indicators, integrated planning, SUMP, and ITS [https://openalex.org/W4388202057||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3142667272||ABSTRACT||000]. query: How the Higher Education internationalization thing help sustainability in higher education institutions, and what the bibliometric analysis find about it from Scopus database?
final_answer: Across the papers, higher education internationalization and sustainability are portrayed as mutually reinforcing: internationalization is said to help sustainability by increasing interaction between HEIs and their surroundings, expanding collaborative networks, and bringing global perspectives into teaching, learning, and research development [https://openalex.org/W4285797265||ABSTRACT||000]. More broadly, higher education is also described as supporting sustainability by raising awareness of students and educators about the SDGs, mobilizing partnerships for SDG-17, and shaping organizational culture and international cooperation activities [https://openalex.org/W3201485561||ABSTRACT||000]. Several papers converge on the idea that sustainability work in HEIs should go beyond classroom teaching and become a whole-institution effort, including policymaking, living labs, science and research for decision-making, and integration of SDGs across departments [https://openalex.org/W3202265498||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4400413260||ABSTRACT||000]. The bibliometric studies based on Scopus consistently show that research on these topics has grown substantially over time, with marked increases in recent years for sustainability-related HEI research and internationalization research [https://openalex.org/W4406778824||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4285797265||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4223628254||ABSTRACT||001]. In the sustainability-focused bibliometric analysis, Scopus yielded 2,221 documents from 1990 to 2023 that were screened to 1,013 eligible articles, with output peaking in 2022 and then declining in 2023 [https://openalex.org/W4406778824||ABSTRACT||000]. In the internationalization bibliometric analysis, Scopus identified 1,412 journal articles from 1974 to 2020 and found rising research interest, with the United Kingdom, United States, Australia, China, and Canada among the most prolific countries [https://openalex.org/W4285797265||ABSTRACT||000]. Another Scopus-based review found 4,410 publications on “higher education” and “sustainability” over the last 30 years, with the United States, UK, Spain, Australia, and Germany as the most publishing countries and with practical implications for governments and HEIs to develop synergies and policies for more efficient investment in sustainability research [https://openalex.org/W4223628254||ABSTRACT||001]. Together, these studies suggest that the literature sees internationalization as one pathway through which HEIs can widen partnerships, embed sustainability more deeply, and strengthen their contribution to the SDGs, while bibliometric evidence indicates a rapidly expanding and geographically concentrated research field [https://openalex.org/W4285797265||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3202265498||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4223628254||ABSTRACT||001].

query: How does the theme of "Green Cluod Computing" connect the discussion of Green IoT with the systematic survey of energy-efficient techniques in sustainabl cloud computing, especially regarding why data centers and cloud technologies are being optimized for lower energy use and reduced environmental harm?
final_answer: Green IoT and Green Cloud Computing are linked in the summaries as parts of a broader ICT sustainability agenda aimed at reducing energy consumption, carbon emissions, pollution, and other environmental harms [https://openalex.org/W4280503421||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4280503421||ABSTRACT||001]. The Green IoT paper explicitly names Green Cloud Computing and Green Data Center technologies as enablers of G-IoT, showing that cloud back-end infrastructure is treated as part of the same green stack that supports a “green and smart world” [https://openalex.org/W4280503421||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4280503421||ABSTRACT||001]. The cloud-computing papers explain why this matters: growing numbers of networked devices and cloud services are driving up data-center power use, heat generation, cooling needs, and carbon emissions, so future cloud systems must become energy-efficient and environmentally sustainable [https://openalex.org/W4385723923||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4281251447||ABSTRACT||000]. Across the survey-oriented summaries, the optimization goal is consistent: reduce electricity use and environmental harm through techniques such as VM virtualization and consolidation, power-aware methods, bio-inspired approaches, thermal management, and integrated workload/resource management [https://openalex.org/W4281251447||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4385723923||ABSTRACT||000]. The data-center-focused papers further show that this push is not only about emissions, but also about operational sustainability, since greener infrastructure can lower operating costs, improve resource efficiency, and support regulatory compliance and brand benefits [https://openalex.org/W4391045525||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4366762583||ABSTRACT||000]. Several summaries also emphasize that software-level and orchestration-level techniques are attractive because they can require less infrastructure and be less failure-prone, which helps explain why cloud technologies are often optimized through management and control rather than only by hardware replacement [https://openalex.org/W4281251447||ABSTRACT||001]. More recent framing expands this idea beyond the cloud alone, describing sustainability as something integrated across design, development, monitoring, refactoring, compliance, and Kubernetes-style resource management [https://openalex.org/W4391566264||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the theme of “Green Cloud Computing” connects Green IoT to sustainable cloud surveys by treating the cloud and its data centers as the energy-hungry backbone of connected systems that must be redesigned for lower energy use and reduced environmental harm [https://openalex.org/W4280503421||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3172706057||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How do sustainable technologies, such as clean energy in manufacturing and green and reverse logistics, support Industry 4.0 innovation and SDG-based growth in industrial enterprises, and what did the analysis find about enterprise adoption and environmental management?
final_answer: Across the reviewed papers, sustainable technologies are consistently presented as enabling Industry 4.0 innovation while also supporting broader sustainability and SDG-related growth in industrial enterprises [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4389484631||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4398200114||ABSTRACT||001]. In particular, clean energy in manufacturing, green logistics, and reverse logistics are described as conditions that can foster industry development and future growth through Industry 4.0 technologies and innovations in an SDG context [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000]. Multiple reviews similarly conclude that Industry 4.0 can improve environmental sustainability by increasing manufacturing efficiency, reducing resource consumption, and strengthening environmental performance [https://openalex.org/W4226256571||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4398200114||ABSTRACT||001]. The literature also frames Industry 4.0 and sustainability as mutually reinforcing: sustainability can guide technology development, and those technologies can strengthen sustainability pillars and reduce environmental impact [https://openalex.org/W4311719782||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4282842216||ABSTRACT||001]. Evidence on enterprise behavior is strongest in the Slovakia-based analysis of 105 enterprises, where more than 82% reported implementing the SDGs and more than 70% preferred environmental aspects in business management [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000]. That study also found significant relationships between environmental management and sustainability in production and logistics, including a confirmed link between renewable energy technology use in the industrial sector and sustainability in logistics [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000]. However, the broader review literature is more cautious and notes that some Industry 4.0 technologies can also create environmental harms such as air pollution, improper waste disposal, and excessive use of raw materials, information, and energy, indicating a gap between intended and actual sustainable practice [https://openalex.org/W4398200114||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the evidence suggests a positive but conditional relationship: sustainable technologies and Industry 4.0 together can support SDG-based growth and environmental improvement, yet adoption and environmental management outcomes appear uneven and context-dependent, especially outside the few studies that report enterprise-level data [https://openalex.org/W3170613256||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4389484631||ABSTRACT||000].
