query: How do sustainable technologies and environmantal management relate in the context of Industry 4.0 and SDGs, and what did the study find about enterprises preference for environmental aspects in business management?
final_answer: Across the reviewed papers, sustainable technologies and environmental management are presented as closely linked in Industry 4.0 because digital and advanced manufacturing technologies are repeatedly described as drivers of sustainability, environmental performance, and SDG-related outcomes [https://openalex.org/W4389484631||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4398200114||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W3170613256||ABSTRACT||000]. Several studies say Industry 4.0 technologies such as Big Data, IoT, cyber-physical systems, additive manufacturing, and analytics can improve manufacturing efficiency, reduce resource consumption, and support sustainable manufacturing or a sustainable environment [https://openalex.org/W4226256571||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W3120619572||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4311719782||ABSTRACT||000]. In the SDG context, the evidence indicates that integrating Industry 4.0 with the SDGs can improve environmental sustainability and create ecological support and better environmental performance, while also helping reshape organizational processes toward sustainability goals [https://openalex.org/W4398200114||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4389484631||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, one paper emphasizes that the relationship between Industry 4.0 and sustainability remains unclear and fragmented in the literature, and another notes that Industry 4.0 technologies can also produce environmental harms such as air pollution, improper waste disposal, and excessive consumption of raw materials, information, and energy [https://openalex.org/W3170613256||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4398200114||ABSTRACT||000]. The papers therefore present a mostly positive but not unqualified view: sustainable technologies are seen as enabling environmental management, yet they may also create environmental risks that need further investigation and better management [https://openalex.org/W4392974914||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4398200114||ABSTRACT||000]. Regarding enterprises’ preference for environmental aspects in business management, the clearest evidence comes from one study reporting that more than 70% of enterprises prefer environmental aspects in business management and more than 82% implement the SDGs [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000]. That same study also found a significant relationship between enterprise environmental management in the SDG context and sustainability in production and logistics, including a relationship with renewable energy technology use in industry [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000]. Other papers either do not report this preference directly or explicitly state that the evidence is insufficient to determine it [https://openalex.org/W4389484631||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4226256571||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4311719782||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How do energy resourses and renewable energy in mining together help with environmental sustainability and sustainable development, and what good effects are said about using renewable energy in mining for sustainability?
final_answer: Across the papers, energy resources and renewable energy are presented as central to making mining more environmentally sustainable and better aligned with sustainable development goals (SDGs) because mining has high energy demand, often relies on fossil fuels, and produces multiple environmental harms such as greenhouse gas emissions, dust, waste, and other pollution [https://openalex.org/W4294647036||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4386805143||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4399883377||ABSTRACT||000]. A more sustainable mining industry is described as one that reduces resource and energy consumption across all stages of mining, from exploration to post-closure, while also minimizing waste and ecological disturbance [https://openalex.org/W4294647036||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4399883377||ABSTRACT||000]. The strongest reported benefits of renewable energy use in mining are lower carbon emissions, reduced energy usage, improved waste management, and decreased environmental pollution [https://openalex.org/W4399883377||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4386805143||ABSTRACT||000]. One paper also says renewable energy in mining can create jobs, support a circular economy, reduce operating costs, and improve sustainable development indicators [https://openalex.org/W4386805143||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4386805143||ABSTRACT||001]. However, the evidence is not uniformly positive: another paper warns that sustainability assessments should not focus only on carbon emissions because renewable energy systems can have a “dark side” and may harm other aspects of sustainability [https://openalex.org/W4396736229||ABSTRACT||000]. Similarly, one mining sustainability study reports increased air emissions, water use, and energy usage for most companies and an absence of improvement in renewable energy utilization, suggesting that better energy management is still needed [https://openalex.org/W3165375152||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the papers agree that renewable energy and improved energy management can help mining contribute to environmental sustainability and SDGs, but they also show that benefits depend on broader technological, regulatory, and implementation conditions [https://openalex.org/W4399883377||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4386805143||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4396736229||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How do innovation, CEOs' sustainability orientation, and green governance relate to sustainability and environmental performance in firms?
final_answer: Across the summaries, innovation consistently appears to be linked to better sustainability or environmental outcomes, but often through mediating organizational mechanisms rather than as a standalone driver. Green innovation is reported to have significant positive relationships with environmental sustainability and innovation climate in industrial firms, with innovation climate mediating this link and green motivational strategies and green abilities strengthening the effect [https://openalex.org/W4388684227||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4388684227||ABSTRACT||001]. A separate study likewise finds that green innovation capabilities influence firm performance indirectly through social and economic sustainability, although not through environmental sustainability, which suggests the pathway from innovation to performance may differ by sustainability dimension [https://openalex.org/W3200508375||ABSTRACT||001]. In addition, sustainability-oriented innovations are associated with stronger economic performance, with green competitive advantage as a strong mediator and green image as a weak mediator, and they are also positively related to green organizational identity [https://openalex.org/W4367603834||ABSTRACT||000]. On the leadership side, environmentally aware or green transformational leaders are found to positively influence green performance, partly because green organizational culture and green engagement mediate that relationship [https://openalex.org/W4401652574||ABSTRACT||000]. For CEOs and governance, the evidence suggests that governance matters most when considered as a bundle: in dirty firms, CEOs, boards, and owners jointly shape environmental innovation, and both powerful and weak CEOs can support environmental innovation when paired with suitable board and ownership configurations [https://openalex.org/W4282035384||ABSTRACT||000]. A broader sustainability-strategy study also reports that genuine sustainability strategy improves firm performance and environmental results, but its effectiveness depends on ownership dispersion and board independence, and the relationship varies by sector [https://openalex.org/W4404618052||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the papers agree that sustainability and environmental performance are enhanced by innovation and governance arrangements, but they also show that effects are indirect, contingent, and context-dependent rather than universal [https://openalex.org/W4388684227||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4401652574||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4404618052||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How do the themes of "energy resources," "clean and distributed energy," and "energy transitions" connect across the context in explaining both environmental sustainability and workforce implications, and what does the context say about the role of clean energy, renewable electricity, and training in this transition?
final_answer: Across the papers, “energy resources,” “clean and distributed energy,” and “energy transitions” are presented as interconnected parts of a broader shift in how energy systems are organized, governed, and evaluated for sustainability [https://openalex.org/W4220773259||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4401335752||ABSTRACT||001]. Several summaries link this shift directly to environmental sustainability, emphasizing reduced greenhouse gas emissions, climate protection, resource conservation, low ecological impacts, and ecosystem stability as core goals [https://openalex.org/W4391762394||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W3154213043||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4400513475||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4407562904||ABSTRACT||001]. The context also frames clean and distributed energy through renewable adoption, resilient grids, storage, and a sustainable mix of renewables with limited nonrenewables to maintain supply quality while minimizing cost and environmental impact [https://openalex.org/W4220773259||ABSTRACT||001]. At the same time, the transition is not purely technical: it is repeatedly described as involving policy coherence, cross-border collaboration, stakeholder values, and tradeoffs among economic development, ecological standards, inclusivity, and pace of change [https://openalex.org/W4391762394||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4283155889||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4401335752||ABSTRACT||001]. Workforce implications are present in multiple summaries, which tie sustainable energy policies to job creation, economic growth, social equity, human capital development, and public engagement [https://openalex.org/W4391762394||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4400513475||ABSTRACT||001]. One paper makes this especially explicit by saying renewable energy use can support sustained employment growth and that governments should invest in renewable energy infrastructure and workforce training to enable green economic transformation [https://openalex.org/W4407562904||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the context suggests that clean energy and renewable electricity are treated as central tools for environmental sustainability, but the transition must also be managed as a social and labor-market process requiring training, institutions, and collaboration [https://openalex.org/W4400513475||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4407562904||ABSTRACT||001].

query: How do the themes of "Environmental sustainability", "Sustainability implementation barriers", and "Sustainable residential buildings" connect when comparing off-site construction research with the barrier analysis in Ghana and the "Mostadam" approach in Saudi Arabia, and what sustainability-related findings are highlighted across these contexts?
final_answer: Across the provided studies, the common thread is that sustainability in construction is treated as an applied, implementation-oriented issue rather than an abstract objective, especially in residential buildings and broader built-environment projects [https://openalex.org/W3168941981||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4310036329||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3120903819||ABSTRACT||001]. In Ghana, environmental sustainability is operationalized through lifecycle-based project indicators, especially water quality, air quality, energy use and conservation, and environmental compliance and management, which are presented as key measures for steering the industry toward sustainability [https://openalex.org/W3168941981||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3168941981||ABSTRACT||001]. In the Ghana residential-building barrier study, sustainability implementation barriers are grouped into management, standards, society, and knowledge, with management-related barriers emerging as the most significant obstacle [https://openalex.org/W4310036329||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4310036329||ABSTRACT||001]. This barrier emphasis is consistent with the Ghana retrofit study, which identifies cultural, economic, technical knowledge, and regulatory barriers and argues that overcoming human-behavioral, cost, skills, and policy constraints is important for promoting sustainable retrofitting [https://openalex.org/W4293340752||ABSTRACT||001]. Similar barrier hierarchies appear elsewhere as well: the Nigeria study highlights poor sustainability education, lack of incentives, ignorance of lifecycle cost benefits, low priority for sustainable construction, and resistance to cultural change, while the Iran study finds economics- and regulation-dependent barriers more influential than market or workforce-experience issues [https://openalex.org/W3145060410||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3132259306||ABSTRACT||000]. By contrast, the Saudi Arabia “Mostadam” source emphasizes sustainable residential buildings, practical strategies, and policy action to transform buildings and cities toward sustainable development and sustainable cities, but the provided evidence does not specify implementation barriers there [https://openalex.org/W3120903819||ABSTRACT||001]. The off-site/prefabrication context also fits the same sustainability pattern: the Southern Africa IPCM study mainstreams sustainability principles into affordable housing and reports higher overall sustainability performance using lifecycle energy, cost, and technical-performance evaluation [https://openalex.org/W4386401188||ABSTRACT||000]. Another housing-focused study similarly links environmental sustainability and affordability through passive design, recycled and local materials, and socio-technical innovations that reduce lifecycle costs [https://openalex.org/W4385389240||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the evidence suggests that environmental sustainability, sustainable residential buildings, and sustainability implementation barriers are connected by a shared concern with translating sustainability principles into measurable project indicators, practical housing design, and policy-supported implementation, while the main obstacles are managerial, educational, economic, regulatory, and cultural [https://openalex.org/W3168941981||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4310036329||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3120903819||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4385389240||ABSTRACT||001].

query: How can healthcare workers balanc innovation with sustainability when reducing workplace emissions and avoid the wasteful use of medical resources in imaging and other care, while still keepin AI benefits responsible?
final_answer: Across the papers, a consistent message is that healthcare workers should treat sustainability as a core design constraint rather than an afterthought when adopting AI and other innovations [https://openalex.org/W4399973910||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4220793133||ABSTRACT||000]. In radiology and interventional radiology, the literature describes significant environmental burdens from energy use, carbon emissions, waste, water pollution, hardware waste, and data storage, while also noting that awareness of sustainability is often higher than actual implementation [https://openalex.org/W4327898048||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4409540874||ABSTRACT||000]. Several papers suggest that AI can still be part of the solution if it is used to reduce low-value imaging, optimize resource allocation, improve workflow efficiency, and support energy efficiency and telemedicine-like sustainable practices [https://openalex.org/W4409540874||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4399973910||ABSTRACT||001]. However, the same evidence warns that AI can also add sustainability burdens and clinical risks, including algorithmic bias, unequal access, and dangerous recommendations, so benefits should be weighed against equity and patient safety [https://openalex.org/W4409540874||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4220793133||ABSTRACT||000]. The most repeated prescription is a holistic governance approach: eco-design, lifecycle assessment, responsible data management, continuous monitoring, policy frameworks, and collaboration are all presented as necessary to keep AI benefits responsible [https://openalex.org/W4399973910||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4409540874||ABSTRACT||001]. More generally, sustainability should be judged through health, justice, and resource conservation, not carbon alone, so workers can avoid wasteful use of medical resources while still improving care [https://openalex.org/W4220793133||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4220793133||ABSTRACT||001]. The evidence also suggests that individual effort is not enough in settings like interventional radiology because some constraints require departmental, institutional, or system-level change [https://openalex.org/W4327898048||ABSTRACT||000]. Finally, there are important uncertainty points: some summaries are radiology-specific, one paper explicitly says it does not provide healthcare-specific strategies, and several papers note knowledge gaps or the need for further research, so the field still lacks fully settled best practices [https://openalex.org/W4403054232||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4392191303||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4394008899||ABSTRACT||001].

The framework also includes a “Knowing” and “Doing” assessment and highlights a missing “Being” dimension, pointing to a gap between what companies say and what they actually do [https://openalex.org/W4364359925||ABSTRACT||000]. In addition, sustainability is presented as a triple-bottom-line orientation and as a strategic driver shaped by employee motivation and managerial attitude, linking environmental action to broader organizational performance [https://openalex.org/W4283697438||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3128290205||ABSTRACT||000]. Multiple papers explicitly connect sustainability to business outcomes such as firm performance, financial performance, and sustainable competitive advantage, suggesting that environmental sustainability can also support how a company is viewed as a successful or responsible business [https://openalex.org/W3128290205||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3132273715||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4280505603||ABSTRACT||001]. The available summaries do not provide the sustainable marketing article itself, so a direct comparison is not possible; however, the supply chain evidence shows the same general logic of linking sustainability with positive company positioning through performance and responsible management [https://openalex.org/W3128290205||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4308101885||ABSTRACT||002].

query: How does the text link economic sustainability and decoupling consumption from economic growth in these two contexts, and what is suggested about making space tourism environmentally sustainable?
final_answer: Across these summaries, economic sustainability is treated as the most plausible dimension of space tourism sustainability, in the sense that the sector may be financially viable even if broader sustainability remains uncertain [https://openalex.org/W4315646741||ABSTRACT||002]. At the same time, the text says that economic burden persists because of the “tyranny of the rocket equation,” where fuel weight keeps costs and environmental costs tightly linked [https://openalex.org/W4315646741||ABSTRACT||003]. In this framing, decoupling consumption from economic growth is not presented as already achieved in space tourism; instead, the literature notes that economic indicators are the most relevant while social and environmental indicators are less developed, suggesting that sustainability assessments still emphasize growth-related economic performance more than a fuller decoupling-based model [https://openalex.org/W4315646741||ABSTRACT||014]. The summaries also agree that social and environmental sustainability are less promising than economic sustainability and need a stronger conceptual and empirical basis [https://openalex.org/W4315646741||ABSTRACT||002]. To make space tourism environmentally sustainable, the text suggests first critically evaluating whether it can be made sustainable and ethical at all, and under what preconditions [https://openalex.org/W4315646741||ABSTRACT||003]. It further recommends developing a theoretically grounded and robust analytical framework adapted from sustainable tourism frameworks to address the current knowledge gap [https://openalex.org/W4315646741||ABSTRACT||002] [https://openalex.org/W4315646741||ABSTRACT||003]. Overall, the evidence implies that environmental sustainability would require more than economic viability; it would require a new framework that can systematically incorporate environmental and social dimensions rather than relying mainly on economic indicators [https://openalex.org/W4315646741||ABSTRACT||014] [https://openalex.org/W4315646741||ABSTRACT||002].

query: How do regional integration and multistakeholder partnerships support Sustainable Development Goal 8 in the Yangtze River Delta?
final_answer: Evidence specific to the Yangtze River Delta suggests that regional integration supports SDG-related progress by linking sustainability analysis and governance across multiple scales, from county to region, river basin, and global levels [https://openalex.org/W3185034769||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4320729134||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4320729134||ABSTRACT||001]. One study argues that SDG planning should integrate land, water, and energy in long-term urban planning and explicitly include multi-sector partnerships, which it presents as a way to coordinate development across scales and sectors [https://openalex.org/W3185034769||ABSTRACT||001]. Another paper shows that county-level, region-wide sustainability assessment in the YRD can reveal spatial differences and autocorrelations, and that regional sustainability improved overall from 2000 to 2015 even though socio-economic sustainability rose in most counties while environmental sustainability declined [https://openalex.org/W3194996912||ABSTRACT||000]. This indicates that integration is useful not because one dimension can be advanced alone, but because economic and environmental objectives need to be coordinated together [https://openalex.org/W3194996912||ABSTRACT||000]. More broadly, the YRD is described as a useful subnational experimental site for studying regional integration and sustainable development, with calls for applicable governance structures, institutions, multi-source data, and interdisciplinary methods to support integrated development [https://openalex.org/W4320729134||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4320729134||ABSTRACT||001]. Multistakeholder partnerships are also framed in the SDG literature as a way to define scope, identify interlinkages, assign responsibilities, and bring together relevant actors for implementation, while linkages across sectors, scales, and actors help determine who should be engaged [https://openalex.org/W4205386374||ABSTRACT||000]. However, the partnership literature is not uniformly optimistic: reviews report limited effectiveness, legitimacy deficits, and weak synergy generation in many partnerships, suggesting that better governance, accountability, and institutional design are needed [https://openalex.org/W4400486548||ABSTRACT||000]. Taken together, the papers imply that in the YRD, regional integration supports SDG 8 mainly by enabling coordinated, multi-scalar governance of economic development, while multistakeholder partnerships provide the collaborative structure needed to align sectors and actors around that goal [https://openalex.org/W3185034769||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4320729134||ABSTRACT||001].

query: How do environmental sustainability reporting practices in Bahrain\"s large industrial sector relate to environmental management and Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), and what evidence from the Industry 4.0 study shows similar links between SDGs, environmental aspects, and renewable energy technologies in industrial enterprises?
final_answer: In Bahrain’s large industrial sector, sustainability reporting appears to be closely tied to environmental management because the studies describe materiality analysis as a way to better monitor and measure environmental performance and to support implementation of the SDGs [https://openalex.org/W4200252599||ABSTRACT||000]. The Bahrain evidence also suggests that using a materiality matrix helps prioritize the most significant sustainability issues, improve report content by incorporating stakeholder views, and raise report quality, which links reporting practice directly to environmental management improvement [https://openalex.org/W4200252599||ABSTRACT||000]. By contrast, other supplied papers do not provide Bahrain-specific evidence, but they do show that SDG-related reporting and sustainability management vary by sector, company size, geography, internationalization, and performance, indicating that sustainability reporting is heterogeneous across industries [https://openalex.org/W4286447895||ABSTRACT||000]. The Industry 4.0 study adds a parallel line of evidence by showing that Industry 4.0 technologies and circular economy practices are linked to sustainable operations and to SDGs 6, 7, 9, 12, and 13, and that this linkage can help organizations realign management practices toward those goals [https://openalex.org/W4210290448||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4210290448||ABSTRACT||001]. A related Industry 4.0 review also models Environmental Management Systems as increasing environmental and sustainability performance while explicitly mapping SDGs onto the model, reinforcing the idea that environmental management and SDG progress are connected [https://openalex.org/W3157489939||ABSTRACT||001]. Another Industry 4.0 review reports that these technologies can enhance sustainability performance, address environmental concerns, and help achieve SDGs, and it offers a framework that classifies SDGs, technologies, and enablers to analyze their connections [https://openalex.org/W4389484631||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4389484631||ABSTRACT||001]. Across these studies, the common theme is that structured management tools, whether materiality matrices or Environmental Management Systems, strengthen the link between environmental performance and SDG implementation [https://openalex.org/W4200252599||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3157489939||ABSTRACT||001]. The Industry 4.0 evidence also points to specific environmental/resource relationships, including a reported alignment between food security and SDG 14: Life Below Water, and it emphasizes the interconnections between SDGs and Industry 4.0 technologies for future research and industrial practice [https://openalex.org/W4389484631||ABSTRACT||001]. However, the Bahrain paper provided here does not include direct details on renewable energy technologies, and the Industry 4.0 evidence only indirectly supports that part of the query through broader sustainability and SDG linkages rather than explicit renewable-energy findings [https://openalex.org/W4210290448||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3157489939||ABSTRACT||001].

query: In the context of Environmental sustainability reporting and Sustainability reporting, how do the Bahrain industrial companies" materiality matrices relate to improved environmental performance, and how does this compare with the UK evidence on whether reporting that follows guidelines and a business-case approach actually improves sustainability performance?
final_answer: In the Bahrain large industrial sector, the available evidence indicates that materiality analysis and materiality matrices are linked to better monitoring and measuring of environmental performance, because they help companies identify and prioritize the most significant sustainability issues [https://openalex.org/W4200252599||ABSTRACT||000]. The Bahrain evidence also says that incorporating stakeholders’ views through materiality matrices can improve the quality of sustainability reports and support implementation of the SDGs, which suggests an indirect pathway from better reporting practice to better sustainability management [https://openalex.org/W4200252599||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4200252599||ABSTRACT||001]. A related Bahrain/GCC study similarly finds that stronger materiality assessment disclosure is associated with better financial performance, lower leverage, and better corporate governance, while also supporting higher-quality sustainability reporting, transparency, and accountability [https://openalex.org/W3134875937||ABSTRACT||001]. However, that study does not say that Bahrain industrial companies’ materiality matrices directly cause improved environmental performance, so the claim is stronger for reporting quality and accountability than for measured environmental outcomes [https://openalex.org/W3134875937||ABSTRACT||001]. By contrast, the UK evidence argues that companies that merely comply with reporting guidelines and use a business-case framing may not capture all sustainability aspects and may not have a real positive impact on sustainability performance [https://openalex.org/W4220852241||ABSTRACT||000]. In that UK study, reports reflecting a broader understanding of sustainability are associated with better sustainability performance, while compliance- and business-centred messages are negatively associated with it [https://openalex.org/W4220852241||ABSTRACT||000]. Taken together, the papers suggest a partial agreement that reporting can matter, but they differ on what kind of reporting is effective: Bahrain evidence emphasizes materiality matrices as a tool for improving environmental monitoring and report quality, whereas the UK evidence warns that guideline-following and business-case reporting alone may be insufficient or even negatively related to sustainability performance [https://openalex.org/W4200252599||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4220852241||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How doeas sustainable marketing relate to enviromental sustainability in shaping a company"s image, and what kinds of consumption changes are described as ways to advance sufficiency transitions?
final_answer: Across the papers, sustainable or green marketing is consistently presented as a way for firms to signal environmental commitment and build a more favorable company image, often by positioning the organization as socially and environmentally responsible or by strengthening legitimacy with consumers and stakeholders [https://openalex.org/W4392716256||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W3137258271||ABSTRACT||001]. Several summaries also link this image-building function to competitive and relational benefits: firms can gain competitive advantage, strengthen relationships with environmentally conscious consumers, and respond to shifts in consumer behavior toward greater social and environmental awareness [https://openalex.org/W4392716256||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4396847081||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4388661115||ABSTRACT||001]. At the same time, one paper warns that profit-centric firms may imitate sustainability practices inauthentically as greenwashing, indicating that sustainability claims can enhance image but also create credibility risks when not matched by deeper sustain-centric commitments [https://openalex.org/W4379928390||ABSTRACT||000]. A related set of papers emphasizes that sustainability marketing should move beyond short-term growth goals toward sustainability, sufficiency, and even degrowth-oriented frameworks, reflecting tension between economic growth and ecological well-being [https://openalex.org/W3126349936||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4282834253||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4379928390||ABSTRACT||000]. However, the evidence is much thinner on exactly how these marketing approaches shape image through environmental sustainability in specific branding terms, since several abstracts explicitly say they do not provide direct evidence on that point [https://openalex.org/W4379928390||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3126349936||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4400608740||ABSTRACT||000]. On sufficiency transitions, the clearest recurring ideas are broad rather than specific: the papers mention sustainable consumption patterns, sufficiency, pro-sustainable behaviour, and degrowth-minded policies, but they do not detail concrete consumption shifts such as reduced consumption, substitution, or particular lifestyle changes in the evidence provided [https://openalex.org/W3126349936||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4282834253||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4400608740||ABSTRACT||000]. One summary does note that sustainable marketing aims to move firms and stakeholders toward upper levels of sustainability and sustainable consumption patterns, while another frames green marketing as engaging consumers in sustainable practices and preserving natural resources [https://openalex.org/W3126349936||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4392716256||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the papers agree that sustainability-oriented marketing can improve image and support pro-environmental behavior, but they also show that the concept is contested, vulnerable to greenwashing, and only loosely specified when it comes to the exact consumption changes involved in sufficiency transitions [https://openalex.org/W4379928390||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4282834253||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How sustainability reporting link with SDGs and sustainability performance, it matter from the supply chain framework too?
final_answer:
Across these papers, sustainability reporting is generally presented as a mechanism for connecting corporate action to the SDGs, but the strength of that connection varies. Some studies argue that GRI-based or integrated reporting can show whether SDGs matter to the private sector and help assess how firms contribute to them, while also supporting evaluation of sustainability strategy with common metrics [https://openalex.org/W4220859323||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4362609606||ABSTRACT||000]. However, other evidence suggests the link is often weak in practice: one large study of 8,500 companies found no correlation in reporting specific goals and a clear disconnection between sustainability performance and SDG reporting, implying that firms may disclose SDGs arbitrarily rather than based on actual performance [https://openalex.org/W4394576889||ABSTRACT||000]. A related study found that companies may mention SDGs in reports without explaining how concrete sustainability initiatives shape their contribution to the Agenda 2030, reinforcing concerns about transparency and substance [https://openalex.org/W4220859323||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, some papers report more positive associations, such as a sustainability reporting score index that integrates SDGs and is said to help stakeholders measure firms’ sustainable performance, and another study that links sustainability reporting to sustainability performance through environmental performance measurement and SDG implementation [https://openalex.org/W4392003298||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4200252599||ABSTRACT||001].

From the supply chain perspective, the evidence suggests that sustainability reporting and SDG-related performance become more meaningful when they are embedded in supply chain or value-chain frameworks. A supply-chain assessment framework based on GRI is designed to measure both companies’ and suppliers’ environmental and social sustainability performance using 91 indicators, showing how reporting can extend across supply chain actors and sectors [https://openalex.org/W4400657024||ABSTRACT||000]. Another paper reports that sustainable supply chain management has positive relationships with both SDGs and financial performance, and that implementing a sustainable supply chain from supplier to customer can improve operational efficiency and reduce environmental and social impacts [https://openalex.org/W4394886303||ABSTRACT||001]. Similarly, a framework paper argues that sustainable supply chain management, technology adoption, and performance measurement are important for promoting sustainability, and that clearer sustainability indicators are needed to support SDG-oriented supply chain management [https://openalex.org/W4327714039||ABSTRACT||000].

There is also evidence that SDG alignment in sustainability assessment is not automatic: some indicators have no direct or indirect SDG connection, partly because of limited life-cycle thinking and limited discussion of workers, consumers, and value-chain actors [https://openalex.org/W4281493513||ABSTRACT||001]. Related SDG–LCSA work says SDGs and life-cycle approaches are complementary but lack a harmonized way to connect them, so more research is needed to consistently link metrics to SDGs [https://openalex.org/W4380365728||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the papers suggest that sustainability reporting can support SDG tracking and sustainability performance measurement, but its credibility and usefulness improve when reports are tied to materiality, performance indicators, and supply-chain-wide assessment rather than broad symbolic disclosure [https://openalex.org/W4200252599||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4400657024||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4394576889||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How do the circular economy and sustainable recycling approaches in textile waste and polymeric membranes reduce environmental impact?
final_answer: Across the textile papers, the circular economy is presented as a way to reduce environmental impact by replacing linear production and disposal with reduce-reuse-recycle systems that extend product lifecycles and turn waste into new resources such as recycled yarn, regenerated fibers, biofilms, biodegradable composites, and biofuels [https://openalex.org/W4406270757||ABSTRACT||000]. Multiple reviews agree that recycling, reuse, repair, repurposing, resale, and rental can lower waste and reduce water, resource, and energy use, while also supporting responsible consumption and production [https://openalex.org/W4406270757||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4406270757||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4403242376||ABSTRACT||000]. Several papers also emphasize that designing textiles and finishes for end-of-life recyclability, and using closed-loop or bio-based processing, can help keep materials circulating and reduce pollution from textile production and processing [https://openalex.org/W3206222416||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4406270757||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, the literature notes that fast fashion-driven overproduction and overconsumption intensify textile waste and environmental pollution, so greener technologies and stricter environmental legislation are needed alongside circular strategies [https://openalex.org/W4407071446||ABSTRACT||000]. For polymeric materials, the plastics review makes a parallel argument: traditional mechanical recycling is insufficient, whereas chemical and biological recycling methods such as pyrolysis, depolymerization, and enzyme-based degradation are described as more efficient and sustainable alternatives that reduce waste [https://openalex.org/W4407870591||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the shared environmental logic is that circular and sustainable recycling approaches reduce impact by keeping materials in use longer, limiting virgin resource demand, and decreasing waste generation and pollution [https://openalex.org/W3206222416||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4407870591||ABSTRACT||000]. However, the papers also caution that recycling is constrained by technological, awareness, and investment barriers, and that existing textile waste management programs have been unsuccessful, so supportive policies, corporate change, and new biotechnologies are needed for these benefits to be realized [https://openalex.org/W4403242376||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4407071446||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How textile waste management can use waste conversion and the adsorption properties in these materials?
final_answer: Across the papers, textile waste management is consistently framed as moving away from dumping and toward recovery, reprocessing, reuse, recycling, and broader circular-economy models [https://openalex.org/W3205047951||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3206222416||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4206622324||ABSTRACT||000]. Several summaries show that waste conversion can turn textiles into new products or resource streams, including conversion into purified fiber fractions, recycled fiber products, glucose, bio-oil, and other valuable resources [https://openalex.org/W4323545673||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4206622324||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4408599276||ABSTRACT||000]. The conversion pathways reported include aggressive mechanical agitation with cellulase-catalyzed hydrolysis, chemical and biotechnological conversion, enzymatic recycling, and fluidized-bed pyrolysis, with pretreatment and solvent recovery noted as important for efficiency and scalability [https://openalex.org/W4323545673||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4408599276||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, the papers agree that textile waste is difficult to process because of mixed fibers, finishes, additives, dyes, and other contaminants that can interfere with degradation and make conversion less efficient [https://openalex.org/W4408599276||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4323545673||ABSTRACT||000]. In contrast, adsorption is discussed mainly in the context of textile wastewater treatment rather than direct conversion of textile materials: it is described as a feasible, cost-effective method for removing dyes and metals, often as part of multi-stage treatment systems [https://openalex.org/W4309710850||ABSTRACT||000]. Thus, if the goal is to use textile waste management for waste conversion and adsorption-based treatment, the evidence supports a combined strategy in which solid textile wastes are reprocessed into new materials or fuels while liquid effluents are treated with adsorption and other complementary processes [https://openalex.org/W4309710850||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4408599276||ABSTRACT||000]. The literature also suggests that biological treatment, especially using microorganisms and enzymes, may generate valuable new products and clean energy, but the summaries do not provide enough detail to show how these approaches compare directly with adsorption-based methods [https://openalex.org/W4407071446||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the evidence supports integrating conversion, pretreatment, and adsorption within a circular waste-management framework, but it does not establish a single universal solution for all textile waste streams [https://openalex.org/W3205047951||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4309710850||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How is the translational regulation of NEDD4 linked to the IGF1 signaling pathway, and what does the context say about NEDD4 in cells that depend on this pathway?
final_answer: The clearest evidence linking NEDD4 to the IGF1 pathway comes from gastric cancer cells, where cells were stratified into IGF1R-dependent and IGF1R-independent groups based on Akt phosphorylation after OSI906 treatment [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||000]. In that setting, Dox-induced NEDD4 knockdown suppressed tumor growth and NEDD4 overexpression promoted growth specifically in IGF1R-dependent gastric cancer cells, indicating that NEDD4 supports proliferation in cells that rely on IGF1/IGF1R signaling [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||001]. The study further concludes that NEDD4 promotes proliferation by antagonizing PTEN’s protein phosphatase activity toward IRS1, with a PTEN-IRS1 axis required for NEDD4-mediated regulation of Akt activation and tumor growth [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||001]. In contrast, in IGF1R-independent cells, changing NEDD4 levels had no effect on proliferation, which supports a context-dependent role for NEDD4 rather than a universal growth effect [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||001]. Other provided papers do not add support for an IGF1-NEDD4 translational link: several explicitly state that they do not mention NEDD4 or IGF1 signaling and instead focus on unrelated pathways or proteins [pmc_PMC9803678||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC4425028||ABSTRACT||001] [pmc_PMC5386455||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4285014207||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W3199735924||ABSTRACT||000]. A related but distinct NEDD4 study in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma shows translational upregulation of NEDD4 and links it to PTEN/PI3K/AKT signaling, but it does not explicitly connect NEDD4 to IGF1 [pmc_PMC5386762||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC5386762||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the evidence suggests that NEDD4 can be translationally upregulated in cancer and that, at least in IGF1R-dependent gastric cancer cells, it promotes growth through a PTEN-IRS1-Akt mechanism, while showing little or no effect in IGF1R-independent cells [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC10063445||ABSTRACT||001] [pmc_PMC5386762||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How are the SDOs linked to policy coherance for sustainable development in the EU context?
final_answer: In the EU context, the SDGs are repeatedly presented as a framework for policy coherence for sustainable development, because they are meant to integrate environmental, social, and economic objectives and prevent progress in one area from undermining another [https://openalex.org/W3134571733||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4200315183||ABSTRACT||000]. Several papers treat coherence as a practical alignment task: for example, the SDGs are linked to the European Green Deal, the European Semester, and Country-Specific Recommendations through a 3D-mapping approach meant to better align EU priorities with the broader sustainability agenda [https://openalex.org/W3194602120||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3194602120||ABSTRACT||001]. Other work suggests that tools such as circular economy policy and Life Cycle Assessment can support this alignment by connecting EU policy design and monitoring to SDG achievement [https://openalex.org/W3209532954||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4210270578||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, the evidence is not uniformly optimistic: one paper argues that SDG-linked coherence can become narrowly technical, mask political incoherencies, and even limit transformative change when framed as “neutral” or “win-win” [https://openalex.org/W4200315183||ABSTRACT||000]. Another paper similarly stresses that coherence depends on political drivers—ideas, interests, and institutions—rather than being only an administrative or institutional exercise [https://openalex.org/W4308113945||ABSTRACT||000]. Across the EU literature, the environmental SDGs appear to be the most complex and least coherent, implying that coherence is weakest in environmental policy areas and especially needs strengthening around biodiversity and climate [https://openalex.org/W3134571733||ABSTRACT||000]. Relatedly, one study says the SDGs are already incorporated into EU strategic priorities to a sufficient extent, but important sustainability challenges identified in the Sustainable Development Report 2020 are still not reflected in the CSRs, showing that coherence remains incomplete [https://openalex.org/W3194602120||ABSTRACT||001]. More broadly, the literature calls for a system perspective, better data, and more transdisciplinary research to capture trade-offs and improve coherence across governance levels and scales of implementation [https://openalex.org/W4366975340||ABSTRACT||001].

query: How are Multi-Criteria Decision-Making (MCDM) and optimization used in sustainability evaluation frameworks for transport systems, and what methods are highlighted for road transport sustainability analysis?
final_answer: Across the papers, sustainability evaluation for transport systems is consistently framed as a multi-criteria decision-making problem because transportation decisions involve multiple, often conflicting criteria that must be balanced under uncertainty [https://openalex.org/W4320918985||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4280576525||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4406996777||ABSTRACT||000]. Several studies emphasize that MCDM/MCDA is used to combine environmental, economic, social, and sometimes circularity dimensions into a single evaluative framework or index, supporting more reliable decision-making than simpler sustainability indices alone [https://openalex.org/W4406996777||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4311545548||ABSTRACT||000]. In transport applications, one paper proposes an integrated spherical fuzzy set approach with SWARA for weighting and MARCOS for ranking sustainable vehicles in Tehran, while another uses an entropy–CoCoSo framework to evaluate road transportation sustainability in OECD countries [https://openalex.org/W4320918985||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4280576525||ABSTRACT||000]. A broader transport case study also uses hybrid MCDM methods—DEMATEL, REMBRANDT, and VIKOR—and compares them with AHP, Fuzzy AHP, TOPSIS, and PROMETHEE in expressway location evaluation, showing that multiple MCDA tools are used in sustainability assessment workflows [https://openalex.org/W3196060399||ABSTRACT||000]. For public transport, the literature review finds MCDM to be the preferred framework type among surveyed studies, and identifies AHP as the most frequently used method, while another public transport framework combines indicators into the Sustainable Transport Planning Index using AHP-based weights and normalization [https://openalex.org/W4315708900||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4363679553||ABSTRACT||000]. Optimization is mentioned more as a general decision-support goal than as a specific transport-method family in the provided evidence, and one review explicitly does not support naming optimization frameworks beyond MCDA-based approaches [https://openalex.org/W3196060399||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4378909343||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the evidence suggests that transport sustainability frameworks favor structured multi-criteria ranking, weighting, and normalization methods, with entropy, AHP, SWARA, MARCOS, CoCoSo, VIKOR, TOPSIS, PROMETHEE, DEMATEL, and REMBRANDT highlighted across the studies [https://openalex.org/W4280576525||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3196060399||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4363679553||ABSTRACT||000].

key_claims.notes: Both cited abstracts explicitly describe transport sustainability evaluation as MCDM due to multiple criteria and note conflicting criteria/uncertainty.

query: How does the study use predictive analytics in the 1-hop work, and what does the 2-hop AI impact assessment say about AI"s role for sustainable development?
final_answer: Across the papers, the 1-hop work uses predictive analytics as an AI method for forecasting, monitoring, and optimization rather than as a standalone end, with examples including deep learning and supervised machine learning for SDG-related forecasting and system optimization [https://openalex.org/W4412514975||ABSTRACT||000], real-time environmental monitoring and predictive modeling for climate change and resource depletion [https://openalex.org/W4392169541||ABSTRACT||000], and advanced predictive models that improve resource monitoring, agriculture, waste management, and cleaner production [https://openalex.org/W4401831154||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4402735735||ABSTRACT||000]. One study also frames predictive analytics as anticipating environmental risks to support sustainability actions and conservation efforts [https://openalex.org/W4396752219||ABSTRACT||000]. In contrast, one provided paper does not supply enough evidence to describe any 1-hop predictive-analytics work at all, so its contribution cannot be synthesized on that point [https://openalex.org/W4220935479||ABSTRACT||001]. For the 2-hop AI impact assessment, the papers broadly agree that AI has strong potential to advance sustainable development through data-driven insights, environmental optimization, climate mitigation, biodiversity support, and resource management [https://openalex.org/W4412514975||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4414098400||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4401831154||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4392169541||ABSTRACT||000]. Several abstracts go further and say AI should play a central or pivotal role in responsible sustainable change, while also noting that environmental, economic, and social dimensions all matter [https://openalex.org/W4412514975||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4402735735||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4396752219||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, the papers caution that AI’s promise is not fully realized and that limitations such as lack of deep sustainability expertise, ecological footprint, bias, and the need for supportive policy and infrastructure remain [https://openalex.org/W4412514975||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4414098400||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4401831154||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the literature presents AI as an enabling tool for sustainable development, but one that requires responsible governance, interdisciplinary collaboration, and further research to translate potential into impact [https://openalex.org/W4414098400||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4392169541||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4405499395||ABSTRACT||001].

query: How the Higher Education internationalization thing help sustainability in higher education institutions, and what the bibliometric analysis find about it from Scopus database?
final_answer: Higher education internationalization is presented as a way to support the sustainability of higher education institutions by expanding collaborative networks and bringing global perspectives into teaching, learning, and research development [https://openalex.org/W4285797265||ABSTRACT||000]. It is also framed as part of a broader higher-education role in sustainability, where internationalization helps HEIs raise awareness of the SDGs, mobilize students and educators for partnerships, and respond to globalization and Agenda 2030 challenges [https://openalex.org/W3201485561||ABSTRACT||000]. More generally, the literature suggests that sustainability in higher education works best through a whole-institution approach in which universities go beyond teaching sustainability and also engage in policymaking, living labs, and research-informed decision-making [https://openalex.org/W3202265498||ABSTRACT||000]. The Scopus-based bibliometric study on higher education internationalization analyzed 1,412 journal articles from 1974 to 2020 and found growing research activity, with the United Kingdom, United States, Australia, China, and Canada among the most prolific countries [https://openalex.org/W4285797265||ABSTRACT||000]. That study also reported increasing use of the term in global cross-cultural and transnational education research, suggesting that internationalization has become a more visible topic in the field [https://openalex.org/W4285797265||ABSTRACT||000]. Related Scopus bibliometric work on sustainability in higher education likewise shows strong and rising publication activity, including 4,410 publications in one study and 1,013 eligible articles in another, with the United States, UK, Spain, Australia, Germany, China, and other countries appearing as major contributors [https://openalex.org/W4223628254||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4406778824||ABSTRACT||000]. However, the available summaries do not provide detailed Scopus bibliometric results specifically linking internationalization to sustainability practices in HEIs beyond the broad claims above, and one Asian HEI study explicitly notes that its abstract does not give specific evidence on how internationalization itself helps sustainability [https://openalex.org/W3212231498||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How does the theme of "Green Cluod Computing" connect the discussion of Green IoT with the systematic survey of energy-efficient techniques in sustainabl cloud computing, especially regarding why data centers and cloud technologies are being optimized for lower energy use and reduced environmental harm?
final_answer: Across these papers, “Green Cloud Computing” is presented as part of a broader sustainability agenda in which cloud platforms, data centers, and connected devices are optimized because their growing energy demand and environmental footprint have become a problem [https://openalex.org/W4281251447||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4385723923||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4280503421||ABSTRACT||000]. The Green IoT paper makes the bridge explicit by treating Green Cloud Computing and Green Data Centers as enabling ICT technologies that support greener modernization while reducing pollution, energy consumption, and electrical waste [https://openalex.org/W4280503421||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4280503421||ABSTRACT||001]. The systematic survey of energy-efficient techniques in sustainable cloud computing reinforces that point by focusing on data centers as a key target for reducing energy use and CO2 footprints through virtualization, consolidation, power-aware methods, bio-inspired methods, and thermal management [https://openalex.org/W4281251447||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4281251447||ABSTRACT||001]. Several papers explain why this optimization matters: cloud and data-center growth increases electricity use, heat output, cooling needs, and environmental harm, so future cloud computing must be both energy-efficient and environmentally sustainable [https://openalex.org/W4385723923||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3172706057||ABSTRACT||000]. Other summaries extend the same logic to sustainable development and environmentally sustainable computing, noting that lower-energy cloud systems can reduce carbon footprints, support eco-friendly practices, and help meet environmental regulations [https://openalex.org/W4366762583||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4391566264||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4391045525||ABSTRACT||001]. The Green IoT discussion also frames the motivation in human and ecological terms, arguing that greener ICT should reduce toxicity, pollution, and waste while supporting a safe, healthy environment [https://openalex.org/W4280503421||ABSTRACT||000]. At the same time, the cloud-sustainability papers note practical constraints: upfront investment costs, renewable-energy integration with fluctuating grids, and technical complexity in advanced cooling systems can limit implementation [https://openalex.org/W4391045525||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the papers agree that optimizing cloud technologies and data centers is necessary not just to save power, but to reduce carbon emissions, operational heat problems, and broader environmental harm across the ICT stack [https://openalex.org/W4391917929||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4385723923||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4366762583||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How do sustainable technologies, such as clean energy in manufacturing and green and reverse logistics, support Industry 4.0 innovation and SDG-based growth in industrial enterprises, and what did the analysis find about enterprise adoption and environmental management?
final_answer: Across the reviewed papers, sustainable technologies are presented as an important enabler of Industry 4.0 innovation because they help industrial firms improve efficiency, reduce resource use, and strengthen environmental sustainability [https://openalex.org/W4226256571||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4398200114||ABSTRACT||001]. The clearest link to the user’s focus comes from the Slovakia study, which states that clean energy in manufacturing and green/reverse logistics, when combined with Industry 4.0 technologies, create conditions for industrial development and future growth in the context of the SDGs [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000]. That study also found that more than 82% of the 105 enterprises implement the SDGs and more than 70% prioritize environmental aspects in business management, suggesting broad but not universal adoption of SDG-oriented practices [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000]. In addition, it reported significant relationships between enterprise environmental management and sustainability in production and logistics, and between renewable energy technology use in industry and sustainability in logistics [https://openalex.org/W4280522772||ABSTRACT||000]. Broader review evidence supports this pattern by showing that Industry 4.0 technologies can improve environmental sustainability and environmental performance, while also helping organizations address environmental concerns in manufacturing and supply chains [https://openalex.org/W4398200114||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4389484631||ABSTRACT||000]. However, the literature also warns that Industry 4.0 technologies may themselves generate environmental harms such as air pollution, improper waste disposal, and excessive consumption of raw materials, information, and energy, so sustainable technology adoption is framed as a corrective rather than an automatic solution [https://openalex.org/W4398200114||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4398200114||ABSTRACT||001]. Several reviews also emphasize that the current state of production remains unsustainable and that there is a gap between current and intended sustainability outcomes, indicating the need for continued implementation and study [https://openalex.org/W4398200114||ABSTRACT||000]. More generally, the evidence shows that Industry 4.0 and sustainability are mutually reinforcing, with management, innovation, and SDG alignment recurring as key themes across industrial enterprises [https://openalex.org/W4311719782||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4389484631||ABSTRACT||000].

query: How was ARDL used to test the nexus, and what long-run association did it reveal for human capital and renewable energy?
final_answer: The provided summaries do not support a precise reconstruction of ARDL being used to test a specific human capital–renewable energy nexus in every paper, but they do show a common pattern of using ARDL-family models to examine long- and short-run relationships among sustainability variables [https://openalex.org/W4313181844||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4312213521||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4315629505||ABSTRACT||000]. In the clearest relevant study, the authors used ADF to test stationarity and ARDL to test the nexus among variables for China over 1986–2019 using WDI data [https://openalex.org/W4313181844||ABSTRACT||000]. That ARDL analysis reported that human capital index and renewable energy consumption/production were negatively associated with carbon emissions and positively associated with sustainable development goals [https://openalex.org/W4313181844||ABSTRACT||000]. The same summary therefore characterizes the long-run association as positive with SDGs and negative with carbon emissions for both human capital and renewable energy [https://openalex.org/W4313181844||ABSTRACT||000]. Another paper also used ARDL, but for multiple energy demands and China’s energy efficiency, and found a positive association between multiple energy demands and energy efficiency rather than a human capital result [https://openalex.org/W4315784444||ABSTRACT||000]. Several other summaries either used different ARDL variants or explicitly lacked any mention of human capital and renewable energy, so they cannot substantiate a longer-run human capital–renewable energy conclusion on their own [https://openalex.org/W4388450586||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4312213521||ABSTRACT||000][https://openalex.org/W4327545694||ABSTRACT||000]. Overall, the evidence suggests ARDL was applied as a time-series tool to test nexus relationships after stationarity checks, and the only directly supported long-run finding here is that human capital and renewable energy were linked positively with SDGs and negatively with carbon emissions in the China study [https://openalex.org/W4313181844||ABSTRACT||000].

query: In the context of Sustainable Consumption, what did the systematic review conclude about the concept’s complexity, its relationship to the circular economy, and the role of government in supporting sustainable consumption?
final_answer: The systematic review portrays sustainable consumption as a complex and nebulous concept, with theoretical fragmentation that gives it breadth but also creates overlapping and unclear boundaries [https://openalex.org/W4381591906||ABSTRACT||000]. It also emphasizes that “being” a green consumer is difficult in contemporary settings, and that consumer awareness does not necessarily translate into sustainable behavior [https://openalex.org/W4381591906||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4322770358||ABSTRACT||000]. Across the reviewed literature, sustainable consumption is closely linked to the circular economy, but the relationship is not presented as straightforward because circularity and sustainability are related yet not identical [https://openalex.org/W4381591906||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3120864615||ABSTRACT||000]. query: What clinical and laboratory findings are associated with elevated FSH in men with non-obstructive azoospermia and chromosomal anomalies, and how do KS and testicular XX DSD compare with the undefined cause group?
final_answer: Across the provided studies, elevated serum FSH in men with non-obstructive azoospermia is linked to less favorable reproductive and testicular profiles, including failed sperm retrieval, higher LH, and lower likelihood of successful sperm extraction, whereas successful retrieval is associated with larger testicular volume and a higher T/LH ratio [pmc_PMC10307674||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC10307674||ABSTRACT||001]. In men with non-obstructive azoospermia and chromosomal anomalies, the Klinefelter syndrome (KS) group had lower average testicular volume, shorter penile length, lower total testosterone, greater height and arm span, higher serum LH and FSH, and more frequent gynecomastia than the undefined-cause group, with gynecomastia absent in the undefined group [pmc_PMC10065101||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC10065101||ABSTRACT||001]. Testicular XX DSD showed an intermediate pattern, with LH, FSH, and penile length values between KS and the undefined-cause group, testicular volume similar to KS, and other clinical data similar to the undefined group [pmc_PMC10065101||ABSTRACT||001]. The comparison therefore suggests that KS is the most distinct from undefined cause, while testicular XX DSD occupies a middle phenotype rather than matching either group completely [pmc_PMC10065101||ABSTRACT||001]. One additional chromosomal-anomaly cohort reported that certain abnormalities should be referred for AZF deletion screening and that only 1% of cases with >1×10^6 sperm/mL had Y chromosome microdeletions, but it did not provide the specific clinical or laboratory associations requested here [pmc_PMC10307663||ABSTRACT||000] [pmc_PMC10307663||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the evidence supports elevated FSH as part of a broader endocrine/testicular pattern associated with more severe reproductive impairment, but direct cross-study comparisons are limited because not all papers report the same subgroups or outcomes [pmc_PMC10307674||ABSTRACT||001] [pmc_PMC10065101||ABSTRACT||001].

query: How do Sustainable Catalytric Technologies support global resource securty and sustainability?
final_answer: Sustainable catalytic technologies support global resource security and sustainability by helping address climate change, pollution, and sustainable energy challenges through innovative catalytic strategies [https://openalex.org/W3136963614||ABSTRACT||000]. They are also framed as enabling a shift from linear to circular production, especially by using sustainable waste resources for fuel and chemical manufacturing and by reducing dependence on fossil resources that harm ecosystems [https://openalex.org/W4397002662||ABSTRACT||000]. Several summaries emphasize that catalysis can support long-term sustainability transitions by enabling early systems change and helping meet more ambitious goals for 2050 and 2100 [https://openalex.org/W4284690057||ABSTRACT||000]. In practical terms, green chemistry and green engineering principles guide catalyst and process choices to minimize harms to human health and the environment, while sustainability metrics help quantify improvements over incumbent technologies and identify remaining economic and environmental problem areas [https://openalex.org/W3156019499||ABSTRACT||000]. These assessments can also inform research investments that may eventually lead to commercialization of green chemical technologies [https://openalex.org/W3156019499||ABSTRACT||001]. The literature further argues that renewable-electricity-powered catalytic transformations and electrocatalytic processes can generate solar fuels and commodity chemicals that support the water-energy-food nexus and many sectors of society, contributing to environmental and social justice [https://openalex.org/W4323925755||ABSTRACT||000]. Resource security is strengthened by approaches such as rational design of earth-abundant catalysts, development of catalysts from renewable resources, and biomass conversion into biofuels and high-value products [https://openalex.org/W4401191227||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4377108088||ABSTRACT||001]. At the same time, the summaries stress that feasibility and real-world benefits depend on techno-economic, environmental, and systems-level analysis, including infrastructure, feedstock mobilization, and integration into existing facilities [https://openalex.org/W4323925755||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4377108088||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4385888760||ABSTRACT||000].

query: In the sustainability assessment of district heating systems, which multi-criteria decision analysis methods were compared, and what did the sensitivity analysis reveal about their suitability and differences in calculation and interpretation?
final_answer: A district-heating sustainability study explicitly compared five MCDA methods: WSM, TOPSIS, PROMETHEE, ELECTRE, and DEA, applied to 12 district heating companies using 8 criteria [https://openalex.org/W4220986058||ABSTRACT||000]. The sensitivity analysis varied criteria weights in three ways: changing them one by one to estimate stability ranges, changing them by a fixed value to test the effect on average scores, and comparing AHP weighting with equal weighting [https://openalex.org/W4220986058||ABSTRACT||000]. That analysis, together with the literature review, concluded that all five methods are suitable for sustainability analyses of district heating systems, but they differ in calculation process and in how results are interpreted [https://openalex.org/W4220986058||ABSTRACT||000]. Other summaries in the set support the broader view that MCDM is the preferred evaluation framework for district-heating sustainability assessment and that AHP is the most frequently used method, but they do not provide comparable method-by-method sensitivity findings [https://openalex.org/W4315708900||ABSTRACT||001]. A separate district-heating study using fuzzy COPRAS also reported a sensitivity analysis that altered criteria weights to validate robustness, but it did not compare alternative MCDA methods or explain differences among methods [https://openalex.org/W4281388694||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the evidence indicates agreement that multi-criteria approaches are preferred and that results depend on weighting choices, but only one supplied study provides a direct comparison of multiple MCDA methods and a clear conclusion that the methods are similarly suitable while still differing in computation and interpretation [https://openalex.org/W4220986058||ABSTRACT||000].

query: In this fouling study, how did Actinobacteria relate ta the microbes on prepainted steel, and what other kinda microorganism was most dominant there?
final_answer: In the fouling studies on prepainted steel, Actinobacteria were reported as part of the microbial community, but their prominence varied by study. One study found Actinobacteria to be one of the dominant microbial groups in the community sequence data from fouled prepainted steel, alongside Bacillus spp., cyanobacteria, and several fungal taxa [pmc_PMC5387312||ABSTRACT||000]. Another study found Actinobacteria at low relative abundance on prepainted steel samples (1.06%) and noted that it was not identified in all samples [pmc_PMC9805769||ABSTRACT||001]. The most dominant organism reported also differed across studies: fungi were described as the most dominant organisms on prepainted steel by fluorescence in situ hybridization imaging in one paper [pmc_PMC5387312||ABSTRACT||000], while another paper reported Staphylococcus as the most dominant genus based on highest average relative abundance (18.88%) [pmc_PMC9805769||ABSTRACT||001]. Taken together, the evidence shows that Actinobacteria were present on prepainted steel but were not consistently the top group across analyses [pmc_PMC5387312||ABSTRACT||000][pmc_PMC9805769||ABSTRACT||001].

query: What did the interviews with retailers and service providers in North America reveal about managing product returns sustainably?
final_answer: The interviews with retailers and service providers in North America suggest that sustainably managing product returns is constrained by several reverse-supply-chain barriers rather than by a lack of interest in returns management itself [https://openalex.org/W4322500966||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4317888257||ABSTRACT||001]. One study found that multichannel retailers, retail experts, and return service providers were mainly focused on the financial impact of returns and had little awareness of their environmental impact, which meant they lacked a comprehensive approach to reducing those impacts [https://openalex.org/W4322500966||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4322500966||ABSTRACT||001]. The same interviews were used to identify barriers preventing retailers from developing environmental sustainability plans for returns management, and the authors proposed strategies and a framework to address them [https://openalex.org/W4322500966||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4322500966||ABSTRACT||000]. A second paper using North American interviews similarly highlights sustainability hindrances in the reverse supply chain, including the need to encourage RE producers to compete and the lack of governmental support for sustainable supply-chain solutions [https://openalex.org/W4317888257||ABSTRACT||001]. Taken together, these findings indicate that sustainable returns management requires both retailer-level attention to environmental impacts and broader system-level support in the reverse supply chain [https://openalex.org/W4322500966||ABSTRACT||001] [https://openalex.org/W4317888257||ABSTRACT||001]. The evidence provided does not include detailed implementation outcomes or quantitative measures of effectiveness, so the practical impact of the proposed strategies remains unclear [https://openalex.org/W4322500966||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4317888257||ABSTRACT||001].

query: How is the public sector related to corporate governance, and what did the study say was stopping sustainable procurement in the Nigerian public construction sector?
final_answer: Across the supplied studies, the public sector is presented as an important setting for sustainability and procurement governance: one paper says previous work had already examined barriers to sustainable procurement in the public sector, while another frames public-sector organisations as shaped by coercive and mimetic forces that influence sustainable procurement and sustainable leadership [https://openalex.org/W3162983557||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4386268572||ABSTRACT||000]. A separate study also says the public sector offers a key viewpoint for understanding sustainability challenges and that public-sector policies should support low tariffs, taxes, and subsidies for sustainable goods [https://openalex.org/W4308695771||ABSTRACT||001]. In relation to corporate governance, one paper states that corporate governance has importance in the public sector and internationally, and is related to the sustainability of modern organisations [https://openalex.org/W10420025||ABSTRACT||000]. That same source describes corporate governance in terms of stakeholder management, governance structures, boards, and manager-board relationships [https://openalex.org/W10420025||ABSTRACT||000]. For the Nigerian public construction sector specifically, the clearest study identified four barrier groups to sustainable procurement: attitude and poor fiscal incentive, financial restrictions, insufficient leadership and knowledge, and regulatory constraints [https://openalex.org/W4308695771||ABSTRACT||000]. The study further said there was no sustainable procurement regulatory framework in the country and that major barriers included lack of government commitment, poor economic conditions, and lack of knowledge [https://openalex.org/W4308695771||ABSTRACT||000]. Other Nigeria-focused papers are consistent with this picture of institutional and capability barriers, emphasizing the need for proper government policies, sustainability education, professional development, and stronger regulatory/policy frameworks [https://openalex.org/W3145060410||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W4220971596||ABSTRACT||001]. Overall, the evidence suggests the public sector matters both as a governance actor and as a policy environment that can enable or block sustainable procurement, but the Nigerian construction-specific evidence points most strongly to weak regulation, limited government commitment, financial constraints, and low knowledge as the main obstacles [https://openalex.org/W4308695771||ABSTRACT||000] [https://openalex.org/W3145060410||ABSTRACT||000].
